Summary

Phainon was having a shitty day. He woke up late, almost got fired, and then got home to find out that the game he's been obsessed with for the last several years was finally too much for his 20-year-old laptop to run correctly. Plus, this OP-as-shit character named Flame Reaver came out of nowhere and almost nuked his character to oblivion.

Oh, then he got fucking transmigrated into the game of Star Rail.

...Why did stuff like this only happen to him?

chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Phainon had already been having a shitty day. He’d overslept, gotten to his shift at the pawnshop late for the third time this month (which wasn’t his fault—the bus was unreliable and he had no other way of making it to work), only to get yelled at by his boss for the trouble.

Then, when all he wanted to do after work was take a shower and relax, he arrived home to a note from his landlord saying the hot water was out and wouldn’t be fixed until the next day—in the middle of November, when it was cold as shit outside and Phainon’s toes were practically frozen solid from the holes in his boots.

Now, Phainon sat in front of his clunky, decades-old laptop, his hair still cold from his (incredibly miserable) shower, and marveled at his terrible luck.

The latest update of the game he’d been obsessed with for the last two years had finally come out, and Phainon had logged in immediately after his shower to finally play it, only to find that the graphics on his shitty-ass 2005 Lenovo wouldn’t load.

The sound worked fine, as did the visuals for the in-game text, as well as the text box at the bottom of the screen, but the background was just…black. None of the character sprites would load, or any of the menu options. He couldn’t even exit the game and restart his computer, since the last save point had been nearly half an hour ago, and he’d have to replay a ridiculously annoying dungeon, which he would like to avoid if he had the chance. Phainon had only barely begun to catch his breath after being assaulted with waves upon waves of enemies, and did not feel like repeating the experience. So far, Penacony was not ending in Phainon’s good graces.

In the dialogue box, a new line scrolled across the screen.

Flame Reaver: You, a mere worm, dare to challenge me? 

Phainon squinted at the screen. Flame Reaver? 

In his hundreds of hours playing Star Rail, he’d never heard the name Flame Reaver, not to mention anything similarly stupid. The latest update had been hinting at the arrival of a big bad, but Phainon had expected it to be a character who had already been shown onscreen. Like Sunday or something. Or even someone like Black Swan, or even Aventurine. Anything but a fucking deus ex machina-ass character named Flame Reaver. 

He tried to tamp down his pessimism. Maybe the ending could still be good. Maybe the devs had a good reason for introducing the Flame Reaver so late.

Exactly forty-two minutes later, Phainon was filled with a fury so large he was sure he would never make it to heaven, because he was about to blow a gasket.

What the actual fuck was this boss?

Flame Reaver had monologued for thirty minutes, then the player went through another ten minutes of flashbacks, and then the game had plunged Phainon straight into a boss fight. Phainon had barely been fighting Flame Reaver for five minutes before he was ready to give up in frustration. 

Why was this boss so fucking hard?

Flame Reaver hit incredibly hard and shot literal meteors (even though Phainon still couldn’t see what was happening on screen, there was a little text popup whenever Flame Reaver summoned meteors, so Phainon was kept in the loop. If only he could actually see it). At least the combat interface had loaded, so Phainon could control his characters’ combat actions, but that was it. Not only that, Flame Reaver was also frustratingly immune to practically any attack Phainon threw at him.

After several minutes of this, Phainon had had enough. He slammed his hands down on his desk with an irritated “Argh!” and immediately regretted it, both for the pain in his hands and the horrifying sight of his entire laptop screen going dark. 

Fuckkk. 

Phainon had accidentally disconnected his laptop from the charging cord in his frustration, and now he was regretting every choice he’d ever made as he scrambled to reconnect it. He plugged the laptop back in, heart pounding, his stomach tight with anxiety.

After staring at the screen for several long moments, Phainon entertained the possibility that he might have just lost all of his progress from the last several hours.

“Shitty fucking game,” he muttered. “Shitty fucking Flame Reaver. What the fuck do you mean, nuking me with your OP-as-fuck meteors, coming out of nowhere? Fucking devs… How do you make a story any shittier? Fuck,” Phainon cursed liberally, suddenly furious with this latest turn of events.

All he’d wanted after his awful day was a nice, quiet evening to recharge by playing his favorite game. Now, his vision was getting blurry, and his head suddenly hurt like a bitch—what on earth was happening?

What a shitty ending to a shitty day.

Stupid fucking Star Rail, was his last thought before he passed out.

[Activation code: “Stupid fucking Star Rail.” System automatically triggered.]

Phainon’s entire body hurt. He tried to roll over, hoping to find a more comfortable spot on the mattress, but a sharp pain in his head quashed any hopes of going back to sleep. Groaning, Phainon sat up and opened his eyes, and whoa—

Phainon was definitely not in his bedroom. 

Huh. Phainon’s dreams weren’t usually this vivid. Wait, if this was a dream, wasn’t he not supposed to know he was in a dream? As in, once he discovered he was in a dream he would wake up, that sort of thing? Or was this lucid dreaming?

Lucid or not, Phainon was pretty sure dreams weren’t supposed to hurt.

His head throbbed with pain, and Phainon winced as he stood up and looked around, taking in his surroundings. He was…in a field. In the middle of nowhere. What the fuck.

Out of nowhere, a chime rang out, and in front of Phainon’s (unbelieving) eyes popped a blue screen, upon which text scrolled, an auto-generated voice reading out loud: 

[Welcome to the System! You have been given the opportunity to experience the world of Star Rail firsthand. We hope you make use of this rare chance to immerse yourself in the new region of Amphoreus as a beta tester. Enjoy!]

Phainon blinked.

What…the fuck.

There were so many problems with what he had just heard. First of all, Star Rail? If Phainon was actually just asleep, this was definitely a nightmare, because what kind of sick joke would it be for Phainon to dream about the game he definitely did not want to think about for the time being.

Second, and most of all the part that signaled to Phainon that he might actually be in deep, deep shit, was the term “beta tester”.

…Did Phainon just get isekaied into Star Rail’s beta program? How on earth would that even work? Phainon wanted to instinctively write off that possibility, but his surroundings were looking awfully real. 

There were a few things Phainon could do to test this theory. He tried the first one.

“Hey, um, System?”

Ding! The blue box popped back up into Phainon’s vision with a chime. 

[How may the System assist you, User?]

Phainon stared at the screen. Somehow, it was even more jarring seeing it the second time. After he didn’t respond, the blue box updated with new text, the mechanical voice grating in Phainon’s ears.

[User can choose to explore the following menus: Stats, Quests, Inventory, Archive, and more. Would User like to see all available menus?]

Phainon cleared his throat. “Uh—no, no thanks.”

The blue box disappeared in a blink, leaving Phainon with a sinking feeling in his chest.

…Damn. He might really be in over his head this time.

Phainon looked at the fields of wheat surrounding him and felt only numbness.

“System?”

[How may the System assist you?]

“Am I…dead?”

He waited, tense, for the System’s answer. 

[No, User Phainon is not dead.]

Phainon let out a breath. He was pretty sure he would have remembered dying, but for all he knew he could have died in his sleep. In any case, that was one question answered. There were still several dozen more, but Phainon was relieved to know that at least he was alive. Back in his own world, at least. 

“Um, you said I was invited here as a…beta tester? Why was I—how did that happen? Why was I selected? What am I supposed to do here?” 

[User was randomly selected to test out Star Rail’s upcoming region, Amphoreus. This playtest will serve roughly the same purpose as a beta test, only providing a broader and more immersive experience. User is encouraged to explore the world of Amphoreus and complete any Quests that arise.] 

Phainon had kind of expected as much. “What kind of Quests?”

[While exploring Amphoreus, User may encounter Main Quests, Story Quests, and Side Quests. Main Quests will follow the main storyline of Amphoreus, which have higher completion requirements but also higher rewards than other type of quests. Story Quests are lower-risk, lore-focused optional quests that are based around either Characters or Locations the User may encounter. Finally, Side Quests are additional optional quests the User may complete to earn extra rewards, including experience, stat increases, or relationship bonuses.]

“...Relationship bonuses?”

[During User’s time in the world of Star Rail, they will encounter all sorts of companions, whether that be friend or foe. User’s choices while traveling through Amphoreus will affect their relationships with these characters. User can earn several types of points with Characters, and can make any Character a friend or an enemy.]

All this new information was making Phainon’s head spin. He’d read stories about situations like this, but never had he imagined it would feel so overwhelming. All he wanted to do was go back to his own bed, his own world, and sleep.

Fuck. “Do I have to? Do this…beta test, I mean.”

The System did not seem apologetic as it confirmed Phainon’s worst fears. 

[Unfortunately, User Phainon has already been bound to the world of Star Rail, and will not be able to return to his home world until the Main Quests have been completed. Would User like to view the Main Quests?]

Phainon sighed. “Fine, yes, I’d like to view my Quests.”

With a sound like a page turning, the screen enlarged, flashing an updated screen before Phainon’s eyes. The screen now read, Quests—Main Quests. Unlocked: 1/?

(1) Make your way to Okhema, the Holy City

…Just one? Phainon thought he’d be able to see all of his Main Quests here. Like, defeat X boss, or make sure Y never does blah blah blah, etc. Seems like it wouldn’t be that easy.

Before he had any chance of dismissing the System and processing the extreme amount of information he had just gained, Phainon heard someone call his name.

“Phainon!”

Phainon blinked. He had heard his name. Why in the actual fuck did someone from Star Rail know his name?

“System?” he whispered, trying to be quiet in hopes of avoiding notice by the unknown person searching for him. “Why does that person know my name? Aren’t I supposed to be like a random character or something?”

[For a more streamlined user experience, User Phainon has been bound to an unnamed character from the world of Amphoreus, and their in-game name has been set to [Phainon] to add to User’s immersion. User’s appearance has also been set to match User’s original appearance.]

That was trippy. So basically, Phainon was just a random background character, except he looked exactly the same as he did in his own world. There were so many questions Phainon had about this whole thing, like—

“Does that me—”

“There you are!” A light female voice sounded from behind him, the wheat stalks rustling to signal their arrival at Phainon’s hiding spot. Phainon winced, afraid to jump right into beta testing right away, but turned around. Standing before him was a short girl, maybe around the same age as Phainon, with bright pink hair and dressed in something that looked straight out of Gladiator. Or 300, maybe.

“I knew you’d be hiding in here again!” The girl announced triumphantly, tossing her hair over her shoulder. Phainon, still startled by being caught, didn’t know what to say, and could only sit gaping at her, dumbly.

“Uh,” Phainon managed out finally. 

“I found you again, so the score is now—Phainon?” The girl stopped in the middle of her sentence, her brows furrowing in concern. “Are you okay?”

Phainon’s head still really, really hurt. He didn’t know how much pretending he could get away with, and he guessed the excuse I’m not actually from here wouldn’t fly very well, so he opted for the good-old amnesia route, which technically was only half-false in this situation.

“I, um. Who…are you?”

The girl gawked at him for a moment, and then laughed. “Come on, Phainon, that won’t work on me.” After a few more moments, Phainon not giving her any indication he was joking, her expression froze.

“You’re…serious?”

At Phainon’s grim expression, the girl stared at him. “Oh fuck, you’re serious. Okay. Okay, well, in this situation, we should probably go back home, right? Yeah, okay,” she muttered, clearly speaking herself through this unexpected crisis. 

“All right!” She grabbed Phainon’s arm and pulled him behind her, Phainon’s vision blurring with the sudden movement. Without waiting for him to adjust, the girl took off through the wheat field, pulling Phainon behind her like a child dragging a doll. Phainon struggled to keep pace, but it was hard as he didn’t know where they were going and couldn’t lead, only able to be dragged along as the wheat whipped and fluttered around them. Occasionally, the stalks would hit Phainon in the face, causing him to sputter and brush them out of his face wildly with his free hand.

After several minutes of this, the field suddenly ended, and Phainon found himself standing at the edge of a small, rustic village, with golden wheat bordering its entirety save for one side that nestled against the sea, with gentle waves lapping against the docks.

Phainon wanted to stop and take it all in, but the girl did not slow down, and kept pulling him behind her as they made their way into the village. 

The village looked old, the houses held together with sticks and thatch, but cozy nonetheless, with embroidered curtains on every window, and all the people were clothed in colorful fabrics. Phainon tried not to stare too hard as he was pulled behind the pink-haired girl, but no one seemed to give him a second glance.

...Huh. It seemed this previously unnamed character had a background written for them after all. Phainon hadn’t really had time to think about what this all meant, but he thought it reflected well upon the devs that they had even written a background for a nameless nobody. Or maybe the game was…alive? And the game that Phainon had played only reflected the parts that were important to the story?

Phainon didn’t really want to think about that.

After running through the entire village, they arrived at a small, quaint house. The girl didn’t hesitate to burst through the door, still holding tightly onto Phainon.

”Audata!” she called. “Hieronymus!”

”Cyrene?” a voice came somewhere in the house, and from around a corner came a woman with greying hair and warm eyes. “Cyrene, what’s wrong?”

”It’s Phainon!” Cyrene said, frantic. “Something’s wrong! He must have hit his head… He said he doesn't know who I am.”

Audata turned her gaze onto Phainon. 

“…Phainon?” she asked, quietly. 

“Um… Hi?” Phainon said, not knowing how to respond. Although, he reflected, he really didn’t know who they were. Or what anything was. It was only because he knew he wasn’t truly this world’s Phainon that he felt guilty.

In any case, what choice did he have but to pretend to be Phainon in this world?

Audata studied him, her expression searching. After a moment, she turned away from him to walk over to the hearth, where several thick armchairs were.

“Let’s sit down,” she said.

Phainon sat. Beside him sat Cyrene, and across from them sat Audata. Phainon cleared his throat, thinking perhaps he should say something. 

“I–”

“Don’t rush,” said Audata. “What do you remember?”

“I…woke up. In the field.”

“Do you remember anything before that?” Cyrene asked, brow creased in worry. 

“...No,” Phainon said.

Before Audata could ask another question, the front door opened, and inside stepped a man. He was tall, his face weathered. Phainon guessed this must be Hieronymus.

“What’s going on?” Hieronymus asked them, sensing something was amiss from the tension in the room. 

Audata stood up and pulled Hieronymus into one of the adjacent rooms, presumably to update him on the current situation. Phainon couldn’t hear what they were speaking about, but he heard whispers and tried not to eavesdrop.

There was movement on his left, and then a gentle squeeze of his hand. Phainon looked over—Cyrene was clearly worried about him, with concern knit into her face and in the shadows of her eyes. Was she his sister? Or perhaps a childhood friend? Phainon couldn’t tell.

“It’ll be all right,” she said, as if Phainon needed comforting.

Phainon couldn’t help but snort lightly at that. “You look like you need to hear that more than I do.”

Cyrene pouted at him. “Hmph. That’s what I get from trying to be nice,” she sniffed. For a moment, she looked like she was going to say something more, but instead she trailed off into silence, her thoughts visibly heavy.

“...Cyrene?”

Her gaze snapped back to him, as if checking to see if he’d remembered. Phainon shook his head, waving his hands as he explained.

“No, no, I still…I just heard Audata call your name…Um. Are you…okay?”

Phainon cringed internally. Of course she wouldn’t be okay, Phainon had lost his memory and she was clearly worried sick about him. What kind of stupid question was that?

“I—” Before Cyrene could answer, Audata and Hieronymus came back into the room, both looking worried.

“Cyrene, fetch the doctor.”

When the doctor arrived, he examined Phainon but could not find a single trace of an injury, not even the tiniest bump on his head. He eventually admitted that he couldn’t find the source of Phainon’s memory loss, but recommended they keep an eye on him for the next few days in case he’d missed anything.

“Will his memories come back?” Phainon heard Audata ask the doctor as she sent him off at the threshold. Phainon could feel their eyes return to him, even though he was faced the opposite way, still seated in front of the hearth.

“...Hard to say. We’ll have to wait and see.”

There was a soft sigh, then the sound of the door closing.

Phainon was feeling increasingly uncomfortable. The character whose life he had invaded was a random NPC, right? Phainon was supposed to be immersing himself in Amphoreus for the sake of the beta test, but why did this make him feel so uneasy?

It felt like he had stolen someone’s life. Someone’s son, someone’s friend.

Phainon knew it was silly, but it felt wrong to be sitting here in someone else’s house and pretend to be their Phainon. …Did this nameless character really have a life? As in, were all these people really alive? Phainon knew this was a game, and the System had said it was a beta test, but…

It all felt so real.

Phainon hadn’t had parents for a long time. And now, under the worried gazes of Audata and Hieronymus, of Cyrene, he felt exposed.

His stomach growled loudly, distracting him from his thoughts. Guilt wasn’t the only thing he could feel in this beta test, apparently.

They ate dinner in relative silence, no one quite knowing how to deal with Phainon’s predicament. It was delicious, spiced stew with bits of lamb, served with watered down wine. 

“Your favorite,” Cyrene whispered from her seat next to him, nudging his hand with hers.

After dinner, Cyrene left for her own home—childhood friend, a small part of Phainon’s brain noted—and Hieronymus showed Phainon his room.

“If you get cold, there’s more blankets in there,” said Hieronymus, pointing to a chest in the corner of the room. “It gets chilly in here—you’d always have to… Anyways. Good night,” he said, lingering at the door a bit awkwardly. 

“Good night,” said Phainon, quietly.

With that, Hieronymus shut the door, and Phainon was alone.

Lying on a bed that wasn’t his, in a house and clothes that didn’t belong to him… Phainon felt miserable. 

He just wanted to go home.

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Phainon knew something was wrong before he even opened his eyes.

His bed was too scratchy, and the sunlight shone directly on his face, making his entire body feel uncomfortably warm.

Wait a minute. His bedroom window never got any sun this late in the year. He cracked one eye open.

…Fuck. Now he remembered. He was in a strange bedroom, in someone else’s house. 

In Star Rail.

Hoping it wouldn’t work, but only half-expecting it not to, Phainon whispered into the empty room, “System?”

With an infuriatingly cheerful ding, all of Phainon’s worst fears resurfaced in the form of a semi-transparent blue screen.

[Good morning, User Phainon! How may I assist you today?]

Phainon groaned, flopping back onto his pillow. “Why am I still here?” he mumbled, shifting his arm to cover his eyes.

[User Phainon has not completed all of their Main Quests, and so is unable to return to their home world. Would User like to review their Main Quests?]

“No!” Phainon almost shouted, but caught himself just in time, the word coming out strangled. “No, I just…”

He was just so, so tired.

“Hahhhhhh…”

Phainon rubbed his face with his hands and thought for a moment. Theoretically, if this was all actually happening and not just an extended mega-nightmare, how long would it take Phainon to complete his Main Quests and return home? 

“...How many Main Quests do I have?”

[Unfortunately, that information is unavailable at this time. Currently, User Phainon only has one Main Quest unlocked: [Make your way to Okhema, the Holy City]. Additional Quests will be available as User progresses through the storyline.]

Of course. Why would this be easy? 

“Okay, fine. Can you tell me how I get to Okhema?”

[User Phainon is still in the tutorial area. Please complete the tutorial first.]

What? What tutorial?! Phainon fumed. First, you say all I have to do is complete my Main Quests, and now I have to complete a tutorial? I have over 1000 hours in Star Rail! Why do I need to play through a stupid tutorial?

”What tutorial?” Phainon asked through gritting his teeth. Why wasn’t anything in this goddamn beta test simple?

[The tutorial will teach User Phainon the basics of completing the beta test. After completing the tutorial, the User will unlock further tools and abilities to aid their progress. Does User wish to begin the tutorial?]

What choice do I have? “Yeah, fine, let’s start.”

[User Phainon has accepted: [Tutorial Quest: Through the Fields of Wheat—Aedes Elysiae]. Open Quest Log?]

Underneath the text flashed two blinking buttons, [Yes] and [No]. Phainon reached out his finger and clicked [Yes], feeling a slight pressure under his fingers as he interacted with the screen. Immediately, the screen enlarged to show his Quests again, only this time, the Tutorial Quest sat at the top of the screen, highlighted. 

[Through the Fields of Wheat (1) — Meet the System!]

…This was going to be one of those annoying, hand-holdy tutorials, wasn’t it?

Ten minutes later, Phainon wanted to bang his head into the nearest wall.

The System had spent the entire time describing the various functions of the System, including defining what an inventory was, how to interpret his stats, and how to navigate through the System archive…as if Phainon couldn’t have figured all that out on his own.

The System had noted some useful details, however—Phainon could apparently use the points he earned from completing quests in the Shop for cool things like stat buffs or medicine, or even special unlockable skills. 

However, it was when the System got to explaining the point system that Phainon really felt lost.

[While progressing through Amphoreus, the User will collect multiple types of points. Progression Points, or PP, can be earned by completing Quests and Achievements, but User can also earn different types of Relationship Points by establishing and deepening relationships with characters throughout the world.]

(Phainon’s inner twelve-year-old snickered a little at the abbreviation PP.)

Plus, achievements? Hell yeah!

At least Phainon had one thing to look forward to in this beta test.

[These Relationship Points are converted to either Friendship Points, FP, or Enmity Points, EP, depending on whether the relationship between the User and the Character is positive or negative.]

…Okay. “What’s the difference? Like, do I get anything special from not getting any Enmity Points or something?”

[As User gains more Relationship Points, additional Story and Side Quests will be subsequently unlocked. If the User gains too many Enmity Points with a Character, they may be unable to access these Quests until their Friendship Points reach a certain level.]

At this point, Phainon didn’t care about Story or Side Quests. All he wanted was to complete this damn tutorial and get a move on to completing his Main Quests. Maybe, on a better day, he might have jumped at the chance to explore the world of Star Rail like this, but something about being pulled into Amphoreus via good old Truck-kun rubbed Phainon the wrong way.

He didn’t care about Relationship Points, or doing any side quest bullshit. He just wanted to go home.

“Can’t I just, like,” he gestured his hand at the entirety of the glowing screen, “mute all this?” Phainon asked, a little helplessly. There was just too much information for him to keep track of, and frankly he didn’t care about any of it.

[Would User Phainon like to mute all System notifications? Or would User only like to mute notifications about changes in point totals?]

“Just the point notifications… Please,” he added as an afterthought. There was no point in taking out his frustrations on the System. Just because the devs created a stupid, convoluted system for this beta test didn’t mean it was the System’s fault.

[Point total notifications have successfully been muted. Additionally, congratulations! User Phainon has completed the first stage of the tutorial.]

Phainon’s eye twitched. First stage?!

[Achievement Unlocked: “Baby Steps” — Complete the first part of the tutorial. +10 PP]

[Achievement Unlocked: “A Whole New World” — Complete your first quest. +10 PP]

Before Phainon could let out the noise of frustration that had been building in his throat for the last fifteen minutes, a soft knock sounded on the bedroom door.

“Phainon?”

Phainon shot up out of bed, hurriedly fixing the mess of tangled hair on his head before opening the door. Audata stood outside, looking tired, but her eyes crinkled as she looked at him.

“Would you like some breakfast?”

Breakfast was flatbread and honey, along with dried figs that left a cloyingly sweet aftertaste in Phainon’s mouth. It was only Phainon, Audata and Hieronymus this time, and the mood seemed somewhat eased in the light of the day.

After they had finished breakfast and the dishes were cleared—Phainon had tried to help but had been shooed away, relegated to the dining table to watch—a knock came at the door, preceding the arrival of none other than Cyrene.

“Oh, Cyrene! Would you take Phainon out for a while?” Audata asked as she finished drying the last dish, replacing it in the cupboard.

As if I’m a dog, Phainon thought mulishly, the unspoken assumption that he needed looking after not lost on him.

“Me? Um…” Cyrene glanced at Phainon, looking somewhat nervous. 

“Go on, Cyrene. It’ll be all right,” said Hieronymus. “We’ve just got a few errands to run today and can’t stay in the house long.”

Cyrene didn’t say anything right away, but after a few moments she finally said, carefully, “All right.” 

They walked to the docks, to a little inlet where the waves softly lapped not far from where a giant tree stood, a single swing hanging from its branches. Aedes Elysiae was prettier than Phainon remembered. The day before, he’d been too busy being pulled after Cyrene to fully take it all in, but now he could see it with new eyes. 

With the sea breeze in his hair, the fresh air in his lungs, the fragrant scent of wheat in his nose, Phainon felt…refreshed. Was that the word? When a place felt so peaceful you couldn’t help but sigh?

Phainon was too lost in his thoughts, not noticing that Cyrene hadn't followed him up to the swing. 

“I…” Cyrene began from behind Phainon, her voice wobbly.

Phainon turned. She looked like she was about to start crying. “Cyrene? What is it?”

“It’s my fault you lost your memory!” she burst out, not looking at Phainon.

“...What?”

“It must have been my fault! If I had been paying more attention that day, I could have stopped it from happening… I’m so sorry, Phainon… I should have been looking out for you,” Cyrene said, sniffling.

“Why would you do that?” Phainon didn’t understand. “You don’t know what happened.”

“But I’m the older one! It’s my duty to protect you!”

Phainon stared at her. “But…I’m clearly the older one here,” he said, gesturing to the height difference between them, where Phainon stood nearly several heads taller than Cyrene.

“You don’t know anything! Girls get their growth spurts after boys do! Plus, I’ve always been the more mature one,” Cyrene blubbered, tears still running down her face.

Phainon couldn’t help but laugh at this childish display. “All right, all right, you win,” he said, wiping her tears gently with his sleeve.

...Is this what having a younger sister was like?

Phainon thought it felt rather nice.

“It’s not your fault, Cyrene.”

Cyrene glared up at him. “How would you know?”

“Ah…” She'd gotten him there. “I just know it wasn’t, okay? I’m sure you did your best.”

Cyrene stared at him, trying to see if he was making fun of her. When she didn’t seem to find any hint of teasing in his face, she looked away.

“Hmph.”

Cyrene moved towards the swing, where there was a rug placed on the wooden slats of the docks, anchored by several stacks of books. She sat down, patting the space in front of her, inviting Phainon to join. He did, unsure of what they were doing, and Cyrene pulled from her pocket what looked like a box of cards.

They were hand-drawn, and intricately designed, with delicate borders of ink and watercolored backgrounds. Phainon’s breath caught at the sight.

“What are these?” he asked.

Cyrene’s mouth twitched. She seemed to be in a better mood after Phainon’s comforting. “Why, my oracle cards, of course! You’ve seen them before—you bought them for me, after all.”

Phainon fought the urge to say, No, I didn’t. The other Phainon did.

That wouldn’t solve the mess he was in. Instead, he leaned forward, so that his white hair almost touched the surface of the cards, trying to read the tiny writing on the bottom of the thick cards.

“Uh uh uh, that’s cheating!” Cyrene gathered the cards and began to shuffle, stopping only after she had shuffled them several times. Then she spread them facedown on the rug.

“Pick one.”

“...Me?”

Cyrene looked unimpressed. “Who else?”

“Um…all right.”

Phainon deliberated. He’d never been one to believe in these types of things, and couldn’t say he had much interest in astrology or fortune-telling. Still, he indulged Cyrene, and chose a card near the leftmost side. “Then, this one.”

Cyrene picked up the card he’d chosen, and then sighed, amusement plain in her voice.

“Ah… How do you manage to pick the same card every time?”

At those confusing words, she flipped the card around for Phainon to see.

The image was that of a lone man standing atop a mountain, raising his sword to the sun. It was gaily decorated, with gold leaf bordering the edges, illuminating the writing at the bottom that read The Deliverer.

“What do you mean, I always choose this one?”

“You’ve always drawn that one, ever since you brought me these cards. Maybe it means that you’re doomed to be my mail deliverer!” Cyrene giggled.

Phainon frowned in mock annoyance. “Hmph,” he said, mimicking Cyrene’s earlier pompousness. “Then where’s my pay?”

“Pay? What do you mean, pay? Don’t you know couriers work for free? You’ve lost your memories, so you must not have known.”

At “lost your memories”, Phainon’s awareness returned to him in a jolt.

…What am I doing?

He was meant to be finishing the tutorial and heading to Okhema, so he could get a move on back to his own life. What was he doing here, wasting time laughing with a character from a video game?

It had been all too easy to get distracted, for him to drop his defenses and forget that he was on a mission.

…But wasn’t that the point? For him to immerse himself in Amphoreus?

Surely it couldn’t hurt for him to loosen up a little, right? After all, it was only a game.

Phainon put his heavy thoughts out of his mind. For now, at least, he would try to enjoy the moment.

They spent the rest of the afternoon laughing and talking, Cyrene telling him stories from when they were young.

“You’re lying to me!”

“No,” Cyrene protested. “You really did act like a puppy for a whole day! You even followed me around on all fours, all the way to school!”

Phainon threw his hand over his face, exasperated. There was no way that the real Phainon had ever done something that stupid. Was that another thing the devs had written into that NPC’s background? Phainon figured it must be an AI of sorts, since there was no way those underpaid, overworked devs would have time to make this detailed a background for every single character in the game. 

That made Phainon wonder—was he the only beta tester in Amphoreus? Were there other people playing in Amphoreus right now as he sat there with Cyrene?

System? Phainon thought in his head, trying to see if he could project his thoughts to the System telepathically. He’d seen it done in more than one isekai anime, so why not? Are there other beta testers in Amphoreus?

The System responded as if Phainon had spoken aloud, making his pulse jump in excitement.

[No, the opportunity to participate in this beta test was extremely selective. User Phainon will not encounter any other Users for the duration of the playtest.]

That was cool—not only was Phainon able to communicate with the System with his mind, he was also the only real person in the game. He’d played a few MMORPGs growing up, but had always preferred single-player games, so Phainon counted that as a win.

Now that the questions had started, there was no stopping them. There was so much Phainon wanted to know—about how he got here, what limitations there were, and how much of the original Star Rail Phainon would be able to interact with.

Phainon waited until Cyrene had taken a break from recounting childhood memories, choosing instead to write in her journal as Phainon feigned a nap, to ask the System the questions that plagued his mind.

Do I get to meet the Trailblazer? Phainon asked. Like, am I playing the Main Quests earlier than everyone else? Or am I just meant to explore Amphoreus?

[The sole instructions for the beta test are to explore Amphoreus and adhere to the main storyline. Additional information is currently unavailable.]

Hmm. That didn’t really give Phainon anything to work with. So is there anything I can’t do?

[There are three restricted actions for the beta test, and if the User commits any of the following actions, a penalty will be put into immediate effect. Prohibited actions include: revealing User’s true nature as a transmigrator, revealing the existence of the System, and revealing the existence of worlds other than Amphoreus.]

Wait, why does it matter if I tell anyone about that stuff? It’s just a game.

[Revealing the existence of outside worlds or technologies may impact the AI’s ability to follow the plot that has been scripted for the beta test. Additionally, partaking in these restricted actions breaks the immersion of the test, and is therefore prohibited.]

Ah. So there was a roleplaying aspect to this as well. All right—what happens if I break any of the rules?

[User Phainon’s Combat Power will be reduced to [0] for a set duration, and cannot be restored until the full duration of the penalty has passed.]

Wait, what? Does that mean if Phainon broke one of the rules, he wouldn’t be able to defend himself or fight back or anything? 

Um… What happens if I die in the beta test?

[When entering the beta test, User Phainon’s soul was linked to the current character. If the User dies in the beta test, their soul will therefore also perish.]

What?! That was very, very bad news. From what he knew of Star Rail, the game was dangerous—there were enemies everywhere! That he had to fight! Fuck, he had to learn how to fight.

“Cyrene?”

She turned to face him, pink eyes reflecting in the early afternoon light. 

“Do I know how to fight?”

Cyrene grinned. “Hehe, as if that’s a hard question to answer.” She stood up from the rug, brushing herself off, and then stuck out her hand to help him up.

“Follow me!”

An hour later, Phainon stood in a stone courtyard somewhere in Aedes Elysiae, panting and drenched in sweat.

He could fight.

Cyrene had tugged him all the way to the courtyard and pushed a sword in his hand, pointing at a dummy that had been hiding in a corner. 

“Swing at it,” she commanded.

Phainon glanced at the sword, and then up at the dummy, and then back at Cyrene.

“Are you sure?” he asked, hesitancy swirling in his gut.

Cyrene rolled his eyes. “Yes, dummy. You’ve been using that sword since you could hold it without falling over, so just try it!” With that, she went to sit down at a low table, not far from where Phainon and the dummy were, positioned with a perfect view of what was sure to be Phainon’s most embarrassing moment to date. 

“O–Okay,” Phainon muttered. Here goes nothing.

Grasping the sword hilt firmly, he swung the sword at the dummy.

Phainon had fully expected the swing to feel awkward, for the sword to hit the dummy at a strange angle and clatter loudly to the stones. Instead, somewhere in the time between him swinging the sword and it hitting the dummy, his grip on the sword changed, the angle shifting so it found solid purchase, hitting the dummy squarely across the chest.

Phainon stared at the sword, and then looked up at the dummy. “Whoa.”

It had felt…natural. As if Phainon’s body instinctively knew what to do.

Hey System, Phainon asked internally on a whim. What do my starting stats look like?

The System interface opened up in front of Phainon’s eyes, displaying such a long list of numbers that it took Phainon a minute to find what he was looking for. He hadn’t really looked at them when the System was explaining what each of his stats meant earlier, but now he wished he’d been paying attention.

Holy cow, he thought faintly. His Combat Power was wayyy higher than what he had expected. Not that he was complaining—at least he didn’t have to build his stats up from nothing! From that one slash, Phainon could tell his muscle memory was chock-full of sword practice.

Phainon took a quick glance further down the screen, and most of his stats looked good except for Stealth, which was almost abysmally low. However, his Charisma was pretty high, so maybe he’d be able to get by in most situations through diplomatic means instead.

…Huh. In less than a day, he’d gone from hating the idea of staying in Amphoreus even a second longer than he had to, and now he felt almost as if he had stuff to look forward to.

Phainon supposed that’s what happened after you found out you had super strength and could wield a sword after picking one up for the first time.

In any case… Maybe he could see himself hating this beta test less than he’d thought.

content warnings for this chapter (includes spoilers!!)

- canon character death

See the end of the chapter for more notes

Hey System, Phainon asked while lying in bed a few days later. He’d been spending the last few days acquainting himself with Aedes Elysiae, and completing the neverending tutorial missions the System gave him. How come none of the people here can tell that I’m not the original Phainon?

The more time Phainon spent in the village, the more he wondered about this specific question. At first, he’d chalked it up to general video game inconsistencies, but now he wasn’t sure if that made sense. Talking with his family and the other people in the village felt so natural, the AI so advanced that Phainon sometimes forgot he wasn’t talking to a real person. 

If these NPCs could act like real people, talk like real people, and remember like real people, then shouldn’t Phainon’s change in behavior behavior have affected the way they interacted with him? Phainon didn’t think the excuse that he’d lost his memories should have excused that much OOC behavior—luckily, he didn’t seem to have an OOC filter of any kind, which Phainon was immensely grateful for, but wouldn’t his strange behavior tip at least someone off that something was wrong?

Could amnesia really explain away a loved one basically being possessed by someone from another world? Phainon didn’t know if he fully believed that.

The System, predictably, had nothing useful to contribute.

[Though the world of Amphoreus has been designed to make the User feel comfortable, User Phainon is the first User to experience living in Amphoreus. Any perception of characters having prior relationships with the User is therefore inaccurate.]

Phainon sighed. He should have expected as much. The System, he had quickly discovered, was basically a glorified field guide. It was like having someone follow you around (constantly—Phainon had had to tell the System to stop giving him tutorial reminders in the bath) and point over your shoulder, saying Look! You should investigate that—you might learn something interesting! Its computer-generated voice irked Phainon to no end, and he had grown tired of its less-than-stellar responses to his (admittedly many) questions.

In the last few days, Phainon had already completed several mini-missions for the tutorial (which, much to his chagrin, was not a two-part mission and instead was the very definition of an unnecessarily long, extremely infuriating multi-part bullshit side quest). So far, Phainon had completed no less than four (4!) fetch quests in the village—as to how this helped him survive in the beta test, he wasn’t sure—and a few more learn-to-navigate-the-System-type quests. 

Naturally, Phainon was at his wit’s end by the end of the second day.

At least being in Aedes Elysiae felt easier than in the beginning. Phainon was growing comfortable there, surrounded by the kind faces and welcoming arms of the villagers. He’d spent most of every day since his arrival with Cyrene, and his parents had slowly stopped treating him as if he were made of glass, letting him help around the house and (re)introducing him to the other villagers.

…Since when did Phainon start thinking of Audata and Hieronymus as his parents? That was a weird realization, and not one Phainon particularly wanted to explore at the moment.

Hanging around Cyrene had been fun—she had shown him around the whole village, and even brought him to what she referred to as their “secret hideout”, pulling him through a hollow tree in a secluded grove of trees not far from the stone courtyard. After Phainon had crawled through the tree, he’d had to rub his eyes and blink, afraid the sight before his eyes was no more than a vision. It was magical—a whole village hidden within the tree, filled with cute, floating things (fairies, Cyrene had corrected him), and Phainon felt a sense of wonder he hadn’t felt since he was a child.

Then there was the general, all-encompassing sense of peace Phainon couldn’t help but feel in his bones. The scent of the wheat, the golden hues of the village, the warmth of the villagers… It felt idyllic. Typical starter village, Phainon thought drily.

Still. Despite his initial reservations, Phainon was starting to settle in to the beta test. Part of him still ached to get home, but that part was slowly getting smaller and smaller the longer Phainon stayed in Aedes Elysiae. 

So it surprised Phainon more than he’d expected when the System gave him the final tutorial quest the next day.

[New Quest Unlocked: In the Fields of Wheat (7) — Leave Aedes Elysiae]

Phainon stared at the message. 

Objectively, he had known he was going to have to leave eventually. Hell, he had wanted to leave from the moment he’d arrived. But now…

Now, he was being told to leave.

Be rational, Phainon chided himself. You were never here to stay anyway.

It still hurt. Just a little.

Phainon broached the topic at breakfast.

“Um… You know that trip I wanted to go on? I think it’s time.”

Cyrene told Phainon that they’d been planning to leave the village before he lost his memories, to travel across Amphoreus and start making their own ways in life, but their plans had gotten put on the back burner due to Phainon’s condition. Phainon had figured he’d use this trip as an excuse to leave, and then get Cyrene to go with him to Okhema.

Audata’s fork clattered against her plate. “Today? But Phainon, you’re still—”

Without your memories. “I know,” Phainon said. “But maybe it’s better this way? I’ll have Cyrene with me.”

It was quiet for a moment. “…Leave tomorrow morning. Not today,” Hieronymus said. “Give you enough time to pack your bags and such.”

Phainon’s heart felt heavy. “All right.”

“By the time you return, perhaps your memories will have come back,” Audata said, smiling gently at him. 

They won’t, Phainon thought bitterly. “What if they don’t ever come back?”

”You’ll still be our Phainon. We’ll love you all the same.”

Phainon couldn’t stand it. His eyes felt hot. 

He stood up. “I’ll go tell Cyrene.”

Cyrene was suitably excited when Phainon told her the news. “They’re finally letting you go? Phainon, that’s amazing! I’m mostly packed still—I just need to finish a few things, then I’ll be ready!” After that, she ran off, leaving Phainon to stand in the middle of the village alone.

Phainon spent the rest of the day wandering around the village, mentally saying goodbye to the place he’d come to feel so fond of in such a short time. He watched the village children play for a while, and then had lunch at home. After that, he sat by the water and watched as the waves lapped at the docks, the breeze blowing gently on his skin. 

Dinner came and went, with his parents preparing another of Phainon’s favorite meals—steamed fish with chickpea salad—to send him off. They helped Phainon pack his things for the journey, making sure he had enough dried meat, water and spare clothing to last for a sizeable amount of time. Phainon had expected to spend a while in bed tossing and turning, but to his surprise he fell asleep the moment his head touched his pillow. 

When he woke in the morning, he sat a while in bed, staring at the System interface.

[In the Fields of Wheat (7) — Leave Aedes Elysiae]

Only after the sun had finally risen, its rays falling warmly into his eyes, did Phainon finally get up.

“Have you got everything?” Hieronymus asked Phainon, adjusting his pack for him. 

“Yes.”

“Food? Water?”

“Yes,” Phainon said. It had been a while since anyone had fussed over him like this, and it felt… Nice.

”Oh, Phainon. Be safe, will you? And visit,” Audata said. She smoothed her hand over Phainon’s forehead, brushing his hair away from his face. 

“I will,” said Phainon, his heart warm.

”And you stay out of trouble, hear? Your mother and I won’t be around to help you out of it anymore.”

“Oh hush, you. Phainon’s plenty old enough to get himself out of trouble now.”

After that, they fell silent. None of them had anything to say that could delay this moment any longer.

Phainon broke the silence. “Time to go, I guess.”

His parents nodded. “I suppose so,” Audata murmured. Then, she stepped forward and enveloped Phainon in a huge hug.

Phainon accepted it, his chest aching fiercely. Hieronymus joined the hug a moment later, burly arms enclosing them both as Phainon was squeezed tightly.

He didn’t want to go.

After a few moments, after Phainon had forcibly made sure his tears would stay put in his eyes where they belonged, he extracted himself slowly from his parents’ embrace.

“All right, then.”

His parents nodded.

“All right.”

Phainon turned around, ignoring his aching chest, and walked out the door.

Cyrene was waiting for him at their spot on the docks, with her own bag packed and slung across her back. 

“Ready?” she asked.

“As I’ll ever be,” Phainon replied. 

“Then let’s set off!” Cyrene declared, a spring in her step as she began walking. 

They had hardly walked for ten minutes and were still walking through the wheat fields surrounding Aedes Elysiae when Cyrene stopped dead in her tracks.

“Oh no!” she gasped, her face falling ashen.

“What is it?” Phainon asked, alarmed.

“I forgot my oracle cards!”

Phainon sighed, both amused and exasperated all at once. “Should we go back and get them, then?”

Cyrene shook her head vigorously. “No! I’ll run back and grab them, I shouldn’t be long!” Without waiting for him to reply, Cyrene sat her pack on the ground beside Phainon and then ran back in the direction of the village. “I’ll be back!” she called over her shoulder.

If Cyrene was going to be a few minutes, Phainon supposed he might as well sit down. There was a low stone wall nearby, so he lugged their packs (why was Cyrene’s so heavy) over to it and rested against it. 

As much as Phainon couldn’t wait to get home, a part of him was disappointed over having to leave Aedes Elysiae so early. At least he’d have Cyrene with him in Okhema until he needed to say goodbye. That reminded Phainon—he still needed to ask Cyrene to go to Okhema with him. He’d ask when she got back. As he sat, Phainon’s eyes grew tired, and he moved his head back to rest against the wall as he closed them. 

Phainon had barely rested his eyes for five minutes when he noticed something was wrong. He opened his eyes, but saw nothing out of the ordinary until he got up and turned around. 

Aedes Elysiae was on fire.

Phainon abandoned their packs as he raced back towards the village. Fire, fire, fire, his heart thundered.

The return journey had taken almost no time at all, but by the time Phainon pushed through the last bunch of wheat stalks the fire had spread quickly. 

The village was ablaze, the houses Phainon had seen whole less than fifteen minutes ago nothing more than ash. Everywhere Phainon looked, there was devastation and the sound of creaking wood as yet another structure collapsed. The air was filled with the thick smell of smoke, making Phainon cough as he inhaled.

Fuck—Cyrene, his parents, the villagers. Where was everyone?

Phainon’s pulse hammered as he ran through the burning village, searching for anyone who might have gotten caught up in the blaze. He searched and searched but found no one—how was there no one? Phainon thought desperately. He kept his eyes open as he searched, ignoring the burn in his chest and the smoke in his lungs, but it was no use. 

The village was deserted. 

Phainon went to his house first, and found it reduced to embers and ash, nothing inside salvageable, with nobody inside. He went to Cyrene’s house next, which hadn’t been completely engulfed in flame yet, but Phainon could see the sparks catching. He charged inside anyway, fully aware of how stupid it was, but he had to see if there were still people inside. 

There was no one on the first floor, nor on the second—why was there no one?

Phainon burst through the last door on the second story, Cyrene’s room, and stopped dead in the doorway.

Cyrene’s oracle cards sat on the nightstand. 

Cyrene hadn’t made it there.

Phainon grabbed the box of cards and ran, hearing the roar of flames envelop Cyrene’s house mere moments after he ran out the front door.

He needed to leave, to get to safety, to run before he couldn’t run any longer. Phainon raced through the village before stumbling on a sight that made him stop dead, heart nearly dropping through his stomach. 

In front of Phainon stood…a thing. It looked vaguely humanoid, but it was more akin to a walking statue than a man, with crumbling black skin cracked through with veins of gold. It was facing away from Phainon, watching the devastation with a gleaming sword of black and gold in its grasp, but turned its head over its shoulder to peer at him as Phainon skidded to a stop.

Phainon couldn’t move. The monster was faceless, only a pit of deep, bottomless black and gold where its features should be. As if sensing his horror, the monster snarled, a harsh, guttural sound that shook Phainon to his core. In a blink, the monster advanced on Phainon, and Phainon’s instincts failed to move him out of the way quick enough.

Phainon’s torso erupted with pain, and he hit the ground, reeling. Phainon tasted dirt and rust as he pushed himself up quickly, only narrowly avoiding the monster’s next strike.

The monster was looking at him, cruelly—somehow even though it had no face Phainon could sense this. He knew then that if he didn’t run now, he was dead.

Cyrene’s cards had been knocked out of his hands when he fell, but as Phainon grabbed them from the ground he was clipped in the head by another blow, and he staggered, falling to his knees. Through his blurred vision he could see a fallen card beside his right hand, so in the next second he grabbed it and ran, leaving the rest of the cards to burn alongside the village.

Vision blurring with grit and tears, lungs burning with smoke and ash, Phainon ran.

Phainon didn’t stop, not until he reached the stone wall where he’d left their packs. He had enough presence of mind to grab both packs from where they lay on the ground, but kept going. 

Phainon just ran and ran and didn’t stop, not even when his throat ached and his lungs burned with exertion. He didn’t stop even when the sun went down, just kept running. The System pinged at him a few times, but he didn’t acknowledge it.

[Tutorial Quest: In the Fields of Wheat—Aedes Elysiae: Complete]

Phainon just kept running.

Phainon didn’t know how long he’d been running for when he stopped to lean over and retch, his breath catching in his throat, bringing to painful awareness the taste of bile and smoke in his mouth. 

He looked up. He was in a forest, surrounded by gnarled, knotted cypress trees with brilliant green leaves. It was this sight, and the fact that he had been forced out of his numb daze, that finally broke Phainon out of his trance.

What was that? Phainon raged. Why am I here? Why was I brought here just to suffer? Why—

Why did Phainon grow to care for people only for them to die?

The System, wisely, did not answer.

Phainon’s head spun. He suddenly felt dizzy, and something dripped onto his hands. Phainon raised his hands to his face so he could see them through his blurred vision.

Phainon had expected tears, but it was something gold instead. Phainon thought it might have been blood.

If he died here, that would certainly put an end to his misery. Phainon instinctively pushed that thought away, and forced himself to stand up.

Fuck that. He was gonna keep going and get himself out of this fuckass game. Standing took monumental effort, but Phainon did it anyway, his head throbbing with the motion. 

He started walking.

This only worked for so long, however, as Phainon’s body seemed to remember that he was injured and in a state of relative disrepair, causing his steps to wobble and his vision to blur from something other than tears. 

It was only when Phainon came upon a cottage that he finally faltered. He hadn’t even made it all the way to the doorway when his legs gave out, black spots peppering his vision. The last thing he saw before his vision went black was the sight of someone rushing towards him, reaching out as if to catch his fall.

Then, Phainon saw nothing at all.

When Phainon awoke, it was dark. His chest felt heavy, and his throat was itchy like nothing he’d ever felt, plus his head felt like it was stuffed with cotton.

He didn’t know where he was for a moment, and then it all came back to him.

Aedes Elysiae, reduced to ash. Cyrene, his family—

A strangled noise came out from his throat, but Phainon didn’t have the strength to restrain it until he heard a rustling from nearby and realized he wasn’t alone.

He sat up sharply—or, tried to. His head swam in protest and his vision went spotty, but it cleared within a few moments. 

“Who’s there?” he rasped out. Somewhere in the back of his mind, Phainon was startled at how croaky his voice sounded, like he’d inhaled a shit ton of smoke—

Oh, wait. He had.

“Your savior,” said the person, standing just out of Phainon’s eyesight in the darkness of the cottage, which was lit by a single lamp on the table, too far to illuminate his features. 

Phainon scoffed, the sound coming out far weaker than he would have liked. “I was doing just fine on my own, thanks.”

”Clearly not, if I had to carry you on my back like a child.”

The stranger finally stepped into Phainon’s vision, allowing him to finally see the stranger’s face, and Phainon’s breath stuttered.

He was beautiful—golden hair and golden eyes, with sharp features and built like a warrior.

And—Phainon was slowly putting the pieces together—he had seen Phainon’s sorry state and had been kind enough to carry him inside.

Phainon felt himself flush. “I—um… I’m sorry,” he mumbled.

“No need to apologize.”

The stranger’s tone was harsh, but his words were not. Phainon didn’t know how to react to this strange dichotomy.

“I’ve troubled you,” Phainon said. “You even had to carry me inside your house.”

”You haven’t,” the stranger said. “This cottage isn’t even mine.”

“Then whose is it?”

”It’s been abandoned for a long time. I come here every once in a while to stay the night.”

”…Oh.”

Phainon didn’t know what else to say. Was he supposed to ask to stay? Or insist he was fine and leave? Phainon was an expert at ignoring his own problems, but he could already tell that he was in no state to leave at the moment. Before he could come to a decision, the stranger spoke again.

“You can stay here, until you’ve recovered.”

“…Okay.”

After a moment, when it was clear neither of them were going to break the silence, the stranger made as if to leave. 

“Hey—wait a moment,” Phainon called out. The stranger turned, his golden eyes glinting in the dim light. He said nothing, waiting for Phainon to speak.

“Um… Thank you,” Phainon said. “For…” Taking care of me, he cringed internally.

The stranger only nodded, gazing at Phainon a moment longer before disappearing into the other room, closing the door behind him.

It had been three days, and the boy still wasn’t speaking.

Mydei didn’t know if he should be concerned. Well, truthfully, he knew he should be concerned the moment the boy had pushed his way through the trees and collapsed in front of him, smelling of smoke and ash and blood. 

What he didn’t know was if he should try to help.

The boy had clearly…gone through something. His wound stank of metal and rust, a specific reek that could belong only to the black tide. And yet, when Mydeimos asked him how long the black tide’s corruption had clung to his body, the boy had only looked at him blankly.

“...The black tide?” The boy’s voice was grating, and he coughed.

Mydei stared at him, disbelievingly. “Have you lost your wits? How can there be someone who has never heard of the black tide these days?”

“I—um… It was my first time leaving home,” the boy said, quietly. “I guess it’s safer over there.” He looked as if he was going to say more, but his eyes hollowed, and he clamped his mouth shut instead.

Mydei figured he knew what he was about to say. 

Was safer. It clearly wasn’t anymore.

After that, the boy didn’t speak at all, only lay on the worn cot Mydei had dragged out from an upstairs closet with his back facing towards Mydei. Mydei took the hint and left him alone.

Three days passed like this, with Mydei spending the days chopping wood for the fire and for fixing up the cottage, which had fallen into disrepair since the last time he’d visited. He liked to come here every once in a while, to clear his mind from the murky state of affairs in Castrum Kremnos. There had been rumors, lately, of his father’s worsening condition, and what it might mean for Mydei’s future—

No. He had come here precisely to escape these kinds of thoughts.

When he could, he took advantage of his relative freedom in the woods to focus on nothing at all. Except this time, he’d had a half-dead boy stumble his way into Mydei’s solitude, which was an excellent distraction from the worries plaguing his mind, and Mydei set his restless anxiety to better use, cooking and preparing medicine for the boy.

The boy ate little and slept restlessly, no matter how much soup or medicine Mydei set in front of him. 

“Eat,” Mydei had said crossly one day, after he noticed the boy picking at his soup.

The boy didn’t say anything, but he shot Mydei a glance that looked suspiciously like a glare, his unruly white hair moving to obscure his face as he picked his spoon back up. Once he had spooned several bites into his mouth, Mydei was satisfied, leaving the table with the sound of his chair scraping loudly across the floor.

“You need to eat more to regain your strength.”

Mydei’s back was turned, so he didn’t see the boy’s expression. He guessed it was probably another indignant glare, but did not turn back around to test his theory.

After three days, the boy’s wound was no longer tinged black, the corruption leeched out despite Mydei’s inexpert apothecary skills, and his voice had returned to normal. The boy was still pale, his complexion closer to the shade of his hair than a healthy one, but Mydei thought it an improvement that he was up and about.

After he pronounced the boy healthy enough to go outside again, the boy rose wordlessly and began gathering his things.

“You’re leaving?”

The boy stopped. He turned to face Mydeimos.

“Yes.” It was the first he’d spoken since Mydei had asked him about the black tide.

Mydei gazed at the boy. He would have looked roughly the same age as Mydei, who was about to witness his twentieth summer, but for the shadows in his eyes and the hollowness of his cheeks. He looked…haunted.

Mydei cleared his throat. “All right.”

Neither of them said anything for a few moments, and then the boy turned back around to finish retrieving his meager belongings, which only consisted of two rucksacks. When the boy was finished, he walked towards the door, but stopped with his hand on the doorknob, turning to look back at Mydei. 

He seemed to want to say something, but nothing came out.

Mydei knew this was the moment he was supposed to ask for the boy’s name, to offer his own, but something in the boy’s eyes stopped him. A flicker of distrust, of fear.

The boy didn’t want him to ask.

Mydei ignored the twinge in his chest. “Then…be well,” he said, not knowing how to send the other off comfortably. The two of them had shared a house for three days, had slept within calling distance to each other, and yet Mydei did not even know his name, nor the very reason he had arrived in such a poor state to begin with.

It seemed it wasn’t for him to know. 

As Mydei watched the boy walk out the door, something deep within his chest ached, wanting him to reach out, wanting the boy to turn his face towards him once more.

Mydeimos ignored it, and closed the door behind him.

It took only half a day for Phainon to finally reach Okhema.

His map was clearly not drawn to scale, as it had looked like it was going to take Phainon a full two days of walking to reach the city, but he certainly wasn’t about to complain.

Standing outside the massive city and its towering walls of stone, something in Phainon’s foggy chest pushed at his lungs.

Wow, it would have said if Phainon had let it. It’s so beautiful, it would have said, in awe.

Phainon didn’t let it.

The gates were massive, built of marble and decorated with long banners of blue and gold. Phainon gaped at them as he passed through, trying not to seem too suspicious to the guards lining the entrance to the city. Luckily, he seemed to blend right in, as everyone else looked just as awestruck as Phainon felt. 

He pushed through the crowds, which were full of people of every age, young and old. The more Phainon looked, the more he noticed that over half looked injured in some way, with some wearing slings or hobbling on crutches, and others leaning on each other to walk.

Were these…refugees?

Phainon recalled the term the stranger had used—the black tide. Was that what these people were running from?

Just like him, his mind supplied unhelpfully. 

Phainon pushed that thought away. He did not want to get into that right now, thank you very much.

He followed the crowds, weaving between the hordes of people as he took in the city around him. Okhema was strangely…airborne? Or maybe that was an illusion. Phainon didn’t know what to think as he caught a glimpse of what looked like wide open sky at the side of the city, seeing only clouds and what looked like entire cities floating in the air. Which was strange because the side of the city Phainon had entered on was definitely on solid ground. Maybe the city was just really, really close to an extremely tall cliff?

Another thing Phainon didn’t want to think too hard about.

As the main road took them towards the heart of the city, a massive statue came into view. It looked like a giant hewn of stone, holding up a radiant globe of light so bright it rivaled the sun, and Phainon couldn’t look at it for too long without his eyes hurting.

Phainon heard excited whispers from close by. “Look, it’s the Dawn Device!” a boy pointed at the massive statue, eyes wide with delight. Phainon had turned to listen, but his eyes caught on his companion, a young girl with pink hair—

Phainon tore his eyes away. His pulse raced, and his chest ached. 

It wasn’t her. It wasn’t, it couldn’t—

He forced himself to look straight ahead and walked a little faster, but the memory of pink hair stuck like glue in the forefront of his mind the rest of the way through the city.

Finally, they reached what looked like the city center, a massive square paved in glossy marble veined with gold. Everywhere Phainon looked, he saw shining buildings and tall, Greek-looking pillars (if Phainon had somehow been confused about the cultural inspiration behind Amphoreus, he had no excuse now, not when everything around him looked like it had been pulled straight out of a Greek myth).

The square was also teeming with refugees, most of whom had raced to stand in a massive line stemming from the furthest point in the square, where several official-looking people and a host of guards stood. Suddenly feeling very small, Phainon fought to orient himself amidst the crowd and the overwhelming grandeur of the city. Of course, the System chose that exact moment to make its reappearance. 

[Congratulations! User Phainon has completed their first Main Quest!]

Phainon had ignored the System since—since that. Afterwards, the System had pinged him a few times, but Phainon had tiredly ignored them, not even having the energy to mute it. Now, it stared Phainon in the face, its bright blue screen glowing almost indignantly.

[A new Main Quest has been unlocked. Open Quest Log?] 

The System’s box continued scrolling with text, clearly not knowing when to be quiet.

Fine, Phainon said silently. If it will get you to shut up.

The System did not reply to that—not like it could—instead, expanding the window so it showed the quest menu, which now read, Quests—Main Quests. Unlocked: 2/?

(1) Make your way to Okhema, the Holy City

(2) Join the Chrysos Heirs

…What the fuck were the Chrysos Heirs? The headache Phainon seemed to get whenever the System spoke was quickly reappearing, and he rubbed at his forehead, annoyed.

Well. Guess he had to find out.

Hey System, Phainon tried. Is there any way to find out how many Main Quests I have?

[Unfortunately, that information is still locked. However, User Phainon may be able to unlock this feature in the future!]

Phainon almost scoffed out loud. As if he believed that. At this point, he didn’t trust any additional information the System gave him. After all, it hadn’t even told him—

Whatever. It was time for Phainon to get a move on. The quicker he completed this next Main Quest, the closer he got to going home.

Before he could make a plan, or even ask the System where to go first, he heard a commotion behind him. Phainon turned, only to see the little boy and the girl with the pink hair standing at the end of the line, cowering under an old man in fine clothing, a thin golden wreath crowning his head.

“You little pests!” the man hissed. “You should know better than to disrespect your elders.”

“But—” the girl protested, the little boy behind her, fighting tears. “We were in line first!”

“It’s true,” an older woman beside them piped in cautiously. “I was h—”

“Lies!” the old man cried. “How dare you try to cheat your way to an audience with the Goldweaver? You’re clearly little Dolosian thieves, here to lie and steal. Better to teach you your place sooner than later!” He reared back, his arm raised as if to slap the girl across the cheek.

Phainon had heard enough. Before he knew what he was doing, he was rushing to place himself between the man and the two children. 

Crack! Phainon’s face stung with the force of the blow.

“Enough,” he said, venom in his voice. “You’d hit a child? For cutting in line?” Phainon was incredulous. “What a sad old man you are.”

The old man was staring at him, shock rippling across his features. “You—you—”

Phainon rolled his eyes, the movement making his cheeks hurt. He already knew his face was going to swell, but he couldn’t bring himself to care. “Yeah, yeah, I get it—”

“…It’s gold,” the man muttered, still staring at Phainon.

Suddenly, Phainon was aware that the bustling of the crowd had stopped, and had been replaced with hushed murmurs. 

Did you see it? That boy… Golden blood, the whispers said.

Golden…blood?

Phainon raised his hand to his nose and felt wetness. He looked at it, and was reminded of a similar moment, in a forest half a day’s journey from here when he had looked at his hands and seen something that should have been blood, should have been red but instead was—

Gold.

Phainon looked up, confused. What did this mean? There was a small crowd of people that had encircled Phainon and the commotion, who were all staring at him as if he’d grown a third arm. 

Was this…good? Bad? Phainon couldn’t tell. 

Before he could figure it out, two city guards were taking him by the elbow and escorting him out of the square. Phainon craned his neck to look behind him, searching for the two children, and caught a glimpse of pink hair just before the guards turned a corner, blocking the square from view.

Several minutes later, Phainon stood in front of a huge, ornate door, embellished with thick curls of brass, coiling into an image of the sun in the center. The guards had brought him there and then released him, moving to stand at both sides of the door. 

He stood there for a moment, and then glanced at the guard on the left. The guard didn’t look back at him.

Phainon steeled his nerves, and then he knocked.

From behind the door came a mechanical whirring, punctuated with several clicks that sounded like locks opening. With a low creak, the door swung open.

“Enter,” came an imperious female voice from inside.

Phainon entered. Inside was a large study, and even though Phainon knew little about Greek-inspired furniture he could tell everything inside was very, very expensive. The very air reeked of luxury, but the most visible proof of this was that most everything in the room was gold. 

Not excluding the owner of the study, who was golden from hair to sandals.

The woman was exceedingly beautiful, and wore a sleek, golden dress that shimmered with white and silver, complementing the gold of her…everything. Her eyes were a bright teal—a color that was less jarring in person than Phainon could have expected—but clouded over. Phainon would have guessed she was blind, but she was looking Phainon directly in the eyes, so he couldn’t tell.

“Sit,” the woman said, gesturing to an ornate wooden chair covered in a silk cushion in front of the desk. After Phainon had sat down, the woman followed suit, sitting delicately in her own chair and affixing Phainon with a piercing stare.

“What is your name?”

“…Phainon.”

“And where are you from, Phainon?”

“I’m from…Aedes Elysiae,” Phainon said, struggling to get the words out.

“Well, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae. Since when have you possessed golden blood?” the woman said, her tone casual but the look in her eyes decidedly…not. Phainon suppressed a shudder. Why did he feel like he was in trouble?

“I…” He didn’t know what the correct answer was. 

“Careful,” the woman said. “I have no need for lies.”

Something told him he shouldn’t test her on this.

Phainon thought. Technically, he personally hadn’t had golden blood until his arrival in Amphoreus, but who knew if the original Phainon had had golden blood his whole life? But, he figured, since the whole thing about the character whose body he was inhabiting was that it was meant to be a user-insert, he guessed the color of his blood must be a plot thing. Plus, if it was so important, shouldn’t he have heard about it before anyway? Phainon hadn’t known anything until after—after the tutorial, right before he’d collapsed in the forest.

Although…the stranger must have noticed, given how he’d tended Phainon’s wounds for three days. 

Phainon still didn’t know enough about golden blood to know what the right choice was in this situation, so he took a gamble. “Since only recently,” he said, hoping the half-truth would allow him to keep his head. Or legs. He wasn’t really familiar with Ancient Greek execution techniques.

The woman didn’t remove her stare from Phainon’s face, seemingly considering his answer. 

“That’s interesting,” she said musingly. “You’re telling the truth.”

Phainon didn’t move a muscle. He felt he’d only narrowly escaped that trap, but he didn’t know if there were more on the way.

“What do you know of the Chrysos Heirs?”

Phainon could have cried. Thank you, plot gods! he shouted internally. He had not been looking forward to looking for the next starting point of his Main Quest on his own. 

“Um…nothing really,” he said honestly, forcing his features to remain impassive, reining in his excitement.

“Hmm. Simply put, the Chrysos Heirs is a group of individuals who have manifested golden blood, which gives them the ability to host divine power.”

Phainon could see where this was going.

“It is hard to say why golden blood manifests, but some have linked it to experiencing…trying events,” the woman said, moving her gaze to Phainon’s torso. Phainon was suddenly very sure she knew exactly what kind of event he had experienced. He pulled his arms across his stomach, as if that could hide the fact that the woman seemed to know where his wound still ached with the remnants of corruption.

She didn’t seem to need confirmation, and continued. “The black tide is moving across Amphoreus quicker than ever before, which is why we need more Chrysos Heirs to join the Flamechase Journey. Only through—”

“I’ll do it,” Phainon interrupted. He knew he was probably being rude, but he didn’t really have the patience to sit through half an hour of exposition right now. Whatever it was, he needed to join the Chrysos Heirs anyway, and he wanted to get that over with sooner rather than later.

The woman stared at him, and then laughed, a soft, high-pitched sound like the chime of a bell. “So impatient,” she said, her cloudy eyes glimmering with mirth.

“Welcome to the Flame Chase, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.”
