Quests—Main Quests. Unlocked: 3/?

(1) Make your way to Okhema, the Holy City

(2) Join the Chrysos Heirs

(3) Unlocks in: 10 day(s)

Phainon opened his Quest Log for the fifth time that hour, as if that would make the countdown deplete faster. It had originally read fourteen days, right after Phainon had officially joined the Chrysos Heirs and completed the second Main Quest, but it had been four days since then and Phainon was beginning to get impatient.

Well, no, that wasn’t true—he had been impatient from the very beginning.

In the meantime, Phainon had been welcomed into the Chrysos Heirs with welcome arms, which came with a hefty set of benefits, including but not limited to a (what had proven to be, if the size of his wallet was any indication) a very generous salary, free room and board, and access to mostly everywhere within the city limits due to his newly elevated status.

All this…due to the color of Phainon’s blood. Phainon knew it probably wasn’t that deep, especially since it was all for the sake of the plot, but something still didn’t sit right with him that all this luxury had practically fallen into his lap.

He knew it wasn’t for free—the Goldweaver, aka Lady Aglaea, aka the woman who had invited him to join (or rather, watched as he invited himself to join) the Chrysos Heirs, had explained that he would have to go on dangerous missions and fulfill duties to the city in order to maintain his status. But when Phainon remembered what his life was like in the real world, with him working himself to the bone only to still struggle to afford rent and food every month…this new state of affairs left a distinctly sour taste in his mouth.

Still. He wasn’t about to start complaining.

Putting aside his reservations for the moment, Phainon tried to focus on the positives. So far, one gigantic point in Okhema’s favor was the utter luxury that was Phainon’s chambers. All the Chrysos Heirs had chambers in the same building, a building of white marble that stood right next to Marmoreal Palace, where the baths were located. When Phainon first stepped into his chambers with Aglaea, he’d pinched himself just to make sure he hadn’t actually died and been isekaied (again) into a world where he actually had money. 

Well. At this point, Phainon supposed that was true.

The room was massive, as most things in Okhema were turning out to be, with a huge four-poster bed swathed in silks of white and cobalt blue. He had his own sitting room and adjacent washroom, as well as a huge armoire beside the bed, which was already stocked with several outfits similar to what Phainon was already wearing, which were suspiciously already his size. Phainon decided not to question it. 

His chambers also came with a strangely thick, heavy set of curtains, which Phainon had not paid much attention to until later that first day, when he had realized that according to his internal clock—which wasn’t always correct, but usually got him pretty close—the sun should have already set, yet still shone brightly though his windows. Phainon walked out to the balcony (oh yeah, his balcony. Phainon was truly living the life) and looked out to see the sun nowhere in sight, the moon instead staring back at him vindictively.

All while the sky was as bright as when he’d entered the city, definitely more than eight hours ago. Phainon estimated he’d arrived in Okhema by…noonish? So by all accounts, the sun definitely should have set by now. Well, he supposed, the sun might have set but the sky was still light, which perplexed him until he turned his gaze further to the right and he was staring at the massive statue he’d noticed earlier and all the pieces finally clicked together.

The Dawn Device. He was staring at the Dawn Device. The Dawn—Phainon mentally facepalmed. The light emanating from the statue was immensely bright, and Phainon had to squint to avoid being blinded. 

An artificial light source that rivaled the light of the sun… Interesting.

That solved the mystery of the crazy heavy curtains. Phainon wished he had a way of telling the time, as there wasn’t so much as a clock in his chambers, but since he had nothing to do the next day (Aglaea had said she’d summon him after a few days so he could adjust—Phainon thought he might know what she meant now) he pulled the curtains shut and tried to go to sleep. 

It was difficult, having been bathed in sunlight the entire day, and Phainon fell asleep only after tossing and turning for several hours, waking up the next day feeling as if he hadn’t slept a wink. He’d ventured out, bleary-eyed, in search of breakfast only to find that a tray of food had been already left outside on a cart with a card signed only with a cursive A.

After eating breakfast (toast with fruit and honey, served with hot tea), Phainon found himself with nothing to do, so he supposed he’d unpack. 

Except…all Phainon had to his name was his two packs. Whenever he looked at them, however, his chest tightened, and his pulse thudded harshly in his ears. So Phainon left them in a hidden corner, beside the desk.

Later, he decided. I’ll unpack them later.

After (not) unpacking, Phainon was out of things to do, so he had gone out to explore the city. He wandered the corridors of the palace, taking in the sights, and had somehow ended up stumbling into a lush garden delicately placed between two outdoor corridors. It must have been bordering the edge of the city, because as Phainon realized he’d nearly walked into a potted tree he had looked up and seen only a vast, blue sky in front of him. 

Birds chattered around him, the wind rustling through the leaves, and Phainon stood there, staring.

The garden was circular, paved in grey stones with potted trees and plants surrounding the edges and a recessed center. The open corridor Phainon had been walking through had deposited him to the garden’s edge, and Phainon could see another corridor at the opposite end of the garden, marked with a wooden pergola. There were trees with fruit and trees without, and the plants were dusted with flowers in every color imaginable. It smelled of herbs and flowers and fresh air all at once, and Phainon was struck dumb.

This world truly was something else.

Out of nowhere, he’d felt a nudge at his foot. When he’d looked down, he’d seen a creature—too small to be a dog, but too fluffy to be a cat, with a mane like a lion and a forked tail. It looked up at him, and let out a noise that could really only be described as a chirp. 

Phainon looked up, and found the garden full of more creatures, all the same type as the one who was currently nuzzling Phainon’s left shoe. They were everywhere, sitting on benches, sunbathing on the stones, or curled up in tree branches. 

Phainon spent only a little while there before deciding to move on. I’ll be back, he promised, petting a little creature on the head before heading back on his way, but not before he marked the garden’s location on the System’s map feature (which had conveniently only unlocked after Phainon had completed his second main quest in Aglaea’s study. Oh, quest-locked quality-of-life features, his beloathed.)

After his romp in the garden, he wandered through the baths, which were huge and shining and iridescent and wayyyy fancier than Phainon had ever figured a bath could be.

Cyrene would love this.

The thought came unbidden, and struck Phainon with the force of its intensity, causing an almost physical weight to land on his chest. All of a sudden, the baths didn’t look so inviting anymore.

Phainon left.

He wandered aimlessly until he came across a bustling marketplace, with stalls selling food and trinkets as well as little shops lining the streets. People meandered through the throngs or waited for a seat at one of the countless food stalls, vendors shouting over the crowd as they peddled their wares.

“Honeycakes! Hot fresh honeycakes!”

“Kalamaki, two for ten balance coins! Just off the grill!”

As Phainon made his way through the crowd, all of a sudden he felt his neck tingle with the unpleasant sensation of someone watching him. He looked over his shoulder to glance behind him, but saw no one overtly staring at him.

Hmm.

Phainon had only turned his gaze from ahead of him for a moment when he was bumped into, rather abruptly.

“Hey! Watch where you’re going, barbárous,” hissed the man whom Phainon had bumped into, knocking Phainon’s shoulder and stalking around him.

By the time Phainon had gathered himself, the feeling was gone.

He hadn’t gone much deeper into the market before someone called him from behind.

“Lord Phainon!”

Hearing an unfamiliar voice call his name, he turned around. Immediately, Phainon’s eyes caught on pink hair (why were there so many characters here with pink hair?) and his heart stuttered. He was stuck in a trance, unable to move or respond, but he snapped out of it after a few moments.

The pink hair was attached to a girl with two rather gravity-defying pigtails, who couldn’t have been half his height. 

Also, somehow…she looked incredibly familiar.

The pigtails, the cheerful aura… Phainon couldn’t quite put his finger on it, but something about her made Phainon feel like he knew her somehow. Maybe it was her face? Just…her whole face?

Something clicked in Phainon’s head, and he blurted out, “Are you…Barbara?”

“Huh? Who’s Barbara?”

Phainon coughed, his face suddenly aflame. What just came over him? And why…why did this girl look so much like a certain healer character from another game in the Star Rail universe?

Phainon only realized he’d been staring after a few moments had passed, and he straightened immediately, clearing his throat. 

“I…um… Anyway. Sorry. What?”

Thanks to whatever gods ruled Amphoreus, but the girl didn’t comment further on Phainon’s weird social habits, only peered at him curiously. “You are…Lord Phainon, correct?”

“Um…Yes,” Phainon answered, even though hearing the Lord at the front of his name made him feel extremely uncomfortable. Ever since joining the Chrysos Heirs, everyone he met had insisted on calling him Lord Phainon, which made this whole Flame Chase-journey-thing feel way too big for Phainon to handle. He knew it was just your typical save-the-world type stakes, but still—being called a “lord” felt weird. For now though, he put that thought aside.

“I knew it!” the girl brightened. “I’m Hyacine. Lady Aglaea asked me to show you around a bit, if you’re up for it!”

Hyacine led him further into the market, pointing out local specialties while she introduced herself.

“I’m a healer from the Twilight Courtyard, near the Grove of Epiphany—have you been there?” she chattered excitedly, eager to make Phainon’s acquaintance. Her energy made Phainon feel uncomfortable—she wasn’t trying to be overbearing, and was probably only being kind, but Phainon didn’t know how to receive that type of attention gracefully just then. So, the only tone he could use to respond to her with was stiff and clumsy.

Be nice! Phainon chided himself. 

He really was trying—it was just that Hyacine’s bouncing energy was too much for Phainon to process at the moment, not to mention the grandeur and scale of his new surroundings. Hyacine could probably sense his discomfort, but Phainon was a little too overwhelmed to tell for sure.

Before his increasing anxiety could grow any thicker, Phainon suddenly heard a ringing sound from beside him. Bewildered, he looked around for the source.

“Sorry!” Hyacine exclaimed, pulling out what looked almost like a cell phone (??? Wasn’t this supposed to be Ancient Greece?) from her satchel. “I have to take this, but I’ll be right back!”

With that, she bounced off, and Phainon was left alone. 

Since he had nothing to do besides wait for Hyacine, he figured he might as well look around on his own. As he was looking around the small square, a sign labeled Treasure of Ages piqued his interest. In front of the store were several shelves of pottery, housewares, and assorted items. 

Maybe an antique shop? Phainon had worked at a pawnshop for the last several years, and though his boss wasn’t the nicest or the most forgiving (Phainon had been on the receiving end of his lectures more times than he could count), he had grown comfortable around the towering piles of old books and crates of cracked porcelain. Seeing a remnant of his life in the real world tugged at him, and made the desire to return home resurface with a sharp twist of his heart. 

Phainon wandered in.

His instinct hadn’t proved wrong—it was indeed an antique shop. The shop was filled with dozens, if not hundreds of old pieces, and the air smelled like dust and the distant tang of oil. 

“A fresh face! Welcome!” came a voice from behind him. 

Phainon startled. He had been so lost in his thoughts that he hadn’t noticed the shopkeeper come and stand behind him. 

“Ah! Hello,” Phainon said.

The shopkeeper peered over his shoulder to look at the piece Phainon had been so engrossed in. 

“Ah… Now that is an ancient Aidonian ceremonial dagger. The bronze is dated to be around eight hundred years old.”

Phainon took a moment to inspect the dagger in its case—it was simple but elegant, with a plain hilt and a sloping, tapered blade. Phainon knew nothing about weapons but could already tell the workmanship was impeccable. 

“It’s in such great condition to be eight hundred years old,” he said. 

The shopkeeper’s chest swelled with pride, and he boasted gustily, “Well, of course it is! I’ve been restoring artifacts since well you were born, son. Eight hundred years is nothing! Why, I’ve got pieces here more than three thousand years old, if you’re interested…”

As the shopkeeper continued, Phainon’s mind wandered.

Three thousand years, huh… It was wild to think of how deep the lore had been developed for this world. Some hidden, niggling part of Phainon wanted to know all of it.

The shopkeeper must have noticed Phainon’s attention wandering, because he suddenly cut himself off with a shake of his head, a rueful smile growing between his sideburns.

“You’ve caught me rambling again—bad habits, I never know when to let things be, my wife says. If you need me, I’ll be over here—name’s Theodoros, by the way. Just give me a holler!”

Theodoros wandered off, and Phainon went back to inspecting the dagger. It looked like there was an engraving carved into the hilt, and he leaned closer to get a better look—

“Whatcha lookin’ at, pretty boy?” came a voice by his ear.

“Ah!” Phainon jumped for the second time since entering the antique shop, and whirled around to see who had crept up behind him this time. 

Standing in front of Phainon was a girl clad in black, wearing a headband with cat ears attached, not unlike something he might have seen in the real world. 

Phainon struggled to contain a snort, but just then he noticed that the cat ears were not, in fact, attached to a headband at all, and actually seemed to just be a part of the girl’s head.

Also, she had a tail. A long, gray tail that flicked behind her, as if sensing that Phainon’s mental reserves were depleting rapidly due to this unforeseen event.

“Oi, Theo!” the girl called, flashing Phainon a wink.

Theodoros wandered back into view. 

“Ah, the little Miss Cipher! Wonderful to see you again. Could I interest you in some porcelain?”

The girl (who might actually be a cat—does that make her a catgirl? Phainon’s head hurt) smirked at him.

“Hmm… Actually, Theo, I was looking for something a bit flashier,” said the (not a cat) girl. 

Theodoros brightened. “Yes! I have just the thing.” He dashed off to the back of the shop, where distant rustling and shuffling could be heard.

Phainon turned his gaze back to the girl right as her hand was slipping into her pocket. “Hey!” he said, astonished. “You can’t—”

“Oh, hush,” Cipher shushed him, her gray eyes glinting. “I gotta have fun somehow.” She pulled something from her pocket and placed it on the shelf, something that looked like one of the coins Phainon had in his wallet but outlined with a faint purple glow. Immediately after it touched the shelf, it began to smoke, and Cipher’s eyes lit up.

“You—Lady Cipher!” Phainon hissed. She shot him a wink, and then the coin exploded into thick gray smoke with a loud pop.

Phainon coughed, waving the smoke from his face. By the time his vision cleared, Cipher was gone. 

Theodoros made his way back to the front of the shop, coughing as well. It was at this moment that Hyacine entered the shop, her already wide eyes growing even larger as she took in the mess that Cipher had left. Luckily nothing had actually exploded, but the antique shop was so full of smoke still that it looked like something out of a post-apocalyptic action movie.

“What—”

“Ah, the Lady Cipher was here…” Theodoros shook his head ruefully. “I should know better than to fall for her tricks by now.”

“Ah…” Hyacine shook her head. “I do apologize, Theodoros. I—”

“It’s all right,” Theodoros interjected, waving her off. “Just a little prank, it looks like. Nothing’s even broken.”

Despite Hyacine’s protests and insistence that they help him clean up, Theodoros shooed them off. 

“Just come by again sometime!” he called after them.

The crowds in the market had thinned by the time they exited Theodoros’ shop. The girl beside Phainon was uncharacteristically quiet, and Phainon fell into his own thoughts.

Just then, he remembered the incident that had occurred earlier. He hadn’t had time to really think about it, but something was strange about the fact that he could understand everyone around him perfectly except for one word.

System? Phainon thought. Why didn’t I understand that word earlier…ba-ba something?

As if it had been waiting for him to ask, the System responded immediately.

[Occasionally, the User may encounter words in Amphoreus that do not have a direct translation to User’s original language. In this case, User Phainon has encountered a word that is difficult to translate, so the System has kept it in its original language in pursuit of accurate communication.]

“Hey, Hyacine,” Phainon began hesitantly. “What does bar—babaroos mean?”

Hyacine stopped short, glancing up to look Phainon in the eye.

“Do you perhaps mean…barbárous?”

“Yeah! Yeah, that’s it.”

Hyacine frowned, her brow furrowing slightly. “Did someone call you that?”

“Um…yeah. I think. Earlier, I bumped into someone, and they called me—that.”

“It’s…” Hyacine hesitated. “It’s not a nice thing to say. It really just means foreigner when people say it nowadays, but its original meaning was barbarian. It’s not the kindest word to use, especially towards a Chrysos Heir.”

What does me being a Chrysos Heir have to do with anything? Phainon wanted to ask. But he held his tongue. Instead, he asked, “I mean… That seems pretty tame to me. I thought he was cursing at me, or something.”

“Lady Aglaea told me your home is somewhere far from the city, and that you might have been sheltered from a lot of the troubles the rest of the world faces, so you might not know… But Okhema is the strongest defense we have against the black tide right now. It used to be that there were many cities able to take on the black tide and could shelter their state’s people, but now… Okhema is really the only one left. Lady Aglaea has made sure everyone feels welcome here, and people travel from all over the world to hide from the black tide here.

“But…” Hyacine’s voice gained a tinge of sadness. “Not everyone here is willing to accept these people with open arms. So they use words like barbarian to belittle those newcomers, label them as if they don’t belong. It’s…become really common, lately.”

With that, Hyacine’s mood grew gloomy. Phainon hadn’t meant to bring up such a heavy topic, but at the same time the situation in the city was becoming more clear. 

Okhema truly was a city at war. Phainon hadn’t really understood it until now, not even seeing all the refugees upon his arrival. 

Phainon looked around. Nothing around him signaled the fact that this city was the last bastion against the black tide—not the wind chimes tinkling from the balconies, not the colorful painted doors, nor the breeze gently rustling through the leaves. 

He could see why some people would want to keep this kind of place to themselves. From all that he’d seen—his mind instantly flashed to the hidden garden—Okhema seemed at peace. Perhaps not all the people within were, but its very foundations—the literal ones, yes, but also its…spirit? Could a city even have a spirit?

“Ah… I didn’t mean to bring the mood down!” Hyacine said suddenly, seeing something on Phainon’s face. Phainon waved her off.

“It’s all right. You really care a lot about this place, don’t you?”

Hyacine was quiet for a moment. “Yeah, I do.” She tugged at the bottom of her sleeves, lifting them slightly so Phainon could see a curling, intricate gold symbol on her wrist. “Even before this appeared, I just wanted everyone to get along.”

Phainon stared at the symbol. “When…that appeared?”

Hyacine looked up at him, eyes furrowing in apparent confusion. “When my marks appeared.”

“Is that…something that happens?”

“Lord Phainon… Have you not seen your own marks?”

Phainon stared. My own marks?

As soon as they parted ways, Phainon rushed back to his chambers and made a beeline for the washroom. Once he got in front of the mirror, he yanked his collar down and stared.

He had a golden tattoo. On his neck.

The tattoo was in the shape of a sun, stretching from a few fingers beneath Phainon’s jaw to just above his collarbone. Phainon traced it with his fingers. It was smooth to the touch, and Phainon wouldn’t be able to tell it was there if not for the barely noticeable warmth.

“Hahhhhhh…”

What the fuck was he supposed to do about this?

chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

The golden marks were apparently “manifestations of golden blood”—aka, they had probably appeared when Phainon’s golden blood first did. That meant that Phainon had been walking around with a golden neck tattoo (!!) for over a week (!!!). 

Fuck.

It was huge. No matter how much Phainon tried to cover the tattoo, it was still visible, the golden tips peeking out just above his collar as if in spite.

He hated it.

It was too big, too flashy—Phainon had never been a fan of fancy clothes or accessories, preferring simple designs over trendy ones. He’d heard many criticisms of his fashion sense in the past, but there was no way anyone could look at the giant tattoo on his neck and think oh wow, that’s so cool.

Why did he care so much about this anyway? Phainon thought about ignoring it for about half a second and then immediately discarded that idea. There was no way he was going to walk around with a fucking neck tattoo, a golden one at that. 

Which brought Phainon to his next question—why the fuck was everything in this world gold?

Phainon’s tattoo, Hyacine’s marks, Aglaea’s whole…everything.

Not like it really mattered, but a boy could be curious.

Lady Aglaea explained the marks to Phainon after she’d summoned him to her chambers for a full debrief on what it meant to be a Chrysos Heir.

Phainon caught unfamiliar words such as Titans, Coreflames, trials, divine authority and thought his head might explode. But finally, he thought he had the gist of it.

“So eventually, I’m going to take on a Titan’s…divine authority?” he asked, tone trailing up at the end in question.

“Yes.”

“Which one will I get?”

“It is not so set in stone, Phainon,” Aglaea said, cloudy eyes glimmering with a hint of mirth. “After retrieving the Coreflame, you would have to pass a trial to prove that you are worthy of it. There are still many yet to be retrieved—you could bear Reason, Earth, perhaps even Strife. As of now, we have but five, the remaining seven still lost to the world.”

“Who…” Phainon wasn’t sure how to ask this. “Where are the five we already have?”

“Some have already been claimed, their trials passed, and some remain unborne. I, for example, bear Mnestia’s Coreflame, that of Romance. My teacher Tribios bears Passage, but the rest remain unclaimed—the authorities of Trickery, Law, and Ocean.”

What a strange collection of gods—no, Titans, Phainon thought. He was used to fictional worlds having their own made-up gods, usually corresponding to an element or feature of nature, like fire, water, electricity, wind, et cetera. These Titans—Romance, Law, Passage… The odd variety certainly was interesting, to say the least.

“So…why…?” Phainon gestured to his neck. “What’s the whole thing with golden blood? The marks?”

“To bear a divine authority is no easy task, Phainon. Without proper fortification, your body would burn to ash the moment you tried to touch it, which is why only those with golden blood are able to bear a Coreflame. I mentioned previously how the manifestation of golden blood is often linked to experiencing events of great hardship. This is only one precipitating factor, but it is a common one. The leading theory is that the Titans send blessings upon those who have experienced immense hardship or displayed great bravery in the face of danger, manifesting in golden blood, granting them great power and strength enough to bear a Coreflame.”

Ah. So it all came down to that. Phainon wasn’t sure what irritated him more, the fact that he hadn’t seen it coming or that all the troubles he had gone through since starting the beta test had been written in from the beginning. But still…wasn’t this too much? To make an innocent person go through something like—something like that all for the sake of the story?

It probably would have been fine if Phainon was playing the game for real, sitting on the other end of a computer screen. But the fact was that he was in the game, living it out in real time as he’d been told to do, which made it feel like it had actually happened to him.

So much so that Phainon thought he was going to throw up from the thought of it.

He left Aglaea’s chambers feeling exhausted, both mentally and physically. It wasn’t as if he’d done anything strenuous lately, but he hadn’t had a good night’s rest since his arrival. No matter how tightly he drew the curtains at night (he had finally discovered that he could use the System to track the time throughout the day) and how exhausted he felt as he laid in his insanely soft bed with its silk sheets, it still took hours of tossing and turning for him to reach sleep each night.

The Dawn Device’s eternal light certainly had an influence on how poor his sleep quality had been, but there was also the unfamiliarity of sleeping in a strange bed that irked Phainon. The nightmares didn’t help, either—more often than not, he had woken up with a heavy weight pressing on his chest, breath coming in gasps as he tried to recover his wits. It always took a long, long time for his heart to stop racing and for his mind to finally settle, after which he would eventually fall into another restless sleep. 

Rinse, repeat. It had been like this for two weeks now, and Phainon thought he might go insane before he even got the chance to complete his Main Quests.

Which, irritatingly, still had not been updated—the System’s Main Quest was still frustratingly blank, even after the countdown had come and gone. He asked the System about it, only to be told in its endlessly annoying auto-generated voice that “the triggering event has not yet taken place”. 

Phainon wanted to tear his hair out.

There was something he could do in the meantime, though. He headed back to the marketplace where he’d met Hyacine, this time on a mission. After searching a few stalls, he eventually found what he was looking for—a choker, nearly an inch wide and made of soft, supple leather. It wasn’t thick enough to cover the entire tattoo, but if Phainon folded up his collars high enough, the tattoo would be hardly visible. It wasn’t as if he could wear a turtleneck instead, not with the sunlight beating down every second of the day.

In his chambers, he tried it on, struggling to thread the clasp behind his neck. When finally it slipped into place, he stared at himself in the mirror.

A familiar face, familiar features…save for the golden tips he could see peeking over his collar. 

He was so fucking tired of this already.

From what he could pick up from his meeting with Aglaea, Phainon could tell the main storyline was probably going to follow the Flame Chase journey as they retrieved the rest of the Coreflames.

There were seven Coreflames left to recover, and if each one took up a single storyline… That was going to take way too long. Just how long was this beta test gonna be? Was he going to have to play the whole story to the end? Or was it going to finish after a certain point, almost like a trial period? Phainon had never been invited to a beta test before, and had no idea how they typically functioned apart from the basics.

He could ask the System, but he also just…didn’t want to. He couldn’t be sure the System was actually going to give him the full truth.

So. At the moment, Phainon was stuck on what to spend his time with. He could go back to his chambers, maybe try to nap a little… No, that would disrupt his (already very disrupted) sleep schedule. 

Then…maybe he could go shopping or something? Phainon discarded that thought as well. He honestly didn’t need anything—Lady Aglaea had clearly anticipated all of his needs, and had stocked his chambers with multiple new outfits, a huge bookshelf, and a refreshment station. He even had a chess table in his chambers, for chrissake.

As Phainon pondered what to do, his mind kept returning to the garden he’d found while exploring the city. 

Hmm. Maybe he’d go there. 

It took him a while to find the corridor that led to the garden, even with the help of the System’s map tracking feature, but eventually he found it. This time, though, the garden wasn’t empty.

“Lord Phainon!”

Hyacine waved at him from across the courtyard, a bright smile crossing her face. Phainon blinked against the brightness that was her expression, and then tried to smile back.

“Hello, Lady Hyacine.”

“What brings you to the Garden of Life?” Hyacine asked, walking up to him with another girl trailing behind her, who kept several steps’ distance even as Hyacine stopped. 

Is that what this place is called?

“I just…wandered by last time, and wanted to come back. What about you?”

“Oh, I come here often, to take a break from my work—” Hyacine motioned to a building near the edge of the garden, “—and to visit the chimeras.”

“…Chimeras?” As if on cue, one of the little creatures Phainon had seen last time came scurrying down a tree, turning back to hiss at another creature who had been chasing it, fur ruffled in annoyance. “Oh—these guys.”

Hyacine giggled, and then her eyes widened a little. “I almost forgot—Lord Phainon, this is Lady Castorice, another Chrysos Heir. You probably haven’t had the chance to meet yet.”

Behind Hyacine, the girl bowed her head politely, her hands clasped in front of her. “Greetings, Lord Phainon.” Her voice was soft and sweet, and the girl seemed almost drowning in lace and lavender, matching the tint of her hair and eyes, which were both similar shades of purple.

“It’s nice to meet you, Lady Castorice,” Phainon said. He supposed he shouldn’t be surprised at this point by the amount of people with vibrantly colored hair in this world—it was Star Rail, after all—but what was stranger still was that Castorice still resolutely stood several steps behind Hyacine. 

“We were actually just speaking about you,” Hyacine piped up, breaking Phainon’s train of thought. 

“You were?”

“Yes, I was curious about your home,” said Castorice. 

Phainon’s heart stopped.

“…Yeah?”

“Hyacine mentioned you’d come from far away, but didn’t remember the name of the city you came from. Is it—”

“A village—Aedes Elysiae,” Phainon interrupted, his head throbbing.

Castorice looked somewhat disappointed. “…Oh,” she said.

Meanwhile, Hyacine’s brows had furrowed, and she didn’t let the matter drop just yet.

“Aedes Elysiae… Where is that?”

Phainon wanted to change the subject, but tried to remember where the sun had been on his trek to Okhema. “West. I think.”

“That’s strange… I didn’t think there were any villages that way until—”

“I’m sorry,” Phainon interrupted once again. He found that he’d hit his limit a lot faster than he’d expected. “I think—I have to go.”

Trying not to run, Phainon left the garden as quickly as he could, stumbling over a potted plant in his haste. He heard it topple over, the porcelain smashing onto the stones as he rushed out, out of the garden that had suddenly grown claustrophobic and away from the memories of home that had sprung into his mind and refused to leave, and Phainon thought he actually might be suffocating to death as he started running.

Talking about Aedes Elysiae shouldn’t have been a big thing, shouldn’t have made him lose his mind like this, but it was as if everything he hadn’t been thinking about for the past few weeks had slammed into him with the force of a charging rhino.

Why couldn’t he just stop thinking about it?

Why did memories of home have to keep coming back to strangle him?

Why did they have to leave?

He didn’t want to go back to his chambers. He didn’t feel comfortable anywhere in this foreign city, knew no one who could comfort him, knew no place to seek safety.

He needed to leave.

Before he knew it, Phainon had escaped the city and was standing in the surrounding forest. He’d finally stopped, chest heaving, and coughed until he thought his lungs might come out that way.

After a long while, Phainon finally caught his breath, and he collapsed against a gnarled tree. It was silent save for the chirping of crickets and the distant croaking of frogs.

In the relative quiet, his heavy mind finally posed the million-dollar question.

Why did they have to die?

Phainon hadn’t cried since arriving in this world, not when Aedes Elysiae had burned to ash or when Cyrene hadn’t returned, not even when he realized that he’d never see his fake parents again or when he’d realized that this beta test had completely, utterly shattered him.

He cried now.

They were ugly, heavy tears, and he was making a lot of noise, but he had no room in his heart to care. Everything reminded him of home—not just constantly having to talk about it with people, with Aglaea, Hyacine, even Castorice, who he’d just met and had probably been extremely rude to, but also hearing the wind through the leaves or seeing just how beautiful the city was, which felt wrong to Phainon that there was still beauty in the world after what he’d witnessed.

Shouldn’t an experience like that taint him? Make him unable to see anything beautiful ever again?

But no, Phainon was reminded of exactly how unjust the world could be as he gazed at the wide blue sky, or when he marveled at the shining plazas of Okhema, or when he lay down to sleep at night and felt the comfortable silk sheets envelop him.

Why did only he get to feel those things? Why was it him who had to feel those things?

And why was everything in that fucking city gold?

Gold, the color his blood had turned after seeing Aedes Elysiae consumed in fire, but also gold, the color of wheat stalks silhouetted against a clear blue sky. Gold, the color of warmth, the color of the edges of his mother’s tunic the day she’d sent him off, and gold, the color of his father’s hair underneath the grey. 

Gold, the color of the border of Cyrene’s oracle cards, which she’d been unable to retrieve the day she’d died.

Gold, the color of death—but also gold, the color of love.

Phainon cried for a long, long time. 

When his tears finally dried, the sky had darkened—he wasn’t far from the city, but apparently far enough that the Dawn Device couldn’t completely illuminate the night around him, which left the sky dimmed in a twilight haze.

Phainon’s throat hurt from crying and he was incredibly parched, but his mind felt clearer. 

Nothing had changed—he was still in the same position as before, but Phainon’s heart inexplicably felt lighter after finally having acknowledged everything.

His parents and best friend since arriving in this world were dead. His home was nothing but ash, and he was still stuck in this stupid beta test. 

But Phainon felt he had a little more courage now.

Out of nowhere, he was reminded of the card he’d picked up after encountering the black tide in the village. Where had it gone?

He needed to find it. He also really should unpack his and Cyrene’s packs, still untouched and hidden from sight beside his desk.

Everything still hurt, but if Phainon was going to finish this beta test and get back to his own world, he was going to have to acknowledge that he was in it for the long run. 

And that meant not pushing things away anymore.

All right—step one, go back to Okhema and sort through his things. Step two, figure out what the “triggering event” for his next Main Quest was, and step three, commence plan. Or whatever.

It wasn’t much, but it was a start. With a sigh, Phainon pulled himself up from where he was leaning against the tree. Then, he began his walk back to Okhema.

When he got back to the city, the sky gradually turning to eternal daylight the closer he got, he went straight back to his chambers. Phainon stared at the two packs beside his desk for a moment, and they stared right back.

He opened the first pack.

Inside were a few changes of clothing, basic camping supplies, and some provisions—the things Phainon had packed. Next, he turned to Cyrene’s pack. Her pack was mostly the same, but there were a few extra things as well.

The first was a letter addressed to him and Cyrene. Phainon’s brow furrowed. Where had this come from? He set it aside for now, and focused on the second thing.

It was the oracle card he’d managed to save from the village. It had been slipped into Cyrene’s pack—most likely by the stranger from the forest. He’d probably found it on Phainon and decided to put it with his things for safekeeping. 

Phainon flipped the card over. 

The Deliverer card stared back at him, its gold lettering reflecting the warm light of Phainon’s chambers. Phainon didn’t know whether to laugh or cry.

“Ah… How do you manage to pick the same card every time?”

Cyrene’s words came to Phainon’s mind, and he swore he could have heard her voice echo in his head.

His eyes felt hot as he put the card down and opened the letter.

Dear Phainon, and dear Cyrene,

You both have grown up so well. We are so proud of the people you’ve become—strong, brave, intelligent and kind. We know this journey is only the beginning of the amazing things you will accomplish one day. Whatever you do, no matter how hard things become, remember that you always have a home here and in each other. 

We are so incredibly proud of you both, and we love you to the moon and back.

Safe travels, and visit soon.

Love,

Mom and Dad

Phainon was crying again. Sniffling, he ran his fingers over the letter and reread it.

His parents must have given this to Cyrene for them to read together, but when? …It must have been when Cyrene had gone back to grab her oracle cards. She had gone to Phainon’s house first, and had spoken with his parents, which is when they would have given her the letter, and then she hadn’t made it home in time. 

If…if Cyrene had still been with his parents when the black tide had struck, that meant that they might have died together. Phainon’s heart clenched. 

If they had to die, at least they didn’t die alone. The thought came too late to bring comfort but warmed Phainon’s heart all the same.

Phainon placed the letter and the card in his desk, and then put away his clothes in the armoire. As for Cyrene’s clothes, he’d have to figure out what to do with them at some point, but for now he put them neatly in a cupboard.

Step one, complete. 

Now, it was time for Phainon to unfuck his life and get back home.

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Reviewing his Three-Step Plan to Making the Most of This Stupid Isekai Situation, Phainon thought he should edit it a little. 

Firstly, it needed to be a little longer than three steps. Phainon mentally began a new list.

Step one, figure out the triggering event for his next Main Quest. That one hadn’t changed, and was still the highest priority.

Step two, find a way to spend his time in Okhema in the meantime. Until Phainon had another Main Quest to work on, he was stuck—and he couldn’t just keep doing what he had been. Phainon had practically explored all of Okhema these past two weeks, and had nothing to do in his chambers other than read or stare out the window at the Dawn Device, which already sounded exhausting to Phainon.

So—what could he do? The obvious answer was his Chrysos Heir duties, but those hadn’t started yet either, and he had no idea as to when that would change. Phainon put that idea aside for now, not discarding it but not counting it as part of the plan. 

Phainon thought for a while, but was stumped until his mind returned to the antique shop he saw the day he’d met Cipher and Hyacine. 

Treasure of Ages… Maybe he could get a second job on the side. Phainon noted that down, and reviewed his updated list.

It was a start.

The next day, Phainon went to Aglaea’s office. He knew he probably should have formally requested a meeting or something, but he had no idea how he could have gone about it. So now, he stood in front of Aglaea’s door, hoping she magically had time in her busy schedule to talk with him.

To Phainon’s surprise, Aglaea let him in, sitting him down at her desk as if she had all the time in the world. 

Before she could even speak, Phainon beat her to the punch.

“I want to start my Chrysos Heir duties,” he blurted out.

The corners of Aglaea’s mouth twitched. “Oh?” she asked.

Phainon hadn’t really thought of an explanation he could give her as to why. “I just—um, I don’t have anything to do,” he said. 

“Hmm… I’d thought to give you some time to gather your bearings, but I suppose we can begin a little early.”

How much time could he possibly need? It had been over two weeks! Phainon was just grateful she hadn’t refused. He breathed out a sigh of relief. 

He would begin the next day—Why not right now, Phainon had almost asked, but stopped himself before he could push his luck too far. Aglaea seemed to sense his impatience and informed him with an amused look that she still had a few things to prepare before he could officially begin.

Tomorrow it was, then.

That gave Phainon time to check off another thing on his list, one he’d felt was important to get done sooner rather than later. Before leaving Aglaea’s office, he paused on the threshold, glancing back.

“Do you know where I could find Lady Castorice?”

Apparently, Marmoreal Palace had a library. As Phainon stepped into the cavernous space, he felt his mouth fall open in awe. It was huge, with shelves of books spanning from the floor to the ceiling, with tall, spindly ladders propped up sporadically against them. The shelves stretched the entire length of the library save for the far wall opposite to the entrance, where high, arched windows took up the entire span of the wall. Through it, Phainon could see off the edge of the city, swaths of blue sky and distant floating cities visible through the fluffy white clouds.

Phainon took it all in for a moment, his heart clenching.

How was he supposed to deal with seeing things like this every day now? It only reminded him of the people who would never get to see it.

He took a few breaths, trying not to drown in the sudden rush of emotions. Then, he proceeded further into the library to find Castorice. 

Besides the shelves along the wall, the main floor of the library was scattered with shelves and tables alike, where people sat whispering or flipping idly through thick tomes and weathered scrolls. It reminded Phainon of the library he’d grown up going to, the public library a few blocks away from his home when he was a child—cozy and familiar, the dark wood contrasting playfully with the gentle light through the windows.

Phainon finally caught a glimpse of light purple hair in a far corner of the library. He turned his head to confirm that yes, it was indeed Castorice, her head bowed low over a book. She appeared so caught up in her reading that she didn’t hear Phainon approach until he said something.

“Lady Castorice?”

Castorice startled, her head shooting up to see who had surprised her. When she saw it was him, her eyebrows lowered in familiarity and she closed her book, moving it away from her on the table.

“Oh, it’s you. Lord…Phainon, was it?”

Phainon nodded. Even though there didn’t seem to be anyone nearby and their conversation was hushed, he didn’t want to disturb anyone, so he asked, “Would you mind if we took a walk?”

They exited the library together, Castorice curiously still keeping a sizable distance between them as they walked. Confused, Phainon turned around.

“Do you… I mean, why…” he gestured to the space beside him, not knowing how to voice his jumbled thoughts.

High Charisma, my ass. He could barely get his own words out half the time.

Thankfully, Castorice seemed to understand. “Ah—I didn’t mean to offend you… It’s a long story.”

They had stopped near an alcove, which overlooked a small courtyard with a fountain and a collection of potted plants. Phainon moved to stand by the balcony.

He didn’t want to pressure Castorice into talking about it, not when it seemed like an uncomfortable subject. So, he spoke first, bringing up the thing that had been on his mind since the day before.

“I wanted to apologize for yesterday,” Phainon said. When she didn’t respond, he added, “When I ran out like that—I didn’t mean to be rude. I just…needed a little space.”

Castorice took a moment to respond. When she did, her head raised to look him in the eye, her voice soft. “I should be the one to apologize. I upset you.”

Phainon shook his head. “No, I—” Breathe. He took a breath. “Talking about home is…difficult for me,” he admitted. “I still shouldn’t have left like that.”

It was quiet for a few beats. Phainon heard the birds twittering in the trees nearby, then Castorice spoke again.

“I…also have difficulties thinking about home.” Her voice was quiet, and she spoke delicately, but her tone was tinged with sorrow. “I was curious, when you arrived, because Lady Aglaea said you’d come from somewhere far away. I thought maybe…it might have been where I came from as well.”

She joined Phainon in looking out over the balcony, but stood about five feet to his left. The mild breeze disturbed a few lavender strands from her braid, causing them to fall into her face, but she didn’t seem to notice.

“I hail from a city called Aidonia, in the far north. In the beginning, they were kind to me, but over time I became…something like a tool for them to use, I suppose.” Castorice looked down at her hands, lacing them together upon the balcony’s edge. “I have a special talent. Anyone I touch dies.”

Phainon didn’t feel as if that was a metaphor. He remained silent.

“I don’t know exactly why, only that I have always had it. In Aidonia, they…” Castorice let out a quiet breath. “They called me the Holy Maiden, but I was only ever their executioner—the person blessed by fate to grant those poor souls an easy death, so they would never have to defile their own hands. And yet…I miss it still.”

After that, Castorice was quiet. The mood had grown heavy, and Phainon thought he now understood the reason behind Castorice’s demeanor, the distance she kept between her and everyone else. Even in the library, she had chosen a table in a far, secluded corner when there were plenty of empty tables—tables that were closer to the giant windows with the beautiful view, tables that had less space between them and other tables, so that one would need to be careful not to knock another’s elbows while carrying a stack of books.

Castorice was keeping herself away from others because she could not touch them—could not touch them nor feel their warmth, couldn’t even feel the comfort of a hand on her shoulder or the feeling of being held in a gentle embrace. Any accidental touch, any brush of fingers against skin, of sleeve against sleeve—

“Oh,” Phainon said, his voice a little cracked through. “Oh, Castorice.” Castorice’s story had made him so sad that he’d forgotten to use her title, but he couldn’t bring himself to care. By the way she looked over at him, eyes dry and smiling, she didn’t seem to mind either.

“Don’t worry about me,” she said. “I just…miss it, you know.”

“Yeah,” Phainon said. “Yeah, I do.”

They stood there in silence for a while, not speaking, and Phainon’s eyes felt wet for far longer than they should have. After a while, he broke the silence.

“Why can’t things just be simple?”

“I don’t know. Why do people have to die? Why are some people cursed with existences of pain and suffering and others aren’t?” Castorice sighed, resting her chin on her hand. “Ask enough of these questions, and they become pointless. It just…is.”

Phainon knew that. He knew there wasn’t any explanation for the injustice of life, of the unfairness of death, but he still hated it.

Phainon had been alone since he was twelve. That year, his parents were caught in a house fire while he was at school, and Phainon hadn’t learned until after waiting to be picked up for hours in the sweltering heat, the sun beating down upon his back until the school receptionist hurried out to fetch him, hand clutched to her heart.

He’d gone to foster care after that. It wasn’t a particularly pleasant time for Phainon, and he’d spent the next six years bouncing from home to home, school to school as he struggled every day to live a life that had suddenly turned upside down. Not that it had been all sunshine and daisies before, but going from having parents and his own room, however small, to sharing a tiny, cramped bedroom with three other kids made Phainon forget what stability felt like.

Any friendships he made after that time never lasted for long. After a few weeks or months of adjusting to a new school, Phainon would eventually make a hard-earned acquaintance, but any chance of it growing into friendship would fizzle out as Phainon would always be transferred before long. It wasn’t his fault he kept getting put into foster homes already stuffed to the brim, the parents at their wits’ end, but he would always end up bearing the punishment for it. Phainon had never had the greatest relationship with his parents, but he would have taken them back in a heartbeat if he’d had the chance.

Unfortunately, death never considered his own preferences.

Now, standing on a balcony in a city a world away, Phainon considered—what would his life be like if his parents had lived? Would he still be here? Would he be a more well-adjusted person and less of a half-baked, unproofed disaster?

Did it matter?

Since arriving in the beta test, Phainon had met people who had treated him leagues better than he’d even been treated back home. His in-game parents, Cyrene— And now they were gone, too. 

What was the point of dwelling on things like this? It’s not like he could change it. Standing there, Phainon breathed out another long sigh, resting his chin on his hand. 

He was where he was now, in the situation he was in now, and there was no changing any of it at the moment. All he could do was carry on. 

Feeling somewhat comforted, Phainon turned to Castorice. “Thank you,” he said.

“For what?”

“For…sharing with me, I guess. Your story. Do you…” Phainon hesitated, his heart racing. “Do you wanna be friends?”

Castorice gazed at him, a soft smile tugging at the edges of her lips. Then, she placed her hand over her heart.

“I’d love to.”

It had been a childish question, but Phainon’s spirits soared with the innocent display of friendship. He mimicked the gesture, and gave her a little bow before bidding her farewell.

“Goodbye, Lady Castorice.”

“Goodbye, Lord Phainon.”

With Castorice’s sweet voice echoing in his ears, Phainon left Marmoreal Palace, feeling more at peace than he’d felt in a long while. 

Next, he headed to Treasure of Ages. Theodoros was ecstatic at the thought of having more help around the shop, even though Phainon rushed to clarify that he’d have to arrange it around his Chrysos Heir duties.

“Don’t you worry a whit about that,” Theodoros waved him off. “I’ll be grateful for any help you’re willing to give. I’m always knee-deep in new donations, you see.”

They agreed to discuss Phainon’s hours and pay after he received more information about his schedule from Aglaea, and then Theodoros waved him a cheery goodbye as he exited the shop.

With those two things settled… The only thing left on Phainon’s list was figuring out how to trigger his next Main Quest. That brought Phainon to another thing, one he’d left off the list, but had been thinking was another (unfortunately) non-negotiable step on the path of figuring his shit out.

Phainon needed to start trusting the System. 

He took a breath, preparing himself. 

“Hey System?”

Ding!

[Hello, User Phainon. How can the System assist you today?]

Hmm. Phainon had avoided using the System as much as he could since leaving Aedes Elysiae, besides the occasional checking of the time or setting alarms for the morning, not to mention its virtual map. Phainon scrunched up his face, trying to think. How could the System help him? 

“Say, do you have any point notifications for me?”

[While muted, User Phainon has accumulated 100 PP and 105 FP. Would the User like to see more details?]

100 Progression Points? And 105 FP? How had he managed that? When Phainon clicked into the menu to read more, he almost choked on his own saliva.

The bulk of his Progression Point increase had come from completing the tutorial, which had awarded him 10 PP for each of the seven parts—add in the points from the Main Quests he’d already completed, plus a few more from exploration rewards, and boom, Phainon was rolling in PP. 

…He really needed to change that abbreviation.

As for Friendship Points, it seemed that Phainon was not disliked in Okhema at all, despite his recent anxiety-addled thoughts. He had gained points with Aglaea, Hyacine, Cipher and Castorice so far—Castorice had so far the most, with thirty, with Hyacine second at fifteen. Aglaea had five and Cipher sat at a solid two, which sounded about right to Phainon.

But…wasn’t he clearly missing some points? Phainon scrolled further down, eyebrows narrowed in confusion, before he reached the bottom of the list. 

…Ah.

Down at the very bottom, friendship bars greyed out but with their progress lines still faintly visible, were three names—Audata, Hieronymus, and Cyrene. His mother and father’s bars were full, with the lines clearly extending past the bar’s length. Cyrene’s was about eighty percent full—maybe he’d gotten on her nerves while they were packing, Phainon thought somewhat wildly.

The bars stood there, the blue screen blinking faintly at him, and Phainon felt his heart squeeze again like some idiot who never learned to move on. 

Fuck. Phainon tried desperately not to cry, and only barely held it in.

He had earned fifteen points each with his parents before he left, and twenty three from Cyrene.

…That many? From not doing anything at all?

Phainon stared at the screen a while longer, his fingertips grazing the screen. After a while, he forced himself to snap out of it and got back on task.

“System, is there any way to find out what the triggering event is for my next Main Quest?”

To Phainon’s incredible surprise, the System actually had something useful to contribute.

[If the User encounters any difficulties while playing through the Main Story at any time, they may purchase Hints from the Point Shop. Go now?]

Phainon clicked [Yes] and navigated to the Point Shop, browsing through the various buffs and powerups he could buy. There was a Combat Elixir that multiplied his Combat Power by 50 for a few hours on sale for—95 PP? Phainon raised his head to glare at where he guessed the System’s head would be if it had one. 

Wasn’t this daylight robbery?

Putting that aside for now, Phainon also saw lots of different types of stat buffs, inventory expansions—oh, and Hints, on sale for 40 PP each. 

Okay, so not the most exorbitantly priced thing for sale, but it definitely wasn’t cheap. Phainon double checked how much PP he had to spend—120 in total—and cringed at the thought of spending a third of his points for a single hint.

Was it even worth it? Was it going to be one of those bullshit story hints that only gave you the tiniest, merest suggestion of a hint? Then again, Phainon didn’t want to waste any more time waiting for the quest to trigger on its own. Who knew what arbitrary condition it could be hinging on to trigger? 40 Progression Points was a lot, but you couldn’t win the lottery without playing it at least once.

Hoping it was worth it, Phainon bought the Hint.

Immediately, a pop up came on the System interface. 

[User Phainon has received a Hint! Activate now?]

Phainon clicked [Yes], feeling his heart jump in his throat. Across the System’s screen scrolled only a few words. 

[Hint: Buy a teleslate! ^o^]

Phainon stared at those four measly words. 

What.

Chapter End Notes

Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

“Hey, have you heard? The king of Castrum Kremnos has finally gone mad.”

The hushed whisper floated through the quiet library, disturbing the ears of whoever happened to sit nearby. Phainon hadn’t meant to eavesdrop, but the topic caught his interest, and so he kept his ears perked as he studied the pages in front of him.

“What do you mean, “finally?” Last I heard, he’s been mad for years.”

“Yes, but this time he even exiled his own son! Ten years ago, the king would have murdered anyone who dared touch a hair on Mydeimos’ head. Now…”

“Haven’t the Kremnoans have always been like that, though? Harsh, cruel, violent—why are you surprised? They’re barbarians, all of them.”

“You don’t get it—things don’t just happen like this for no reason. What changed?”

What changed? That question lingered in Phainon’s mind long after he left the library, his mind entangled in thought.

After using the Hint, Phainon had bought a teleslate. It was the very device that Hyacine happened to use when she showed him around the city, and happened to be extremely similar to a smartphone. It wasn’t exactly the same—there was no good old World Wide Web, after all—but there were both calling and messaging functions available, as well as a camera. 

Hyacine was astonished to see Phainon pick up how to use the teleslate so quickly. “Are you sure this is your first time using it? Usually it takes people forever to get used to their first teleslate!”

Phainon had to press his lips together to keep them from twitching. “I’m just good with technology, I guess.”

Hyacine had accompanied him to buy it from a girl who turned out not to be a girl at all, but instead a lady who had split herself into a thousand versions of herself but now was reduced to three, red-haired childlike pieces—Tribbie, Trianne, and Trinnon. That earned Phainon an achievement for meeting all the Chrysos Heirs in Okhema, which then triggered Phainon’s next Main Quest.

Which was to recruit Mydeimos, Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos, to the Flame Chase.

Aglaea had briefed Phainon on Kremnos after calling him to her office, including the fact that Mydeimos, after coming of age, had been suddenly exiled from his own kingdom, forbidden to ascend the throne and allowed never to return. Since the briefing, Phainon had had poor luck in gathering information, finding the more he searched, the less he found. 

It seemed Phainon would have to change strategies.

“I want you to go search for Mydeimos.”

Now, Phainon stood in front of Aglaea, hands clasped behind his back. Aglaea had mentioned that this mission would be difficult as no one had much information about Mydeimos, especially now that he had been exiled. Kremnos had been an enigma from the very beginning, and recent events did not help that in the slightest.

In the past, Okhema and Kremnos had been bitter enemies, fighting over both land and resources to fortify their own against the rising threat of the black tide. But that had been far earlier, long before Okhema had become the fortified bastion it was now, and before Kremnos had established itself on one of the countless floating cities in the sky.

Apparently, one used to be able to see Castrum Kremnos from Okhema, a long time ago—but now, the city had drifted farther and farther away as the winds shifted, moving even giant floating rocks along in its current.

And now, Kremnos seemed to mostly exist in stories and fairy tales, with only the slightest whisper of Kremnoan affairs ever making their way to the Holy City—until now. Mydeimos’ exile was clearly a matter of great importance, taking everyone who heard it by surprise. As far as Okhemans knew, King Eurypon doted upon his only son, Mydeimos, and the shattering of expectations by exiling him instead quickly brought the matter to everyone’s attention, capturing the city’s interest by storm.

Now, Phainon was being sent to search for the exiled prince. He had a feeling this mission was going to be a lot more hands-on than he was used to. He’d already been feeling in over his head, but he wasn’t the type of person to back down from a challenge. It was just… Searching for Mydeimos was going to be his first real task in this world. Phainon would have to travel alone, survive somehow without getting shanked by the first big bad he came across, and somehow find a lost prince that no one seemed to know anything about.

Phainon wasn’t going to refuse this mission—not like he could, anyway, for the foremost reason that it was a Main Quest, but also because that’s not who he was—but he didn’t have to like it. 

Something told him that this quest was going to take a while.

Not two days later, Phainon was regretting ever taking on this godsforsaken mission. He should have refused, should have found a loophole or something. Surely he could have found a way to search for Mydeimos while in Okhema? At the very least, he could have paid someone else to go find him, what with the massive salary he now had.

Traveling was exhausting. Phainon had set out from Okhema with a rucksack on his back and an (albeit forced) positive mindset, which had quickly faded as the day went on. Aglaea had recommended he start with visiting the outlying villages of Okhema to gather information, and to see if anyone had heard anything about the exiled prince’s whereabouts. Phainon had already been to two, and no one had been able to tell him anything he hadn’t already known. 

I don’t know anything about that damned prince. 

Kremnos? What’s that?

Crown prince, huh? Never heard of him.

No, I haven’t heard anything.

By the end of the second day, Phainon had had it. The first night, he’d slept in an inn in the village, struggling to sleep amidst the smell of livestock and the hay tickling his nose. He’d meant to spend the second night in another inn, but on the way to the planned third village he’d somehow taken a wrong turn—or maybe the map was wrong somehow—and he found himself in a forest instead, watching the sun set through the trees with a shiver running through his bones.

Guess he’d be camping tonight.

After trying and failing several times to start a fire, Phainon gave up, pulling out the sleeping mat he’d packed just in case and curling up against a knotted tree, shivering. He was exhausted. Although he’d traveled through the wilderness once already since arriving in the beta test, he hadn’t entirely been in his right mind then. Now, of (relatively) sound mind and body, Phainon was reminded of just how harsh traveling could be. With the sky darkening into blues and blacks, the Dawn Device no longer visible in the distance, Phainon tried not to think of the chances of him freezing to death.

Instead, he thought of Mydeimos.

Mydeimos was the key to him escaping this world, to returning home—Phainon just had to find him, first. Phainon fell asleep to thoughts of exiled princes, mad kings and the scent of blood.

Phainon awoke to someone standing over him, their shadow falling imposingly across Phainon’s face. 

“How is it that I keep finding you in situations like this?”

Phainon scrambled to his feet. At first he couldn’t place who the voice belonged to, but as he turned his gaze to the other’s face he blinked. 

Golden hair, golden eyes, sharp like a cat. 

“You!”

The stranger from the cottage had his arms crossed upon his chest, staring at Phainon with a glint in his eye. 

“What are you doing here?” Phainon asked, rubbing the sleep from his eyes. 

“Isn’t that something I should be asking?”

Phainon looked around. In the light of day, his surroundings became clearer than they had last night. Giant cypress trees, a dense forest—

And a familiar-looking cottage, nestled between two bent trees, not twenty feet away.

??? Was all Phainon’s mind could produce for a moment. Really? Here, again?

Thankfully, the stranger didn’t actually look upset. His pose looked haughty, but Phainon knew better.

“Ah… Sorry,” he said, scratching his head. A few leaves fell to the ground at the movement, and Phainon cringed internally.

The stranger didn’t say anything, but his lips twitched in what Phainon suspected was amusement. He cleared his throat, and the expression vanished.

“A more paranoid man would suspect you of following me.” 

Phainon gawked at him. “Me? You—I don’t even know who you are!”

“Exactly.”

“What is that supposed to mean?”

The stranger narrowed his eyes. “It means, perhaps you were looking for an opportunity to catch me off guard. Rob me, or kill me.”

This conversation was steering wildly off course—not that it had started anywhere to begin with, but this was just too much. “I—no!”

“Then how do you explain showing up at my cottage out of nowhere for the second time?”

“You said this wasn’t your cottage! Besides, wasn’t I the one caught off guard here?” Phainon gestured wildly. “I was literally asleep! How does that make me an assassin?”

The stranger considered Phainon, the sunlight catching on his golden hair. After a moment, he spoke. 

“It seems you’re either a very good liar or extremely terrible at your job.”

“I am neither of tho—” Phainon gritted out, before tossing his hands up in frustration. “Whatever! It doesn’t matter. I need to get moving.”

As if Phainon had actually been isekaied into a Saturday morning cartoon, or perhaps a really, really long and extremely vivid fever dream, his stomach took that moment to make its emptiness known with a growl.

A very, very loud growl.

The stranger stared at him, and then scoffed. “Hmph. If you promise not to kill me, then come inside.”

Without saying anything more, the stranger turned his back and headed back to the cottage, leaving Phainon to stand there in disbelief.

What on earth was up with this man?

Phainon was acutely aware that he did not really have the skills to find himself breakfast. How had he thought this mission would go? Why didn’t he have the foresight to actually, you know, prepare for it? Phainon mentally berated his own stupidity and followed the stranger inside, ears burning in shame.

The last time Phainon had been in this cottage, he had been half out of his mind. To be honest, he didn’t really remember much of it, even though it hadn’t been more than a month ago. Phainon hadn’t been in the business of thinking about things for a while, but even so, the memories of the cottage were less than pleasant, tinged with the acrid tang of rust and death.

All Phainon could remember was that it hadn’t been comfortable being there.

“Do you want anything to drink?”

Phainon shook his head. He still had his flask of water, which he drank from as the stranger poured himself a goblet of something red and thin. Nauseated, Phainon could only think of blood.

“Pomegranate juice,” the stranger said crossly, noticing Phainon’s expression.

“…Ah.”

The stranger sat down at the table, placing a bowl of stew in front of Phainon. Phainon knew he’d been invited in for food, but this turn of events still felt strange.

“Are you sure?” he asked, peering up at the man.

“Just eat.”

Phainon ate. The stew was thick and hearty, warming Phainon’s chest as he swallowed. They ate in silence, the only sound being the clink of their spoons on the bowls. After they’d finished, Phainon sat for a moment, unsure of how to proceed, but thankfully, the stranger beat him to it.

“Now will you tell me what you’re doing here?”

“Oh.” That wasn’t the question Phainon expected. “I’m looking for someone.”

“You? In that state?” The man snorted derisively.

“In what state?” Phainon asked, peeved. What about him screamed bad at living off the land?

“How long were you planning to look for this person? You didn’t bring nearly enough for an extended search.”

“I—” Phainon protested, but found he had no defense. Why hadn’t anyone told him how to prepare for this damned mission?

“You truly would make a terrible thief.”

Phainon glared at him. “What makes you think I would want to be a thief in the first place?”

Ignoring the question, the stranger sat back in his chair, considering Phainon with his arms crossed. “Last time, too…”

“Last time?”

“I thought this last time, but you really didn’t pack enough for traveling at all,” said the man.

Phainon’s heart twisted at the reminder. He said nothing, his pulse pounding heavy in his chest.

“How—” the man stopped, an unreadable expression passing through his features. “What happened? Last time.”

Ah. Now that was the question Phainon had been dreading.

“I, ah…” Phainon broke off. “Was going through something.”

He heard a snort. “Clearly.”

“I…” Phainon didn’t know how much to share, how much he wanted to share. He started with the basics. “I left home for the first time, with my closest friend.” The mere mention of Cyrene still hurt. Would it ever not? “She forgot something, so she went back to get it. By the time I noticed anything was wrong, the village…burned. It was gone—she was gone. So I left, and came here.”

The words burned coming out. Phainon lowered his head, trying to keep his eyes from watering again. He felt like he’d become a broken hose, good at keeping the water from dribbling all over the pavement until the pressure got too high and it would explode in a burst, causing it to leak and the hose to kink.

“Your wound.”

The stranger’s words startled Phainon. “Huh?” he said, looking up, forgetting the warmth beneath his eyelids.

The stranger was looking at Phainon. “Has it healed fully?”

“I—yeah.”

It was silent. Then—

“Let me see it.”

“It’s fine now.”

“Show me.”

“No, seriously—“

“Why are you being so stubborn? Just show it to me.”

“I’m fine!”

The stranger glared at Phainon. “If you didn't want my help, then why did you follow me in here?”

You offered me food! That’s not the same thing! Phainon wanted to yell in exasperation. But seeing the stranger’s features narrowed in intent, Phainon relented. “Fine,” he grumbled, lifting the edge of his shirt. The bandage around his torso had long been removed, leaving only an angry red ridge of skin that was only beginning to scar. 

The stranger got up, making his way to the other side of the cottage, where Phainon could hear faint clinks and the sound of rustling. After a moment, he returned, a small brass container and bandages in hand. 

Phainon watched as the stranger opened the container, a bitter, earthy smell rising from it. The stranger noticed his curious stare. “To prevent infection,” he said, dipping his fingers in and spreading the cool salve on Phainon’s skin. The wound had been large, extending from right above Phainon’s hipbone to the center of his stomach. 

Phainon was both intensely uncomfortable and stuck in a curious trance as the stranger rubbed soothing circles into his skin. He felt like he could hardly breathe, his chest tight until the stranger finally withdrew his fingers, returning only to apply the bandage. When he was done, he tugged Phainon’s shirt back down, and sat back. “There,” he said.

Phainon loosed out a breath. “Thank you.” He felt shaky and a little exposed, which was silly. It was just a bandage.

“The black tide leaves nothing unconquered.”

“…What?”

The stranger had been looking down, recapping the salve, but looked into Phainon’s eyes at the question. “Your home is not the first, nor the last to fall to its might.”

Phainon felt a surge of something well up in his chest. “What do you mean?”

“Countless cities have fallen before the black tide. Mine…” he trailed off for a moment, his eyes far away, before hardening. “Mine has not yet, but it is only a matter of time. I only mean that no matter what you think, you could not have done anything to stop it.”

Phainon’s breath caught in his throat. “I didn’t…”

“No. But you thought it.”

Phainon couldn’t force his words to come out. How had he known? How had the stranger known that Phainon kept himself up at night with countless thoughts of what if, had tortured himself with the thought that he might have been able to stop it, might have been able to save Cyrene, his parents, that everything was his fault—

“You…” Phainon croaked out. He couldn’t finish his question, couldn’t form words, could only wrench his head away from those golden eyes as he struggled to keep tears from filling his vision, from choking his breath from his throat. He stayed like that for a long time, refusing to let the stranger see more than he already had. 

Finally, after what felt like an eternity, he felt stable enough to return his gaze to where it had been, and found the stranger watching him. Phainon didn’t feel like staying any longer in that oppressive atmosphere, so he shakily stood up, pushing his chair away from the low table with a clatter. 

“I—I got to go,” Phainon said, turning his back on the stranger as he headed for the door. “Thank you for the food—”

From behind him, a clear voice rang through the quiet cottage. “You never told me who you’re looking for.”

Phainon turned. The stranger was standing, his sharp features muted by the dim lighting inside the room. Phainon’s sudden departure from the table had disturbed dust motes in the air, causing them to float lazily around the stranger’s face. What little light there was caught on his golden hair, and Phainon just stood there for a moment, listening to the sound of the trees outside as he gazed at the stranger.

“It’s Mydeimos, the crown prince of Kremnos. The person I'm looking for.”

The stranger’s eyes were unreadable in the dim light. “Why?”

“I don’t want to lose another home.”

Okhema wasn’t his home, didn’t feel like one yet, but it could be. Besides needing to find Mydeimos to progress his Main Quests, Phainon felt this answer was also true. Besides, even if it wasn’t his home yet, it was home for countless others—for Hyacine, Aglaea, Castorice, the refugees—

If Mydeimos joined the Flame Chase, he could protect Okhema, keep the Okhemans from ever losing their home again. 

The stranger didn’t answer for a moment. Then, he dipped his head to Phainon, a gesture of respect, of acknowledgement—Phainon couldn’t tell.

“Then I wish you luck on your search.”

Phainon stood there for a moment longer, letting the stranger’s words fall into the empty air. Finally he nodded, glancing back up to look into those sharp eyes.

“Be well, then.” Then, he turned back around and left, closing the wooden door behind him. It didn’t occur to him until well after the sun had peaked in the sky that he’d once again left without asking the stranger’s name.
