Chapter Notes

See the end of the chapter for notes

Mydeimos was everywhere and nowhere all at once. No matter where Phainon looked, he could not find any trace of Mydeimos, and yet news of the crown prince had only grown. Mydeimos was on a quest for support, presumably so he could challenge his father and retake the crown. 

Stories arose from every corner of Amphoreus of Mydeimos arriving in another city to ask for help, only to be denied at every turn—everywhere the crown prince went, he was turned away, but still Mydeimos remained elusive, seeming to disappear once it was known his presence was unwelcome. Phainon had seen neither hide nor hair of the prince through four months of searching.

It didn’t help that at first he didn’t know exactly who he was looking for—news of Kremnos had historically been sparse, and the kingdom had kept its royal court isolated for the last several centuries, save for the king emerging on the sporadic occasion of war. Now, however, things were different. The more cities Mydeimos visited in search of aid, the more solidified a description of the crown prince became—a broad, built warrior with golden hair, with a body tattooed in lines of crimson. 

Phainon was grateful for the knowledge, as it had been difficult searching for a man people only knew by name, but he still had nothing to show for it. Four months of searching, of traveling the wilderness and asking travelers along the road for any news, of trying but failing to make progress on his Main Quest. 

Phainon was exhausted.

In between expeditions, he had taken on more Chrysos Heir duties back in Okhema, which often were mundane things such as attending council meetings and understanding nothing, helping maintain various places around the city, and training with the city guards. The training had been the part that Phainon was most excited for—since his first stint out of the city while looking for Mydeimos, he had realized that he was very much unprepared to be going on (possibly dangerous) expeditions the way he was.

He needed to learn how to survive in Amphoreus by himself very soon, or he would never get the chance to go home.

So Phainon had looked forward to training with the guard, which proved to be a tiring, albeit useful endeavor. His Combat stats already gave him a leg up, so he wasn’t completely starting from scratch, but Phainon relished the opportunity to learn something as cool as sword fighting more in depth.

Training consisted of running, strength training, and sword drills—although Phainon had some sword experience from training on his own in Aedes Elysiae, he was placed with the new recruits.

“No one gets special treatment here,” Meliton, the captain of the guard, said to Phainon with a level gaze. “Not even Chrysos Heirs.”

Phainon was grateful for that—it meant that he would have the chance to actually get accurate feedback on his training. Phainon carved out half of his day to train with the guards, and after a month or so of swinging his heavy greatsword around and running countless laps around the training arena, he felt like he’d actually made some progress.

Meliton watched as Phainon slashed at a training dummy one day, his arms folded loosely over his chest. “Your form’s improved,” he said. “But your aim’s off.”

Phainon glanced over at the captain, a broad grin breaking across his face. “Let me try again,” he said, and did it again, and again until his aim struck true every time and even Meliton had nothing to critique.

His search for Mydeimos meant that Phainon was often out of the city nowadays, usually only spending half of each month in Okhema, but whenever he had the time outside of his duties he liked to spend it with Castorice. They had grown closer ever since that mild afternoon on the balcony, and Phainon found he truly enjoyed spending time with her. They often took walks around the city or hung around the library, speaking in hushed whispers about whatever book Castorice had recommended recently until they were glared at enough to flee to the Garden of Life, where they would laze in the sun and read or talk for hours while petting the chimeras. 

Castorice had become a true friend, something Phainon had been sorely in need of for a long time. Besides Cyrene, the last person he could honestly call a friend had moved away while he was in university back in the real world, leaving him alone and with no one to talk to. Now, hanging around Castorice reminded Phainon how freeing having a friend could be. It was something he hadn’t really realized he was missing, or maybe had forgotten the feeling from so long of not feeling it.

Cipher often joined them, too—apparently she and Castorice were close friends, which had surprised Phainon at first glance. Castorice was reserved and polite, whereas Cipher was impish and teasing, constantly pulling pranks or calling out playful insults whenever she was inclined to. They made an odd pair, but both of them genuinely seemed to like each other and got along well, so Phainon supposed it really didn’t matter in the end.

The past few months had also included another addition to the Flame Chase, another Chrysos Heir—a man named Anaxagoras, a sage from the Grove of Epiphany who had been both Hyacine and Castorice’s teacher at one point, had arrived in the city to aid the Flame Chase. Phainon had returned from one of his expeditions and arrived at Aglaea’s office to discuss his findings when he found him, a short, frail-looking man with long hair the color of jade in a ponytail slung neatly over one shoulder, sitting in Aglaea’s chair and filing his nails. 

The man’s sharp gaze snapped up to Phainon’s as soon as he entered the office. “You’re not Aglaea,” he said.

“…No.”

The man sighed, an exasperated, long-suffering sound that seemed as if the man was exceedingly tired by the thought of having to confront an unexpected visitor to an office that was not his own. “Can I help you?”

“I was looking for the Lady Goldweaver.”

“Well, as you can see, she isn’t here at the moment,” the man said. 

“…Right.” Phainon didn’t know how to manage this strange situation. Who was this man to be sitting in Aglaea’s seat, to address her so casually? It must be someone close to her, or at least someone of at least the same authority, if not higher. So Phainon left, deciding to return later in hopes of speaking with Aglaea. 

However, it turned out that that man—for it was none other than Anaxagoras, also known as Anaxagoras, the Great Performer, or Anaxagoras, the infamous Blasphemer of Titans, or simply Anaxagoras the Foolish—was only another Chrysos Heir, a sage who dared question the Titans’ authority yet one of Aglaea’s closest confidants. Anaxagoras apparently saw their relationship as that of academic rivals, Aglaea said with a playful glint in her eye, but that was something for another time.

Although Anaxagoras had been invited to the Holy City in order to aid the Flame Chase, he would not be taking on duties such as the ones Phainon found himself doing. Most of the Chrysos Heirs had their own specialty—Hyacine was a skilled healer, and so spent most of her time at the infirmary, while Castorice took on administrative duties with her sharp eye for detail. As the bearer of Passage, Tribios assisted in managing transportation and communication throughout the city, while Cipher…didn’t really have a lot of duties aside from attending meetings and helping out around the city, but she mostly skipped out on those and pulled little, but ultimately harmless pranks instead. Phainon’s specialty had yet to be discovered, but for now he and Aglaea decided he would focus on honing his combat capabilities, and would participate in meetings and general support duties in the meantime.

Anaxagoras—Phainon really didn’t want to have to keep using that unreasonably long name, even in his head… Maybe he’d just call the professor Anaxa instead. He’d just have to be careful not to use that nickname to Anaxa’s face—the professor was extremely particular about his name, demanding everyone call him by his full name at all times, no matter how unwieldy that name was.

In any case, Anaxa’s specialty was academic in nature—although he had little faith in the Titans and the Flame Chase as a whole, he was still deeply moved by academic opportunities, and seemed very excited to debate abstract academic theories with his students. Phainon knew this fact because he had suddenly become one of Anaxa’s students; after their encounter in Aglaea’s office, Anaxagoras had informed Aglaea that he would be conducting a lecture series effective immediately, and that every Chrysos Heir must attend by virtue of needing more academic stimulation. Apparently, Phainon’s mumbling countenance had not inspired hope in Anaxa for the future of the Flame Chase Journey, so now they would all be subjected to surely boring, droning lectures about the most boring subjects known to man.

Except that Anaxa’s lectures were actually really interesting—Phainon had grudgingly arrived at the first one, expecting to spend the next several hours zoning out into space, but Anaxa had immediately begun that lecture with the question of What is the nature of truth, and the atmosphere in the amphitheater was immediately astir, with everyone raising their hand to voice their opinion, and Phainon was hooked.

As the weekly lectures continued, one turning into two, and then three and four and on and on, it became clear that Anaxa taught through debate, valuing the strength of his students’ convictions and encouraging independent thought. He did not care whether students disagreed with him, only that they had the clarity of mind to follow through with their argument, and would admonish those whose arguments fell apart upon opening their mouths. Many Okhemans attended these lectures, and although Phainon and the others had been required to attend, none of them (except Cipher, but only on occasion) skipped a single lecture. 

Through these lectures, Phainon learned more and more about this world within a game. So many of the citizens had complex and differing thoughts, which surprised Phainon more than he’d expected, after living in the beta test for almost five months. He’d expected a lot of the points raised to be more…elementary, or at least less fleshed out in their complexity. This realization, as surprising as it was, reminded Phainon to be less ready to underestimate his surroundings. 

No matter how “fake” this world may be, it was real in the eyes of its people. Phainon vowed not to forget that again.

The lectures were also very useful in gathering information about the world at large, particularly regarding the history of Amphoreus and its current state of affairs. Phainon listened as the participants discussed how Okhema had become the Holy City, how Styxia had fallen victim to the raging tides, how Aidonia had been besieged by the black tide and then buried under the endless falling snow. It was a lot to take in, and Phainon struggled to keep it all straight in his head, but slowly it became easier to understand, and after a while Phainon felt he finally had a grasp of Amphoreus as a whole.

The impatience Phainon felt with every unsuccessful mission in search of Mydeimos was lessened when he had other things to focus on—training with the city guard, attending Anaxa’s lectures, spending time with Castorice… And just like that, four months passed in a blink of an eye.

In the fifth month of Phainon’s time in the beta test, he finally got a lead on Mydeimos.

Over the past few months of searching for Mydeimos, Phainon had asked every village he visited to send him a letter if they heard any news of the Kremnoan’s location. He investigated every lead he was sent, but he would always get there too late, with only campfire ashes to mark where Mydeimos and his supporters had been.

This time, though, was a true lead. Phainon felt his heart race as he read the most recent letter, sent from a village half a week’s journey south of Okhema. 

There’s been talk that Mydeimos will go to Tretos in the coming weeks. I don’t know how true it is, but this news came from someone who used to travel to Kremnos frequently, and says he has connections within the Kremnoan detachment. I wish you luck.

It was a lead, the biggest and most promising one yet. Phainon wasted no time in preparing to leave.

The road to Tretos was long, with Phainon often having to dismount his horse and walk, the road winding through the mountains with a path so narrow Phainon feared he’d trip and fall off the side and into the nearby ravine. Luckily, that part of the journey only lasted a day, and he was able to set up camp on the other side of the mountain in a forest clearing, munching on the trail snacks he’d bought along the way.

Since his first mission, Phainon had learned a lot about how to survive in the wild. Now he knew how much he needed to pack if traveling for a week or two, how much clothes and food and water he’d realistically need, and how to find shelter if the weather turned nasty. Sure, he still overpacked once in a while, and once he’d accidentally bought dromas food instead of his normal trail snacks (in his defense, the shopkeeper never said it was dromas food, only looked at him strangely when Phainon said he was excited to try all the flavors of the snack bar he bought), but Phainon was still alive. That was enough for him at the moment.

On the fourth day of traveling, Phainon was getting anxious. What if his intel was wrong? What if he didn’t find the detachment? What if he got to Tretos only to be told he’d missed Mydeimos by an hour, a day, a week?

What if Phainon never found him?

Before his thoughts had any chance to spiral further, he heard a commotion from off the road, deeper into the forest. Phainon spurred his horse in the direction of the sound, pulse thrumming with anticipation. 

The source of the commotion quickly became clear—it was an ambush. Several people were huddled against a cliffside in one corner of the clearing, all paths of escape blocked by monstrous figures of black and muddled gold.

Titankin—the black tide.

Phainon leapt into action. “Stay back!” he yelled to the group of people, hacking his greatsword at the nearest Titankin, taking it by surprise and dissolving it into golden dust. He cleaved through several of them before they had the mind to return his blows, turning their focus away from the others and solely onto him. 

A Titankin slashed at him, but Phainon dodged, leaping to the side to stab his sword into its stomach. Another came barreling at him, raising its weapon above its head, and he struck first, black blood and golden dust exploding onto him. 

“Look out!”

Phainon looked behind him only to see one raise a bow—since when did the black tide use bows—and managed to dive out of the way just in time, an arrow whooshing through the empty air above him. After a while of fighting and dodging, Phainon had eventually wiped out the ambushing monsters. He stopped to catch his breath, his chest heaving.

The people that had been huddled against the cliffside slowly returned to the center of the clearing, staring at Phainon. Phainon glanced at them—he hadn’t had the chance to notice before, but now he saw it was four men, all wearing red uniforms with gold insignias, with some carrying brass helmets under their arms—soldiers, Phainon thought to himself.

He opened his mouth to ask if they were all right, but one of them beat him to the punch.

“You’re an Okheman,” one of the men spat. Phainon looked down. His clothes were his normal travel wear, but it seemed like everything he owned now were in shades of blue and gold, reminiscent of Okhema’s standard.

“I am,” Phainon said. “Is that a problem?”

“Of course—” the man began, but another stopped him, his hand moving in front of his comrade’s chest. 

“It’s not,” the second man said. “You saved our lives. For that,” he said, shooting a look at the first man, “we should be grateful.”

“What happened?” 

“An ambush. We were taken by surprise,” the second man said, gesturing to a pile of weapons and supplies on the other side of the clearing, “and had no way to fight back. A shameful mistake.”

A thought had been forming in Phainon’s head as soon as he’d noticed the soldiers—the uniforms of red, the hostility they bore for Okhema—

“You’re from the Kremnoan detachment.”

It wasn’t a question. Phainon knew it as soon as he said the words out loud, but the reactions from the soldiers confirmed it. The hostile one glared at Phainon, while the other one who’d spoken stiffened, his eyes hardening, while the other two remained silent. Phainon could see their fingers twitching, though, and clarified.

“I don’t mean any harm. I just want to meet with your leader.”

“An Okheman? Meet with the prince?” scoffed the hostile soldier. “As if we’d—”

“Quiet, Damasos,” the other one hissed. “He saved our lives. It’s the least we can do.” Turning to Phainon, he nodded, ignoring Damasos’ angry glare. “We’ll take you to him.”

Phainon led his horse by the reins as he followed the soldiers. It was nearly half an hour later when they finally arrived at a large camp outside the forest, coils of campfires and the tops of white tents visible in the distance. The soldiers led Phainon through the camp, where he was stared at with a mix of curiosity and hostility as the Kremnoans noted the blue of his tunic, the gold thread of his traveling cloak.

They arrived at the center of camp, a huge bonfire marking its position. The kinder soldier turned to a boy sitting beside the fire and said something, which made the boy leap up and run off deeper into the camp. It wasn’t long before the boy returned with an older man with greying hair, his face weathered with age and littered with scars.

“Thank you, Kosmas,” the man said to the kinder soldier. “You’re dismissed.”

With that, the soldiers departed, with only Damasos shooting a look over his shoulder to stare at Phainon before he disappeared around a corner. Phainon held his gaze for a moment, and then returned it to look at the older man.

“I am Krateros, second in command of this detachment.” The man placed a hand over his heart and gave Phainon a slight bow of his head. He straightened and affixed Phainon with a piercing look. “But who are you?”

“I am Phainon, from Okhema, here on behalf of the Flame Chase Journey,” said Phainon. Krateros’ eyes narrowed. 

“What would an Okheman want with the Crown Prince of Kremnos?”

“I…The Goldweaver wants him to join the Flame Chase, so we might have a chance to repel the black tide before it takes Okhema too.”

Krateros considered Phainon for a moment. “What makes you think the prince would want to help you?”

Phainon had considered this point during his search and could not come up with a definitive answer, one he knew could convince anyone to join his cause. However—

“Mydeimos is said to be just and righteous. If he pledges himself to the Flame Chase, Okhema would offer something of equal value in return for his support.”

“Equal value…” Krateros paused. “What could be of equal value to a prince’s aid?”

To that, Phainon had no response. Krateros waved him off.

“No matter. Let us walk around while we await Mydeimos’ return.”

So Mydeimos has already left for Tretos, thought Phainon. He had been so close to losing the detachment, but luck had been on his side this time. Phainon decided to trust it and hurried after Krateros, who had started walking before him.

As they wandered through the mass of tents, Phainon took it all in with a sense of awe, watching soldiers clad in crimson hurry through the camp. He turned to Krateros. “How long did it take for you to gather all these troops?”

“Four months. Of course, there were those who have been here from the beginning,” Krateros added. “But most of them have come slowly, one by one. It’s been a fight to get anyone to join our cause.”

Four months since Mydeimos was exiled, four months of nonstop gathering troops and begging for support… Phainon couldn’t imagine it.

“It’s impressive,” he admitted. “Though you started small, you’ve amassed such a great force.”

Krateros snorted. “Great force? You should see the armies of Kremnos—this is nothing compared to the royal cavalry. Like this, we don’t stand a chance.”

Somewhere on the edges of the camp, a horn blew. 

“Well,” Krateros said. “We wouldn’t, if not for Mydeimos.”

The sound of horses galloping echoed through the camp. Phainon turned, following the noise, and saw a small troop making their way to the center of camp, where he and Krateros stood. From that distance, the leader’s features were too hazy to make out, but Phainon caught little details as the horses thundered closer.

A flash of golden hair, a brush of crimson.

Phainon’s mouth went dry.

The horses stopped right in front of them, and the leader dismounted his horse with singular authority, without a flourish or hint of pomp to be seen.

“You,” Phainon said.

Mydeimos stood before him, his figure as if shaped from bronze, golden hair and eyes reminiscent of the setting sun. Crimson tattoos swirled across his entire body, his bare chest adorned in brass necklaces. His cloak and armor were all shades of red and gold—symbols of the Kremnoan royal family, an homage to spilling blood in pursuit of eternal glory.

It was the stranger from the cottage, the one who had saved Phainon’s life, the one whose sharp eyes still visited Phainon’s dreams to that day.

The stranger was no other than Mydeimos, crown prince of Castrum Kremnos.

Chapter Notes

hi so um. sorry for this chapter being *checks notes* three weeks late, i lowkey have been going through it but we’re here!! we’re back now!! anywho this chapter is a little shorter than normal, but i hope you enjoy :)

“You,” Phainon said.

Mydeimos regarded Phainon. “Yes.” He made no motion to acknowledge that he remembered Phainon, that Phainon knew of his deception, but Phainon could see the recognition in his eyes, in the angle of his shoulders.

Mydeimos had known Phainon was looking for him the last time they’d met and had said nothing. Phainon stared at him. 

Was he angry by Mydeimos’ deception? Phainon didn’t know.

Mydeimos regarded Phainon a while longer, and then turned to Krateros. “Teacher, I’ve returned.”

“Any luck?”

“Not this time,” Mydeimos grimaced. “They refused, saying they couldn’t turn their backs on my father after all he’s done for them.”

Krateros’ face darkened. “Hmph. Have they forgotten he let them starve when they begged for his help against the black tide? Just because he favors Tretos now… Pah.” With that, Krateros squeezed Mydeimos’ shoulder. “It’s good you’ve returned.” 

Releasing Mydeimos, Krateros turned to Phainon. “I’ll leave you two be.” Then he walked off, leaving Phainon on his own with Mydeimos.

While they were talking, Phainon’s blood had begun to curdle in his veins. “Why didn’t you say anything? Back at the cottage.”

Mydeimos’ gaze was unreadable. “Let us speak somewhere else.”

Phainon followed Mydeimos to a large tent near the front of the camp, not far from where the troop had dismounted. Mydeimos lifted the tent flap and stepped through, holding open for Phainon to follow behind. The interior was sparsely decorated, with a worn cot in the corner and a small table with several chairs surrounding it in the center of the tent. 

Mydeimos sat down on one of the chairs. When Phainon didn’t immediately follow suit, he nodded his head in the direction of the other chair. Phainon sat, glaring at the other. When Mydeimos didn’t speak, Phainon broke the silence.

“You lied to me.”

“I never lied to you.”

“I told you I was looking for the crown prince of Kremnos, and you said nothing.”

“Has the definition of lying changed since I went to school?”

Phainon glared at Mydeimos. “You’re being obtuse.”

“I was in hiding,” Mydeimos said with thinly veiled irritation. “What makes you think I would reveal my identity to an Okheman, of all people?”

Phainon said nothing to that. Of course Mydeimos wouldn’t want to reveal his identity to a random stranger, much less one who belonged to his homeland’s ancient enemy. But when Phainon thought of how Mydeimos had saved his life and nursed Phainon back to health for three days after Phainon escaped the wreckage of Aedes Elysiae—

I just thought…

Nothing. He had thought nothing. Mydeimos was right. Who would trust a random stranger who had arrived at their doorstep not once, but twice? Not only that, but what was a person to do when said stranger just so happened to be looking for them the whole time? Phainon had to admit how fishy it looked.

But…for all of Phainon’s searching these last four months, trekking across nearly half the continent, trusting no one and suspecting everyone, how had Mydeimos slipped under his nose?

Indeed, the man sitting across from Phainon now looked like the very picture of nobility—the golden jewelry, haughty attitude, clothing made from fine fabrics that surely cost more than Phainon’s annual income. But the man Phainon had met in the forest had been different—yes, the person was the same, but something underneath had been lighter, perhaps, or freer.

Whatever it was, it made Phainon look like a fool.

Something else had changed about Mydeimos’ appearance—the addition of crimson tattoos curling upon bare expanses of skin, covering nearly his entire upper body. Phainon couldn’t keep himself from staring. Crimson whorls dissolved into golden skin, making Phainon feel lightheaded.

“Spacing off already?” The sound of Mydeimos’ voice broke Phainon’s trance, and Phainon straightened. 

“Ah,” he said, clearing his throat. “I suppose I wouldn’t trust me in that situation either. But in any case, I’ve found you now. I’ve come to offer you a proposition.”

Mydeimos glanced askance at Phainon. “You? A proposition? Who are you to approach me in that way?”

“I am…” Phainon faltered, only now realizing that Mydeimos still did not know his name. “I am Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, here on behalf of Lady Aglaea of Okhema.”

“The Goldweaver?”

“Yes. She… We would like to invite you to join the Flame Chase Journey, to protect Amphoreus against the black tide.”

Mydeimos said nothing for a moment, his features undecipherable in the dim light of the tent. Then, he spoke. “Why?”

“…Why?”

“Why me?”

Phainon didn’t know what answer Mydeimos wanted to hear, so he settled for the truth. “Although Kremnos and Okhema have not been close in the past, Okhema has seen how Kremnos has made a name for itself on its strength and power. The black tide has become too strong for any one city to handle by itself, whether that be Okhema or Castrum Kremnos. But if we joined forces, we could handle it together.”

Mydeimos considered Phainon’s words, tracing the base of his cup with his gauntleted fingers. Then—

“No.”

Phainon stared at him. “What?”

“I will not join the Flame Chase.”

Stunned, Phainon could say nothing. He hadn’t counted on denial.

“If you need assistance in reclaiming your throne—”

“No,” Mydeimos said again. “This is something I need to do with my own strength. Only by rallying my people myself will I be worthy to reclaim my place in Kremnos. I do not need your Lady Goldweaver pulling the strings in order to triumph. The duty,” Mydeimos’ grip on his cup grew tight, “of repelling the black tide has always historically belonged to Kremnos. To forsake that duty would mean to forsake the values that uphold Kremnos itself.”

Phainon understood. He really, truly understood. However, this was his only option—only through Mydeimos joining the Flame Chase could he return home. 

But…

Mydeimos, exiled from his own home, was in the same position as Phainon. They stood opposite of each other, clad in the colors and emblems of each other’s enemy, but they were both fighting for the same thing—the chance to return home. If their positions had been switched, wouldn’t Phainon be trying to do the exact same thing? 

Relying on one’s own strength was something Phainon was intimately familiar with. It was an innate need, a selfish desire to prove oneself—a declaration that if something was not done out of one’s own strength, it was not worth doing at all.

Sitting there, in a small tent in the middle of a war party, Phainon had no choice but to accept defeat.

“All right.”

Mydeimos paused. “All right?”

“I will accept your answer for now. But you must promise me something in return.”

Golden eyes narrowed. “And what would you ask of me?”

“When you are finished, when you have reclaimed your throne, you must come to Okhema.”

Mydeimos scoffed. “You would have the gall to ask something like this, after I have refused you?”

“It would be an exchange—when you have accomplished your goal, come to Okhema, and the Lady Goldweaver will offer you anything you desire in return.”

Aglaea had prepared Phainon for the possibility that Mydeimos would ask for something in return, but he definitely had not been given the okay to hand over a blank check. Aglaea was too shrewd to offer something as valuable as this, and would never have allowed Phainon to suggest it if she’d known—he was originally supposed to have Mydeimos negotiate his terms with Aglaea herself.

However, Aglaea was not here now, and Phainon was determined to do whatever it took to gain Mydeimos’ trust. If Mydeimos could not join the Flame Chase now, then Phainon would convince Mydeimos to join as soon as the chains holding him back had been broken.

“Why would I trust you?”

“I—” Phainon stopped, and then fumbled around in the satchel he’d brought along with him. His pack was strapped to his horse, but the satchel he wore across his chest held all of his important items. His money purse, the letter from his parents, and—

Something fell out of his satchel as he rummaged through it, landing on the floor beside the low table. Before Phainon could retrieve it, Mydeimos leaned over and picked it up, turning the item over in his hands as he stared at it.

““…The Deliverer?””

It was the Deliverer card, the one Phainon had carried with him from the wreckage of Aedes Elysiae. Since finding his parents’ letter in Cyrene’s pack all those months ago, Phainon had kept both the letter and the card enclosed together on his person at all times, as if keeping it close to him would keep the memories from leaving too.

“It’s nothing,” Phainon snatched the card back, slipping it back into his parents’ letter where it belonged. “I was looking for this.”

The last thing he kept in his satchel was a golden badge, a small round piece of brass emblazoned with Kephale’s symbol, the symbol of the Flame Chase. Aglaea had given it to him upon joining the Flame Chase, and only those belonging to the Flame Chase had one. 

“If you show this to anyone in Okhema, they will know you can be trusted.”

Mydeimos gazed at the badge. “What if I never return it?”

“I doubt you would do that,” said Phainon. “Because you don’t seem to be the type of person to ignore favors.”

“How would you—” Mydeimos started and then stopped, irritation flashing across his face. “Why are you so—”

He did not finish his sentence, only glowered at the badge on the table in front of him. After a few more moments of consideration, Mydeimos raised his head to look Phainon directly in the eye.

“All right. I accept your proposition.”

Phainon opened his mouth to say something, but Mydeimos interrupted him. “—But you must promise that you will grant whatever request I ask of you when I arrive.”

“I promise,” Phainon said, willing his tone to reflect the depth of his honesty. “You will have whatever you ask for.”

Mydeimos did not remove his gaze from Phainon’s. “Then, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, I will hold you to your word.”

In the corner of Phainon’s eye, the System appeared with a new message scrolling across the screen. 

[Main Mission Updated: Await Mydeimos’ arrival in Okhema.]

The memory of those golden eyes followed Phainon the rest of his journey back to Okhema, through forests and mountains and cold nights. The closer Phainon got to the Dawn Device on the horizon, the more fortified his heart became. 

Mydeimos was going to join the Flame Chase. 

Phainon was one step closer to returning home.

Aglaea did not express her dislike of Phainon’s plan to his face, but he could tell through the glint in her eyes that his offer to Mydeimos was not something she was eager to fulfill. Luckily, he managed to escape a lecture, given that Anaxa barged in right after Phainon had finished his debriefing, insisting on discussing something with Aglaea right away, something about an important research breakthrough he’d had which, no, could not wait another minute.

Phainon was dismissed with a tired look from Aglaea, not even she possessing the power to deny Anaxa the opportunity to talk about his research. Phainon nearly skipped out of Marmoreal Palace, very aware the only reason he’d avoided Aglaea’s ire was due to Anaxa’s unfortunate timing, but determined not to let the vision of her wrath dampen his mood.

He was one step closer to completing his Main Quests—one step closer to going home.

Phainon could have cheered. 

It had been almost a week since his departure for Tretos, and he was itching to see his friends. Castorice was bound to be in the library at this time of day, so Phainon headed there next, his sandals whisking lightly upon the pavement as he fought to keep his excitement in check.

Phainon had cut through a small alley on his way to the library, but as he turned a corner heading towards the main street he bumped into someone, causing him to stumble to keep his balance.

“What are you doing?” the person snarled.

Phainon rushed to apologize. “I’m so sorry, are you—”

“You’re going to ruin everything.”

Phainon’s words died in his throat. “...What?”

The person he’d bumped into was tall, clad in a heavy cloak that covered him from head to toe, obscuring his face, but his voice was deep and masculine.

“You weren’t supposed to meet him until later. It’s all out of order. How did you fuck things up this badly?”

The person stepped into Phainon’s space threateningly, and Phainon’s back hit stone. His breath caught in his throat—what the fuck was happening? His hand inched to his belt, where he’d stashed a dagger for protective measures, but the man didn’t seem to care. 

“Get your act together,” he hissed in Phainon’s face, his breath hot. “Or it’ll be—”

The sound of laughter came from the main street not far from where they stood, as if someone was about to witness their compromising position, and the man jerked back. “Fuck. Just—fix this,” he spat.

Without another word, he turned to leave, not sparing Phainon another glance. 

Wits returning in a burst, Phainon rushed after him, turning the corner. 

“Wait—”

But the figure was gone, disappeared as if he’d never been there in the first place.

…What the fuck?

“Phainon!” Castorice’s eyes lit up as he plopped down into the seat opposite her, her features bright with surprise. “You’re back… Are you all right?”

At Castorice’s concerned tone, Phainon turned his gaze over to her, and blinked. “Yeah, I… It’s nothing.”

Clearly doubtful but too kind to say anything, Castorice let Phainon’s excuse slide over her, instead changing the subject. “How was your mission?”

“It went well,” Phainon said, and then filled her in on his deal with Mydeimos, omitting the part that revealed he’d actually met the exiled prince not once, but twice before. That part of Phainon’s pride was still sore, so he skillfully evaded any mention of their previous meetings. Castorice hummed in approval at his recounting of events, even though her eyes widened at the part where Phainon admitted to handing away a carte blanche to a potential ruler of one of Okhema’s oldest enemies.

“How did Aglaea take it?”

“She didn’t yell at me, but that’s only because Anaxa didn’t give her the chance.”

Castorice giggled. “It sounds like everything turned out for the best, though. Good job, Phainon,” she said, her eyes curving upwards as she smiled. “You did it!”

“You’re going to ruin everything.”

The man’s voice from earlier popped back into Phainon’s mind, throwing his mental state off balance.

What the fuck had he meant?

What was Phainon about to ruin?

The more Phainon racked his brain, the less answers he could come up with. The man’s words made absolutely no sense, and so Phainon dismissed them as the ravings of a madman. Whatever the man was talking about didn’t have anything to do with him, or else Phainon would know. 

Right?

Chapter End Notes

Chapter Notes

please forgive me for the late update ;; i’ve had a pretty busy month, but i’m back to some semblance of a routine!! in return please accept this monster of a chapter as an offering

See the end of the chapter for more notes

Mydeimos had been preparing for this moment since before he’d been exiled. Standing in the arena now, facing the mottled figure of what was once his father, disfigured by disease and hate alike, he still felt as if he wasn’t ready for this.

It didn’t matter whether he was ready or not, he thought as he twisted his gauntlets. He was still going to have to take this accursed dynasty down with his own hands.

It didn’t matter whether he felt a rip in his chest as he sliced his father’s head clean off his body, he thought. It didn’t matter whether the sight of his own blood, now glowing golden beneath his tattoos, made him remember sunny afternoons reading his essays to his father in their favorite courtyard, the sun streaming through the stones and illuminating his father’s face, lit up with joy and pride.

It didn’t matter. It wasn’t as if he could go back.

After it was done, Mydeimos cleaned the blood off his gauntlets, wiped the smudges from his shoes. He’d gotten nicked a few times—his father was his first teacher, after all—but the wounds had already closed, leaving nothing but a mixture of dirt and gold upon his skin.

He was alone now, the arena empty of all but the tang of rust and the weight of what he had done.

He was no longer Mydeimos, crown prince of Castrum Kremnos. Now, he had spilt his father’s blood as fate had always intended, fulfilling his destiny to become a mere cog in the neverending wheel of fate and patricide.

Now, not only was he a king-slayer, but a father-slayer as well.

Mydeimos left the arena. The city had looked a little worse for wear when he’d left, just about a year ago now, but now he could clearly see how his father’s neglect had left its mark. The once glorious city, with its shining marble halls and strong walls of stone, was nothing more than a crumbling ruin now. 

Mydeimos could still remember the time where his father had seemed like a great man, a great king. When he was younger, Mydei’s tutors could do nothing but heap praise upon his father, urging Mydei to hurry up and catch up to him, but over time, that had slowed and then stopped altogether as his father’s illness twisted him further and further into madness.

The Castrum Kremnos of today, nothing but aging stone and hardened attitudes, bore no resemblance to that shining city of memory.

Mydeimos took it all in as he walked through the city, the streets empty, its windows shuttered. Once, in the time before his father had devolved into paranoia and greed, these same streets had been lively and bustling, peoples’ faces flushed and rosy. Even despite Kremnos’ thirst for glory, the kingdom had not yet become a single-minded empire focused solely on conquest.

Mydeimos wandered for a long time, not wishing to return to the detachment just yet. They surely would have heard the news of his victory by now, and would be anxiously awaiting his return, eager to heap praises and boasts of his might upon his shoulders. Typically, Mydeimos relished the feeling of camaraderie he shared with his people, glad for the reminder that he wasn’t alone in this. But today, for the first time since the moment he realized his father would never return to that shining, upright figure from his childhood, Mydei wanted to remember.

His father dead by his own hand, the prophecy finally fulfilled. Had victory always been this empty?

It was a long time before Mydeimos finally returned to the detachment where they were camped outside the city walls, the day long passed into night. There were still many people milling about and huddled around campfires, cheerfully sharing stories of their own conquests, and they cheered as Mydeimos passed them and headed deeper into the camp.

Krateros was waiting for him outside his tent, and his piercing gaze seemed to pass through Mydeimos as he approached. But he said nothing of Mydeimos’ state, only bowing his head to acknowledge his return.

“Welcome back.”

“Thank you, Krateros,” Mydeimos exhaled. He wanted to do nothing more but retreat to his tent and sleep, but there was still a victory feast to be held, one that was bound to be long and loud but had surely been delayed until his return. So he went. And he’d been right—it was a long, boisterous feast, his people loud and elated, for their prince had finally slew the vicious tyrant, the villain king Eurypon.

Now we can return home, his people cried. Now we are free.

Sitting at the head table at the front of the tent, surrounded by his most loyal supporters and his staunchest defenders, Mydeimos recalled the promise he had made to that Okheman all those months ago.

“When you have accomplished your goal, come to Okhema, and the Lady Goldweaver will offer you anything you desire in return.”

What did Mydei desire? Sitting there, the memory of his father’s blood staining his hands, the sound of his peoples’ voices in his ears, Mydei asked himself for the first time. It did not take long for him to arrive at his answer.

His father may have abandoned his people in pursuit of eternal glory, but Mydeimos would not. He would be the one to lead his people back home, back to a place they could thrive—and that place was no longer Castrum Kremnos, too marred by the past and stained in blood, its pervasive reek even following them now, in his peoples’ eyes as they recounted Mydeimos’ victory, as they proclaimed eternal glory for Kremnos.

No, Kremnos had been forsaken long ago. Now, Mydeimos had the choice to lead his people to freedom, show them a life free of bloodied burden.

It was time for Mydeimos to fulfill his promise. 

Phainon had been keeping very busy. Nearly eight months had passed since meeting Mydeimos at Tretos, and he was getting more impatient by the minute. Since getting Mydeimos to promise to come to Okhema after accomplishing his goal, Phainon had buried himself in a mountain of tasks—helping out at Treasure of Ages, patrolling the city and attending Flame Chase meetings, going to Anaxa’s lectures, assisting Hyacine at the infirmary, taking care of the chimeras, helping out at the dromas workshop, and basically taking on every single odd job he could within the city so he wouldn’t have to just sit and wait for Mydeimos to arrive. 

He’d also been keeping an eye out for the hooded man he’d encountered after returning from Tretos, but had seen neither hide nor hair of him since. It prickled Phainon’s skin, remembering that incident, but he had no way of knowing what lay behind those strange words. As the months went on and nothing out of the ordinary happened, Phainon tried to push the incident out of his mind to no avail. The figure’s words still stuck in his mind—

It’s all out of order. Get your act together. You’re going to ruin everything.

And yet, nothing happened.

Through his mad dash of rushing through tasks, Phainon had completed dozens of side quests and racked up a not-insignificant amount of PP. However, since he had yet to find a meaningful way to spend them, they had just been sitting unused in his System bank. At some point they were sure to come in handy, but for now Phainon was just letting them pile up.

An unexpected side effect of running around the city completing side quests happened to be that everyone in Okhema seemed to know him now, and Phainon could hardly walk to the market without being bombarded by aunts and uncles who wanted to make him dinner for helping to find their lost cat, or by friendly shopkeepers who promised a discount for recovering stolen items by street bandits. 

It had been overwhelming at first, the reminder that he had forced his way into a community of people that saw him, that cared for him, but Phainon had gotten used to it. Mostly. There were still some times he felt smothered by all the free things they shoved into his hands, telling him to pocket it and save it for later—valuable and expensive things like brass belt buckles, or a new sheath for his greatsword—

“Timo, for the last time I can’t accept this,” Phainon protested weakly, pushing the pocket timepiece that he was pretty sure was plated with real gold back into her palm. “This is too much!”

“Nonsense! A man needs a good way to track the time, especially one with a fancy job like you!” insisted Timo, pushing the timepiece  right back into his hand. Timo ran the spice stall next to Treasure of Ages, and she had long since taken it upon herself to provide Phainon with everything he could ever need. Which Phainon’s incredibly large salary already took care of, but Timo was notoriously stubborn and refused to accept no for an answer.

“Are you saying you don’t think I could make it to things on time without this?” Phainon said, only half joking as he refused to take the timepiece. “Besides, this is too expensive.”

“What do you mean, too expensive? You’re surrounded by expensive things all the time.”

“I thought you were saving up for a new scale,” Phainon said gently. “I really can’t take this.”

“Pah,” Timo said. “I can still buy things while I save, can’t I? You didn’t let me pay you last time.”

The time Timo was referring to was the time a month ago Phainon helped fix her stall, which had been damaged in a street fight by a drunk pair of men during the night. She couldn’t afford to pay a handyman to fix it, and Phainon had happened upon her when she found it in the morning, muttering curses under her breath as she tried to figure out what to do. She had tried to pay him then, too, but Phainon had refused, since it had only been a quick fix and it wasn’t as if she had hired him in the first place. Ever since then, she had been trying to find ways to pay him back, but every time Phainon refused.

“Besides, the man said no refunds. You take it,” she said, closing Phainon’s fingers over the timepiece, pushing it away from her. “I already have one, so there.”

Phainon was at a loss. It looked like there was no getting out of this now. “All right,” he said. “I’ll take it, but don’t try to pay me back again. I’m pretty sure your scale won’t last much longer.” The scale in question was old and made of cobbled-together metal that Phainon was sure had been stuck together with paste and hope. He was surprised it had lasted this long without affecting Timo’s business—but if she said she was saving, he was sure it would get replaced before long. As much as he nagged her about it, Timo was very frugal and had a keen eye for quality, and never tried to extort her buyers.

“Bah. It’s lasted thirty years, what’s a little longer?” Timo waved him off. 

“Thirty years?” Phainon found it hard to believe the scale, old and corroded as it was, had ever been anything other than a piece of scrap metal.

“It was a wedding gift,” Timo said, her normally severe features softening with the memory. “Basileios bought it after he proposed. He said we’d need good equipment if we were ever to make a living off a street stall.” Her eyes were far away for a moment, lost in thought. 

Phainon had heard of Timo’s husband, Basileios—mostly from other people, as Timo didn’t bring him up often, but everyone knew how difficult it had been for her after his death. He’d been a kind man, who could often be found teaching children to play pentei grammai in the streets, who would take the best scraps of meat from his own plate to give to the stray dogs who lingered around the market at dinnertime.

There had been a plague going around in the lower streets of Okhema years ago, brought in by some refugees fleeing the black tide during that time, and Basileios had taken ill. They were never able to have children, so when Basileios eventually passed away Timo was left all alone, with no one around to help her mind the stall or to braid her hair or to bring her gifts, as her husband had often done. 

Phainon liked Timo. She’d had it rough, but still stubbornly stuck around, unwilling to let her life pass by as she wallowed in grief. She was sharp and witty, her words often cutting, but her hands gentle, and she proved how much she cared through her actions, not words. Seeing her always left Phainon feeling an inexplicable sense of comfort.

“Enough about that,” Timo said suddenly, interrupting Phainon’s train of thought. “I’ve got things to do, so hurry along now.”

“Sheesh, all right,” Phainon grumbled. “It’s not like I asked to be stuck here talking to you.” He couldn’t maintain the facade for long, however, and gave Timo a cheery grin as he waved. “See you later!”

Phainon heard Timo muttering irritably under her breath as he walked away, and stifled a laugh. 

Now, what was next on his list? He’d already swung around Treasure of Ages that day, helping Theodoros with cleaning up some old vases, and didn’t have any official duties scheduled until tomorrow. 

Before Phainon had fully gone through his mental checklist of things to do, his teleslate buzzed in his satchel. It was Tribbie, with a slightly concerning message.

Snowy, you should head to the plaza

There’s something you should see

I would deal with it but I don’t have the time right now

Besides, Agy says it’s your responsibility

…The plaza?

Even before Phainon had arrived at Kephale Plaza, he could hear the sounds of a commotion. He hurried his steps, his chest tightening with the beginnings of anxiety. Before long, he reached the plaza proper and was halted by a large crowd of people, jeering and muttering amongst themselves. It was too loud for Phainon to eavesdrop on any one conversation, so he moved through the crowd, pushing his way to the center of the commotion.

When he finally made his way to the front of the crowd, all he saw was the back of a man, broad and clad in a light traveling cloak, who was currently being confronted by what looked like nearly half a squad of guards.

“What business does one of your kind have in the Holy City?” one of the guards spat. 

“I told you, I have business with the Lady Goldweaver,” a measured voice came out from beneath the cloak.

“The Goldweaver? Bah! As if any of the Chrysos Heirs, much less the Goldweaver, would have anything to do with someone like you.” Phainon’s eyes narrowed. Someone like who? 

The guard continued, seemingly eager to vent his frustrations upon someone beneath him, someone who would not stand up for themself. “The last Kremnoan to step foot in this city was beheaded for being a murderer and a spy—why would I believe you to be any different?”

Phainon’s heart stopped. The last Kremnoan—

“It was a Chrysos Heir that invited me here in the first place. I am here to fulfill a promise I made to both him, and the Flame Chase,” the man said, pulling something out of his bag to show to the guard. The guard choked out a cough.

“How—how did you get that? You must have stolen it, that’s—” 

Phainon had heard enough. Without a second thought, he stepped out of the crowd and towards the cloaked man, who the more Phainon looked at seemed more and more familiar, the curl of golden hair barely visible from behind, the upright posture, the unflappable countenance—

For who else could it be but Mydeimos?

Phainon stopped at Mydeimos’ side, facing the guards. Mydeimos did not look over at Phainon, staring directly at the guards in front of him, still holding out Phainon’s badge that had been given to him all those months ago, but the guards did, expressions flickering with unease and surprise. 

The guard who had been sneering at Mydeimos turned his gaze to Phainon, his hard eyes glinting. “Ah, look who it is, the Goldweaver’s most loyal dog. Here to butt in on something that isn’t your business again, mutt?”

Phainon retorted, “The way I see it, this is my business, as I’m the one who invited this man.”

The guard stared at Phainon, his eyes wide with condescension. “Do you not see who this man is?” he said, gesturing to Mydeimos, who despite wearing a traveler’s cloak and hiding his face was still wearing robes of bright red and gold, betraying his heritage to anyone who glanced at him for longer than a second.

“So what if he’s Kremnoan? This is official Chrysos Heir business,” said Phainon, his voice hardening. “If you have an issue, take it up with Lady Aglaea.” Without another word, he turned to leave, but stopped to look back at Mydeimos. The Kremnoan was looking over at him for the first time, gaze impassive. Phainon raised his eyebrow in question, and Mydeimos nodded, and when Phainon turned to leave, he heard Mydeimos following behind.

The plaza let them pass, the sound of murmuring and muttering all around, but no one stopped them. When finally they left the plaza, heading in the direction of Marmoreal Palace, Phainon slowed his steps so they were walking side by side.

“So,” he said.

“So,” said Mydeimos.

“You’re here, then.”

“Yes.”

“Well,” Phainon said. “I’m glad.”

Mydeimos looked over at him at that, his brows furrowing minutely, but said nothing for a moment. “…Hmmph,” he said finally.

They did not speak again until reaching Aglaea’s office. Unsurprisingly, Aglaea had clearly already heard through her golden threads of Mydeimos’ arrival and was waiting for them when they arrived. She rose from her chair as they entered, crossing to stand in front of her desk. 

“Crown Prince Mydeimos. Welcome,” she said, sharp eyes seeming to pierce through him. 

“Lady Aglaea,” Mydeimos replied in greeting, bowing his head slightly.

“I take it you have succeeded in your mission?”

“Yes,” he said. 

“And may I presume you have come to follow up on your promise?”

“I have,” Mydeimos said, his voice level even as he gazed upon Aglaea, who Phainon had been terrified by (and admittedly still was) the first time he’d met her. But Mydeimos did not show any signs of being intimidated, despite Phainon’s knowledge that Mydeimos had absolutely heard the rumors of the Lady Goldweaver. Instead, Mydeimos looked calm and untouchable.

The conversation moved on, with the two of them discussing logistics of Mydeimos’ role in the Flame Chase for a while, until the discussion finally moved to what Phainon had been wondering about for the past eight months.

“And what would you ask of me?” Aglaea asked. “As promised, in return for your service to the Flame Chase Journey, you may ask for whatever you desire.” Phainon felt her sharp gaze slide over to him, and he shivered.

“That…” Mydeimos hesitated, something passing over his face momentarily, but then he straightened, the expression gone as fast as it had appeared. “I would ask for the protection of my people in Okhema.”

Aglaea said nothing for a moment, and then made a small hum of amusement. “I said I would offer anything, and you choose this?”

“Yes.” Mydeimos’ answer was firm, resolute.

“Others would kill to be on the receiving side of this offer. You could ask for control over Okhema’s military, or access to the city vaults. Riches or glory or power are up for the taking, and yet you ask for our protection?” 

None of Aglaea’s outlandish offers seemed to sway Mydeimos. “Yes,” he said again. 

“Why?” The words were out of Phainon’s mouth before he could stop them. 

Mydeimos glanced over at him, the line of his jaw determined. “Because it is time for Kremnos to find a new path. My father—” the word seemed to falter coming out of Mydeimos’ mouth—“lost himself in his quest for glory, and the whole of Amphoreus has suffered for it. The black tide is a threat that cannot be stopped by one city alone, and Kremnos does not have the strength it had in the past. Kremnos needs to learn that it cannot rely on itself any longer. We need the support of Okhema, and Okhema needs the might of Kremnos.”

Phainon stared at Mydeimos. That was what Phainon had said to him, right before Mydeimos had originally refused his offer.

Mydeimos continued. “I would not ask for anything else. My people need to learn to rely on others, and break free from the hatred that runs through their veins, or else they will burn themselves to ashes before the black tide ever gets the chance. That is my answer.”

At that, Phainon sat back. Aglaea was silent, seemingly considering for a moment, and then finally answered. 

“Well, then. I accept your terms.”

Phainon did not leave Marmoreal Palace immediately after they were dismissed; instead he waited for Mydeimos, who exited Aglaea’s office not long after he did. The Kremnoan did not look surprised to see him waiting, only giving him a cursory glance as he stopped in front of where Phainon leaned against the wall.

“…What?”

“Hungry?”

Mydeimos stared at Phainon, slight disbelief crossing his face. Phainon snorted. “You don’t have to look at me like that. Come on, I’ll treat you to some food.”

“I’m not hungry,” came the reply. Phainon leveled a look at the other. 

“Yeah, and my mom’s a turkey. Just—come on.”

“…What’s a turkey?”

Phainon had already turned and started walking, so he used the fact that Mydeimos couldn’t see his face to avoid answering the question. How was he supposed to answer that? Oh, turkeys are a bird back from where I’m from. Oh, they don’t have turkeys in Ancient Greece? Whoops.

It was easier to just ignore the question, so he did. 

To Phainon’s surprise, Mydeimos followed him all the way to the market, where Phainon gestured broadly to the clusters of stalls before them, all selling their own specialties. 

“Take your pick,” said Phainon, feeling rather magnanimous. He’d mooched off Mydeimos more than a few times and was aching for the chance to pay him back. The least he could do was let Mydeimos choose what they had for dinner. 

Mydeimos seemed a little lost for words for a moment, his jaw working as he took in the sight. The market had not yet filled up, the hour still being a little early for dinner, but the few people milling about still looked at the two of them with distrust in their eyes, clearly having seen the crimson and gold of Mydeimos’ clothes beneath his cloak.

Mydeimos ignored them, saying finally, “Porridge.”

“…Porridge?”

“Yes.”

Phainon didn’t question it, having given Mydeimos full authority in this matter, but he looked askance at him before replying. “All right, then.”

The stares did not lessen as they made their way to the stall and ordered, nor did they lessen as they sat down to eat. Rather, they had gotten stronger, the market filling out as Phainon spooned barley porridge into his mouth. It was plain, seasoned only with olive oil and salt, but still filling. Phainon had expected Mydeimos’ tastes to be a little more…extravagant, to say the least. 

But then he remembered the food they’d eaten in the woods. Lentil soup, lamb stew, figs with fruit and honey… He’d thought the food had been simple because of the whole being out in the woods thing, but maybe Mydeimos just preferred simpler food. Phainon glanced over at him. Mydeimos was staring into his porridge, spoon in hand, jaw clenched.

“What is it?” Phainon asked quietly.

Mydeimos didn’t answer for a moment. “…It’s different,” he said finally.

“Different? How—oh.” It hit Phainon then, all of a sudden. Mydeimos’ unease, his reluctance to eat. 

Mydeimos was missing home.

“You don’t have to finish it,” Phainon said, moving to stand up, but was stopped by Mydeimos’ hand gripping his forearm. 

“It’s fine,” Mydeimos said, though the words were quiet coming out of his mouth. “I’ll eat it.”

Phainon watched as Mydeimos ate the rest of his porridge in silence, both of them ignoring the chatter and bustle around them, the whispers of a Kremnoan, here? reaching their ears, accompanied with muttered insults and unsavory words spoken as if Mydeimos could not hear them. But still Mydeimos ate, saying nothing until he had spooned the last bite of porridge into his mouth and stood from the table. Phainon stood with him, grateful for the chance to escape the claustrophobic atmosphere. 

“Let’s go.”

Phainon could feel the stares on his back long after they left the market, but he kept his gaze forward as he walked side by side with Mydeimos. 

They walked back to the palace in silence. Phainon had so many things he was curious about, like if Mydeimos was all right, how the last eight months had gone, what he had been up to during that time, but he held his tongue with no small effort. He didn’t want to overwhelm Mydeimos more than he already had. 

Mydeimos had been given a room on a separate floor of the palace, and Phainon stopped in front of his door. It looked the same as Phainon’s from the outside, but who knows if Aglaea had outfitted his room differently on the inside. 

“Here,” Phainon spoke for the first time since they left the market. Mydeimos looked at the door with its ornate lock, and then looked at Phainon.

“Thank you,” Mydeimos said, his eyes clear, betraying nothing of what thoughts currently brewed behind them. Phainon wanted to ask, wanted to know, but he pushed those thoughts away. 

“I’ll see you tomorrow, then,” he said instead.

Mydeimos only gave him a slight nod. “Tomorrow,” he acknowledged.

Tomorrow, Mydeimos would have to confront Okhema once again, faced with jeers and curses and the prejudiced views of the city. Phainon had gone through his own struggles when he’d first arrived, but that was nothing compared to this. For one, Phainon hadn’t come from an enemy territory, and had faced no more resentment than that against any typical foreigner. 

Mydeimos was going to have to weather all of Okhema’s hatred, all for the sake of the Flame Chase and Phainon returning home. It was Phainon’s responsibility to make sure Mydeimos made it through unscathed.

Phainon certainly had his work cut out for him.
