Phainon woke slowly. 

The sheets were still luxuriously cool, resistant to the heat of his body, and Phainon relished the feeling of being allowed to rest in the comfort of his own bed. Abruptly, Phainon realized he felt more well-rested than he’d felt in weeks, and the thought was jarring enough that it woke him fully. 

Phainon’s eyes opened and he found himself staring at a canopy of scarlet silk, barely visible in the near complete darkness of the room. 

Scarlet silk, threaded with ripples of gold. This wasn’t his bed at all.

Phainon turned his head, where beside him lay none other than Mydei himself. Mydei was still sleeping—thank God, Phainon thought to himself, for the thought of facing Mydei in the light of day after remembering his shameless actions the night before made him want to throw himself off the nearest balcony. 

Mydei stirred, and fine strands of hair fell across his eyes as he shifted, the darkness sifting around him as if to make room for the gold of his entire being. Phainon stared; he had never seen Mydei asleep. Mydei had slept in an adjacent room when they had shared the cottage so long ago, and now was the first time Phainon had had the chance to see Mydei entrenched in the tranquility of sleep.

Sleep suited him, Phainon thought, as he looked at the lines of Mydei’s face, unweathered and unmarked, his skin as smooth as if he’d never let the light of the sun touch his skin, the illusion broken only by the golden tint that covered Mydei’s entire body. 

Immortal body, Phainon was reminded. 

As if sensing his stare, Mydei’s eyes opened to meet Phainon’s. Phainon startled, jerking his gaze away, heart pounding as he tried to think of a reason why he was staring at Mydei as he slept. Nothing came to mind, however, and Mydei’s voice floated over his shoulder as he spoke first.

“How long have you been awake?”

Phainon’s words took a moment to leave his mouth. “Not long.”

Mydei exhaled. “Not long as in a moment or so, or meaning you didn’t sleep at all?”

“No!” Phainon scrambled to sit up, looking over at Mydei. Mydei was fully awake, his brow knitted with concern. “No, I slept. Really well, actually. Thank—”

“Don’t,” Mydei said roughly, sitting up to match Phainon. “It’s fine.”

“But—” Phainon tried again, but Mydei shook his head.

“No,” Mydei said. “Enough.”

With that, Mydei got out of bed and opened the curtains, allowing brightness to flood his chambers. Phainon blinked at the sudden light and got up as well, painfully aware that he was still in his sleeping clothes. 

He chanced a quick check to the System—it was barely seven o’clock, and they usually grabbed breakfast at around seven thirty before morning duties, so he had time to go back to his room and change. “I’ll just—” he started, then stopped, suddenly feeling self-conscious.

Mydei glanced over at him from where he was rustling through his armoire, golden eyes sweeping up to his face. He must have been able to sense Phainon’s discomfort, as he nodded swiftly. 

“I’ll see you at breakfast,” he said.

Phainon echoed his nod, both grateful and embarrassed. “I’ll see you then.”

The whole way back to his chambers, he berated himself for being so childish. You need someone to hold you to sleep to keep the nightmares away? Really, Phainon?

Well, it worked, a small, snarky part of him retorted. And Phainon couldn’t argue with that, so after quickly changing into his dayclothes, he rushed to meet Mydei for breakfast.

Phainon was sure that asking to share Mydei’s bed twice in a row would definitely be crossing a line, so he didn’t ask. After breakfast, they parted for morning duties—usually, they would also see each other later in the afternoon for their usual spar, but today that had been superseded by a request from Aglaea regarding a civil dispute that needed his attention. 

So it happened that Phainon hadn’t seen Mydei all day when they met for dinner, another tradition they had upkept in the guise of Phainon helping Mydei acclimate to Okhema, when in all honesty Mydei really didn’t need his help anymore. Mydei was calm and unflappable, his initial homesickness worn smooth over time, and now he seemed relatively at peace with his position in the Holy City. 

Phainon supposed a more accurate reading of why they continued to eat meals together (excluding lunch but not really, since it was when all of the Chrysos Heirs got together to eat) was that really, he just liked the company. Not just that, he liked Mydei—the way the two of them had seemed to just fall into an easy routine, their camaraderie natural and unforced. Never had he expected to find such a reliable friend as he had in the seemingly uncaring, stoic Kremnoan—but oh, if that wasn’t farther from the truth. 

From the first time they met, Phainon could tell that Mydei was anything than uncaring, his actions seeming wholly divorced from his words, concerned hands betraying his true intentions where sharp words kept them concealed. But despite this, the knowledge that Mydei cared about him, and would want to help Phainon if only he asked—despite this, Phainon could not make himself ask to share Mydei’s bed again. 

Too much, Phainon’s brain nagged at him. You’re asking too much, eventually he’ll see you’ll always ask for too much and give nothing in return.

Phainon pushed away those thoughts, and tried to turn his mind toward dinner. 

Scooping the last remnants of lentil soup into his mouth, Phainon stood up from the table, where Mydei was still finishing his food. He looked up at Phainon, confusion marring his brow. 

“Well,” Phainon said, eager to escape the weight of his unspoken words. “See you tomorrow, then.”

Mydei set down his bowl and spoon. “Tomorrow?” he asked, carefully.

“Yeah, for breakfast,” said Phainon, pasting a smile across his face. He wasn’t sure it fit, anxious as he was about returning to another night full of restless sleep. When Mydei didn’t respond, he began gathering his things to leave. 

“All right—”

“Are your nightmares gone?”

Phainon stared at Mydei, bowl and plate and utensils stacked precariously in his arms as he stopped. “Er—”

“If not, then just come over again,” said Mydei, interrupting Phainon’s half-formed excuse with a weighty stare. Phainon squirmed, very aware that he was in danger of dropping his dishes. 

“It’s fi—”

“It’s not,” said Mydei. “And it is fine, for you to keep doing it, so just sleep with me for the time being.”

Sleep with me, Phainon’s brain repeated, the words heady. He knew Mydei didn’t mean them that way, but they sent a bolt of something down Phainon’s spine anyway. Sleep with me, just sleep with me.

Phainon blinked away his stupor, aware that he hadn’t said anything in several moments. “I—no, I just—”

Unable to finish his thought, unaware what he even wanted to say, Phainon shut his mouth. He forced himself to nod, the motion harsh and sudden, and made the word come out of his mouth, the action feeling disproportionately difficult. 

“…Okay.”

Mydei’s gaze was still heavy on his, but his body seemed to loosen at Phainon’s answer. 

“All right,” he said. “Now sit back down.”

Phainon sat, feeling rather chastised, somehow managing not to drop his dishes in the process.

He’d arranged to meet with Castorice and Hyacine that evening to talk about the latest book they were reading—at Castorice’s insistence, they’d started a book club, which made Phainon marvel at how much he’d changed since arriving in Amphoreus. Old Phainon never had the patience (or the friends) to join a book club, but that wasn’t the case now. 

Often, their book club meetings consisted of the three of them plus Cipher, who had showed up to one on accident, having come to the library to pester Castorice, and had decidedly refused to join but so far had yet to miss a single meeting. Phainon found it incredibly amusing to watch as Cipher’s interest noticeably grew with every meeting, having clearly read the book but too proud to admit she had, so she just sat in twitchy silence the entire meeting atop the couch, perched to the right above Castorice’s shoulder.

So after Mydei finished his dinner, they parted under the expectation that Phainon would be sleeping in Mydei’s room that night. 

The whole time at the library, Phainon couldn’t get Mydei’s words out of his head. 

Sleep with me, sleep with me.

Phainon spent the whole meeting lost in his thoughts, barely registering the conversation at all, out of sorts for an entirely different reason than he’d been the last few weeks. That had been because he was sleep deprived, this was—

This was what? 

Phainon didn’t know. It just distracted him, was all.

When the meeting concluded, Castorice caught his attention before he left with a gentle wave in front of his face. “Are you all right?” she asked, concern etched across her features. 

Even as muddled as his thoughts were, Phainon couldn’t help but feel glad that he had someone such as her to look out for him. 

“Yeah, I’m all right,” he said, and gave her a smile before he left.

When he got back to his chambers, the day had passed well into Curtain-Fall Hour, which according to the System started roughly at eight o’clock and lasted until five o’clock the next morning, at the start of Entry Hour. Phainon took a moment in his room to gather both his things and his courage, then made his way to Mydei’s chambers.

He hadn’t even knocked when Mydei swung the door open, already ready for bed, by the looks of it. Phainon stared at him curiously as he stepped inside, Mydei closing the door behind him.

“How did you do that?”

“Do what?” Mydei turned to look at him from the threshold. 

“Know I was there. You did that last time, too.”

“Habit, I guess.” At Phainon’s strange look, Mydei clarified. “I got used to listening for footsteps with the detachment. Better you know who to expect walking up to your tent, otherwise you might end up with a knife to your neck.”

Phainon didn’t point out that they weren’t in tents, they were in enclosed chambers, with several inches of thick stone separating Mydei’s chamber from the corridor, so how would he even hear Phainon approaching, let alone recognize Phainon’s footsteps, because what was the point? Of course Mydei of all people would have precisely tuned instincts; Phainon felt silly for having even asked at this point.

Mydei’s voice shook those thoughts away. “Come to bed, Deliverer.”

Phainon ignored the strange feeling that arose from those words and took off his outer jacket. Mydei watched as he set his things down and came around to sit atop the bed, having given him the same side as the night before.

Phainon sat there waiting, unsure until Mydei got under the covers and Phainon followed, lying on his back with the sheets pulled up tight, his arms crossed over his chest. From beside him, Mydei’s gaze was lightened with amusement.

“Phainon.”

“Yes?”

“Can you sleep like that?”

“Yes,” said Phainon, stubbornly refusing to meet Mydei’s eyes.

“Hmmph.” Without another word, Mydei’s arm pulled Phainon toward him, so that Phainon’s back was pressed against Mydei’s chest and Mydei’s arm was tight across his torso. Phainon breathed out shakily, the pressure and the intimacy of their new position putting him off-balance. Every inch of them were touching; Mydei’s chin was atop his head, Phainon’s hair brushing his neck, and even their legs were pressed together, entwined as though Mydei was trying to push himself into Phainon’s very being.

It was near claustrophobic and Phainon could barely breathe, yet it was exactly what he needed. In an embarrassingly short amount of time, Phainon could feel himself drifting off, Mydei’s weight and scent around him inexplicably comforting.

That night Phainon did dream—

There were only a few of them left now, the vision of the others strewn amidst the destruction of the Holy City refusing to leave Phainon’s eyes. Still he fought, swinging Dawnmaker again and again, a primal scream leaving his throat as he chopped and cleaved and thrust. 

It was up to them now. They would not fail, they could not—

And yet as that thought passed through Phainon’s fevered mind, he heard a muffled grunt behind him.

Phainon jerked his head around to find the source of the sound, and his heart fell into his stomach.

Mydei had been fighting his own section of the black tide not three steps away from Phainon, but now he stood facing him, his face grimacing in uncharacteristic pain. 

“Mydei?” Phainon managed to force the words out. “What—”

And then he noticed the blade. Long, curved, and sticking out of Mydei’s stomach from the back, as if it had been stabbed right at—

“Mydei,” Phainon breathed, and Mydei’s knees gave out as the blade was pulled out from his body.

Phainon saw red. The Titankin was a shower of golden dust before it had the chance to reorient its attention, and Phainon wiped out the rest of the wave around them before rushing back to Mydei and dropping to his knees at his side. Mydei was breathing harshly as Phainon propped him up on his knees. 

“Mydei, you—”

“It’s fine, Deliverer,” said Mydei, interrupting whatever Phainon had been about to say. “They were too quick.”

Too quick for Phainon to stop, but not too quick for Mydei to jump in front of their blade, to throw away his own life for Phainon’s because he was too distracted to notice.

Phainon’s throat was closing up. “Mydei—” he tried again.

“Enough,” Mydei said. “You’re not finished here.”

Phainon stared mutely at Mydei, at his golden hair matted with sweat, at his skin that was clearly becoming too pale, too fast.

“I can’t—”

“You must.” Mydei’s words were harsh, but his eyes were softened—with pain, with death, with sentiment, who could know? All Phainon knew is it felt like his heart was losing time along with Mydei, for he felt bloodless, a walking corpse. Mydei couldn’t die, couldn’t leave. Mydei was immortal. He’d surely come back this time, too.

“I can’t,” Phainon repeated, his voice hardening. He felt as if his entire body was turning to stone and then cracking, at any moment in danger of disintegrating altogether and turning to dust, just like the thousands upon thousands of Titankin he’d slayed in the past several days. “Not without—”

He forced his eyes shut, trying to gain control over himself, centering himself in the feeling of Mydei’s warmth on his thighs. By the time he opened his eyes, Mydei was dead.

A terrifying numbness passed through Phainon’s body as he witnessed Mydei’s vacant body, his empty eyes, the immortal golden tint of his body never to return. The numbness quickly gave rise to a golden, pulsing anger, so immense that it filled Phainon’s heart and veins and made his vision turn gold for a moment, so gold that for a moment he felt—

He was dying, he couldn’t breathe, everything was so dark—

“Phainon!” Someone was shaking his shoulder. “Wake up!”

Phainon’s eyes shot open. It was still dark, but Mydei was sitting beside him, helping him sit up, grasping his shoulders tightly. Phainon wanted to cry. 

“Breathe,” Mydei said. 

Phainon opened his mouth and tried to breathe but choked instead, and coughed for a long while until air started gradually seeping its way into his lungs. By then, Phainon’s wits had mostly returned to him. 

He’d had a nightmare. In Mydei’s bed. 

Phainon reared up. Suddenly, he didn’t want to be here, he couldn’t be here, not when he’d just had a breakdown in Mydei’s bed and now he never wanted to show his face around Mydei again, not when Phainon was this pathetic and clearly he couldn’t ever have anything nice and—

A hand gripped his arm, stopping Phainon from getting up. Phainon tried to shake it off. “Let go,” he tried to snap, but the panic still lingered in his voice, making it come out shaky instead. The grip tightened instead of releasing him.

“No,” Mydei said. “I won’t.” As if illustrating his point, Mydei’s other hand reached to gently pull at Phainon’s sleep shirt, and Phainon went easily, the fight having drained out of him as easily as it had come. Now, Phainon was sitting on the side of Mydei’s bed, Mydei sitting cross-legged beside him.

They sat there, Mydei’s hand a heavy weight on Phainon’s back, until Phainon’s breath calmed and his vision cleared. Even after Phainon was certain he wasn’t in danger of dying or hyperventilating or falling apart in Mydei’s bed, he said nothing, staring at his fingers twisted into the sheets beneath him.

Finally, Mydei spoke. “What was it?”

Phainon’s grip on the sheets tightened. He didn’t want to talk about it.

This time, Mydei didn’t let it go. “Phainon.”

“No.” Phainon jerked his head around to glare at Mydei. “I’m—”

He stopped short. All of a sudden, he didn’t want to lie to Mydei. He was so tired of pretending like everything was fine, like he could handle it on his own.

Phainon thought of the dream, of the way the original Phainon seemed to hide himself away from the others, refusing to let them get too close. Phainon didn’t want to become like that, he could see himself going down that path, and he didn’t like it.

Phainon didn’t want to push people away anymore.

“It—” At first, the words refused to come out. Phainon cleared his throat and pushed. “It was…you. Dead. And everyone, they—” Fuck fuck fuck. He couldn’t do this. But he had to at least fucking try. 

It took an embarrassingly long time for Phainon to get the words out, but he wouldn’t let himself stop. In his mind, he could still see that other Phainon, the way he deflected and hid and refused to let anyone get close, not even Mydei. And then Mydei had died right in front of him.

A deep breath. “Mydei. Mydeimos, you died. Right in front of me, and all I could do was watch. Aglaea, Hyacine, Castorice—” Fuck, Phainon’s voice was breaking. His eyes were hot and he had to do this without crying, had to get the words out, so Phainon forced them out roughly. “Everyone died, and I couldn’t—I couldn’t save you—”

The emotion he had been trying to hold back, to keep from overwhelming him finally broke loose as he let out a sob, Mydei’s arm bringing his face to rest upon his chest. Phainon cried into Mydei’s bare chest, his tears running down crimson whorls and leaving him feeling empty.

“It was a dream,” said Mydei, his voice spoken above Phainon’s hair. Phainon shook his head mutely, unable to voice the fact that it was real, that it had happened, and that Phainon was sure it would happen again if he didn’t change, if he didn’t get his shit together and pushed everyone away like he always had, like the original Phainon always did.

The past and the present were blurring together, fact and fiction confused until Phainon didn’t know which way was up and which exit was real. He needed to go home, to leave this fucking beta test, as everything in this world seemed to be doing its damndest to confuse him, to convince him that this was real, this was his life, and there was no escaping it.

The tears kept coming and Mydei just let him cry, pulling them down to lie beneath the covers as Phainon sobbed into Mydei’s chest, the other’s arms an anchoring presence around his back. Eventually, Phainon fell asleep, his tears still wet upon his cheeks, and he slept a heavy, dreamless sleep.

The morning was nearly the same as the one before, except this time, Phainon’s eyes were puffy and his head throbbed, but also because he had thought to pack a bag, he was able to change in Mydei’s washroom and they left together for breakfast. 

Mydei didn’t treat him any differently after witnessing the weight of Phainon’s emotions, and Phainon was heartened by his easy presence in the light of day. Mydei had seen him like that—weak, unsure, afraid—and still wanted him around. Unexpectedly, Phainon’s nerves were abated at the acknowledgement of this fact; Phainon had expected to feel shamed, or at least embarrassed by the fact that he had cried himself to sleep in Mydei’s arms, but the only thing he felt the next day was naked relief. 

Gradually, this grew into a routine, with Phainon spending the nights in Mydei’s chambers and Mydei easing away his nightmares with firm hands. Every time Mydei wiped away Phainon’s tears, or pulled him closer to his chest, Phainon felt a wave of misery rise within him. There was no way he deserved this comfort, this intimacy—Mydei had to know what he was saddling himself with, had to know that this was an unequal transaction.

Still, Phainon burrowed himself deeper into Mydei’s arms at night, feeling impossibly warm.

Over the next few weeks, this routine became familiar, and Phainon took no small amount of comfort in it. Phainon had a friend, a person in Mydei, and he’d be hard pressed to turn it down. 

Every time Phainon opened the System to check on his progress—Mydei’s trial was slated to take place the next month, as it was tradition for all of the Chrysos Heirs to be present for a Coreflame trial, and Anaxa was back at the Grove until the end of the month—he was presented with his points summary, which Mydei’s name was always at the top of.

[User Phainon’s Relationship with Mydei has gained 5 FP.]

[User Phainon’s Relationship with Mydei has gained 7 FP.]

[User Phainon’s Relationship with Mydei has gained 3 FP.]

[User Phainon’s Relationship with Mydei has gained 6 FP.]

And so on and so forth.

It occurred to Phainon one day that he didn’t know if Friendship Points had a cap. If they did, what happened then? Not like it mattered, really—no matter how many points he gained, it didn’t actually feel like a friendship could be accurately represented with points. 

Clearly, he was wrong, because the very next day he received a notification for a new quest.

Phainon had just left the training grounds after his afternoon spar with Mydei when all of a sudden, the System popped into Phainon’s vision with a ding.

[User Phainon has unlocked a new Side Quest! Go now?]

Phainon frowned. He didn’t think he’d done anything to trigger a new quest. Curious, he clicked into the Quest screen. 

It read: [New Side Quest: Love is in the Air!]

…What. Phainon squinted at the quest description. Hey System? What the hell is this?

[User Phainon has unlocked the Romance feature! The User will now be able to gain Romance Points (RP) with characters across Amphoreus, which can be used to deepen relationships and unlock further intimacy levels.]

Of all the things that had surprised him since entering the beta test, this clearly made the top of the list. Romance? Dating? In my Star Rail?

Also— “Wait a sec, how did I unlock this? I wasn’t even doing anything.”

[The Romance feature unlocks as soon as the User first maxes out Friendship Points with any character.]

Who could Phainon possibly have maxed out already? He navigated to the Points page and scrolled, stopping when he found the culprit about three-quarters down the page. 

Beside Mydei’s name was a bright green bar, glowing brighter than the others to indicate that it had been filled up.

Wait, so he had maxed out Mydei’s Friendship Points, and now the System was telling him to fall in love with him? Where the fuck did that come from?

Phainon mulled this over until he got back to his chambers, washing the dirt off his face and hands, and then finally sat down at his desk with a huff.

Okay, System, what the fuck? “Why—what—” Phainon didn’t know how to begin, staring at the System interface, who only blinked innocently at him. 

Phainon cleared his throat. “Since when was there dating in Star Rail? There’s never been any in the original games.” That was his biggest question at the moment. 

[User Phainon is correct! This feature has yet to arrive in Star Rail, but the Romance feature has been added to the beta test to provide the User with a more immersive, well-rounded experience, and is expected to be added to Star Rail in future updates.]

And I need dating to get that so-called well-rounded experience? Phainon thought, somewhat peeved. 

Well, no. Peeved wasn’t the right word to describe how Phainon felt at that moment. If he really searched, a more accurate descriptor would be…disappointed.

In the real world, Phainon didn’t really have time to go on dates often, nor the money, but he’d always thought it would be nice to have a partner, someone to rely on emotionally. On all the dates he’d been on, no one had really clicked. No one had really gotten him, or made him feel as seen as—

Well, as seen as Mydei did.

That was stupid. It wasn’t as if Phainon had feelings for Mydei. No, Phainon pushed that thought down. Phainon was just confused, surprised—never had he thought the beta test would throw something like this at him. Yeah, the System had been blathering on this whole time about giving Phainon “an immersive experience” but…dating? That felt a little too much for Phainon. 

Dating was something reserved for the real world. Even if it was only a game, he didn’t really want to do anything like that, especially given how realistic this beta test had proven itself to be. If anything went wrong, Phainon didn’t know that he’d be able to deal with the heartbreak.

Besides. Dating? Mydei? Phainon didn’t know how to make those two things fit together.

For a while, Phainon just sat there, staring blankly at the System interface. 

What should he do?

Option one: He could just…accept the Side Quest, unlock Mydei’s Romance route, and see where that took him. Maybe there would be something cool waiting at the end of it—definitely more Mydei lore, and getting closer with Mydei was always a plus.

Except the more Phainon thought about it, the more he realized he didn’t want to do Mydei’s Romance route. Something in his gut tugged the wrong way when he thought about it, the same feeling as when Phainon lay in Mydei’s bed at night, or when Mydei turned his golden gaze upon Phainon’s. The feeling seemed to tighten Phainon’s bones and shiver through his skin, and he didn’t know how to begin untangling it.

In any case, it was probably best not to begin the side quest anyways. For one, Phainon had more important things to focus on. And really, dating? Now? Secondly, would beginning the side quest mean that Mydei would develop feelings for him? Something about that part specifically made Phainon’s heart clench—Mydei, in love with Phainon because of a quest. Because of a choice Phainon made, without any choice of his own.

Also, this was still just a fucking game. Phainon needed to get his act together and leave.

And for that, Mydei needed to complete the Trial of Strife. So that only left option two—ignore. With that decided, Phainon closed out of the Quest screen and put all thoughts of the Side Quest out of his mind.

Anaxa returned from the Grove three weeks later, having completed his project earlier than expected, so Aglaea arranged for the Trial of Strife to be held a few days after his arrival. There wasn’t much for Phainon to do in preparation, so he mostly just spent his days sparring and patrolling outside the city with Mydei until the appointed day arrived.

The morning of the Trial, Phainon felt an unaccountable nervousness set into his bones. “Why am I nervous?” he muttered to Mydei as he helped him put on his armor in their now-shared chambers. “It’s not like I’m the one about to do battle with my deepest fears.”

Mydei snorted. “At least you’re aware.”

Phainon tightened the last strap upon Mydei’s shoulder and stepped back, surveying him. “How come you don’t look nervous at all?”

Mydei leveled at him a glance. “Have you ever known me to look nervous?”

“Fair enough. Anyway, what do you suppose you’ll see? Hyacine was telling me that the Trial of Strife is notoriously one of the most difficult of the Coreflame Trials.”

Mydei was silent for a moment, considering. “My friends. Comrades, everyone I’ve lost. Everyone I might lose,” he said, looking over at Phainon.

Phainon’s heart tightened. “That's what you fear the most?”

“Yes,” Mydei said.

Phainon thought about everyone Mydei had lost before coming to Okhema—his father to madness, his comrades to war. And his closest friends, the companions he’d shared everything with from childhood through his year of exile, only to lose all of them before they had a chance to see Mydei liberate their homeland from Eurypon’s tyranny.

Mydei had told him this one night, the words spoken quietly from behind Phainon’s back as Mydei’s hand clutched Phainon tight to his chest. Phainon’s heart had ached, then, and it ached now, to think of Mydei reliving his worst fear. 

It was one thing to know one’s worst fear, and to have already lived it and come out the other side. It was entirely another to have to confront it willingly, knowing the horror and pain it would undoubtedly inflict. 

As much as Phainon’s own terror still haunted him, his own past still clutching onto his coattails, he still wanted to turn back time and tell Aglaea yes, I’ll take the Trial if only to spare Mydei from the pain of it.

Except part of Phainon knew he wouldn’t be able to handle it, which is why he’d passed on the Trial in the first place. He knew that, and yet still he wished to take Mydei’s place. 

The System popped up with an alert in Phainon’s peripheral vision, reminding him that it was time to leave for the Trial. Wiping the melancholy thoughts from his head, Phainon glanced over at Mydei. “Time to go.”

The Trial was held in the Vortex of Genesis, and mostly everyone had already arrived when they got there. Everyone except for Aglaea—Phainon craned his neck to try to find her, but she apparently hadn’t arrived. 

Hmm. Phainon straightened and turned to Mydei at his side, who was fidgeting with his gauntlet, but stopped as soon as he saw Phainon looking over.

“Ha!” Phainon let out a laugh. “So you are nervous.”

Mydei glared at him, not even deigning to bestow upon him a response, but Phainon couldn’t even find it in himself to mind. This closeness, this friendship—this is what he stood to lose if he’d accepted that Side Quest.

Why on earth was he still hung up on that? This was not the time to be distracted, Phainon scolded himself. This was Mydei’s moment, and Phainon had to support him.

Mydei, who wasn’t looking so nervous anymore, a smile tugging on the corners of his lips, and Phainon’s heart seemed to tug along with it.

Fuck. Phainon turned his thoughts away from Mydei and towards a somewhat safer topic—the Trial.

Phainon did not want to think about what Mydei was about to see in that Trial, but he couldn’t stop the images from flooding his brain. Mydei’s friends, dead at his feet, his father dead by his own hand, his kingdom stained in blood. 

Mydei had lived a life surrounded by blood and violence, something no child should ever have to go through. And now he had to do it all over again.

Phainon’s chest thudded painfully. “Mydei—” he began, reaching for Mydei’s arm.

He was interrupted by the door to the Vortex opening, and Aglaea stepping through. 

Except she wasn’t alone. Phainon squinted. The Vortex was dimmer than the other side, which connected to an outdoor corridor, and light flooded Phainon’s eyes. There was someone else behind her, which was strange because hadn’t everyone else had already arrived?

Phainon wasn’t left in suspense for much longer because in the next moment, the door thudded closed and his vision returned to normal. Blinking, Phainon finally could see who had accompanied Aglaea to the Vortex.

Only to see it was none other than the Trailblazer, baseball bat in hand.
